questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is a true statement about apoptosis?
options: There is enzymatic digestion of cellular contents
It is associated with adjacent inflammation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Plasma membrane remains intact

The plasma membrane remains intact in apoptosis.

Apoptosis literally means falling-off in Greek. It is a pathway of programmed cell death.

Apoptotic cells break up into fragments called apoptotic bodies. These apoptotic bodies have intact plasma membrane but altered structures. Hence, they are subjected to phagocytosis without eliciting inflammation.

Necrosis is an unprogrammed form of cell death that includes:

• Enzymatic digestion
• Adjacent inflammation
• Karyolysis
questions.learning: Plasma membrane remains intact — The plasma membrane remains intact in apoptosis. Apoptosis literally means falling-off in Greek.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In the diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis, which of the following findings is not typically associated with the condition?
questions.explanation: Bacterial Vaginosis (BV) is diagnosed using Amsel’s Criteria, which requires three of the following: 1) A thin, homogenous greyish-white discharge. 2) A vaginal pH greater than 4.5 (Option C). 3) A positive Whiff test (a fishy odour upon adding 10% KOH) (Option D). 4) The presence of clue cells on wet mount microscopy (Option A) . Thick, white, "curdy" or "cottage cheese" discharge (Option B) is the hallmark feature of Vulvovaginal Candidiasis (yeast infection), not BV. Candidiasis is also typically associated with a normal vaginal pH (around 4.0–4.5). BV results from a shift in the vaginal flora where normal lactobacilli are replaced by anaerobes like Gardnerella vaginalis. Because BV is characterized by a thin, malodorous discharge rather than a thick white one, Option B is the incorrect feature for this diagnosis. Management usually involves oral or topical metronidazole
questions.learning: Bacterial Vaginosis (BV) is diagnosed using Amsel’s Criteria, which requires three of the following: 1) A thin, homogenous greyish-white discharge. 2) A vaginal pH greater than 4.5 (Option C).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Shoulder dystocia is diagnosed when delivery of the anterior shoulder is delayed beyond how much time after the delivery of the fetal head?
questions.explanation: Shoulder dystocia is defined as a delivery that requires maneuvers beyond gentle traction to deliver the shoulders. A specific clinical criterion used is a head-to-body delivery time exceeding 60 seconds. It occurs when the anterior fetal shoulder impacts the maternal symphysis pubis. A key clinical indicator is the "turtle sign," where the fetal head retracts against the perineum. Options A, B, and C represent timeframes shorter than the standard diagnostic threshold. Management involves a sequential series of maneuvers, starting with the McRoberts maneuver, which involves hyperflexing the maternal thighs to increase the pelvic outlet. Suprapubic pressure is also applied to rotate the shoulder. If these fail, more invasive rotational maneuvers like Wood’s corkscrew or delivery of the posterior arm are attempted. This condition is an obstetric emergency due to the high risk of neonatal brachial plexus injury and maternal soft tissue lacerations
questions.learning: Shoulder dystocia is defined as a delivery that requires maneuvers beyond gentle traction to deliver the shoulders. A specific clinical criterion used is a head-to-body delivery time exceeding 60 seconds.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the most common causative organism for verruca vulgaris?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Human papillomavirus-2

Verruca vulgaris or common wart is most commonly caused by human papillomavirus-2 (HPV-2) but is also related to types 1, 4, 27, and 57.

Common warts are usually asymptomatic. They show acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, and papillomatosis and present as firm papules with a rough horny surface. The most commonly affected sites are on the backs of the hands and fingers, and, in children on the knees. Pseudo-Koebner phenomenon may be observed.

Treatment is usually with topical agents such as salicylic acid, caustics, glutaraldehyde, formalin, or with laser, cryotherapy, surgical removal.

verruca vulgaris.
questions.learning: Human papillomavirus-2 Verruca vulgaris or common wart is most commonly caused by human papillomavirus-2 (HPV-2) but is also related to types 1, 4, 27, and 57.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is responsible for producing the changes in blood pressure and heart rate depicted in the image shown below?
questions.explanation: The graph demonstrates a significant increase in mean arterial pressure and a paradoxical decrease in heart rate. This specific pattern is characteristic of Norepinephrine. Norepinephrine is a potent agonist at alpha-1 receptors, causing intense systemic vasoconstriction and a sharp rise in blood pressure. This rise in pressure activates the baroreceptor reflex, which increases vagal tone to the heart, resulting in reflex bradycardia. Isoproterenol (Option B) is a pure beta-agonist that increases heart rate while lowering blood pressure. Epinephrine (Option C) typically increases both blood pressure and heart rate (due to direct stimulation) except at very low doses. Dopamine (Option D) usually increases heart rate at medium and high doses. The reflex bradycardia shown in the tracing is the definitive clue for norepinephrine's primary alpha-mediated vasopressor effect. Clinicians use this drug in the management of septic shock to restore perfusion pressure while being mindful of the potential for reflex heart rate slowing
questions.learning: The graph demonstrates a significant increase in mean arterial pressure and a paradoxical decrease in heart rate. This specific pattern is characteristic of Norepinephrine.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with difficulty initiating urination and urinary retention. Ultrasound shows a post-void residual volume of 130 mL. Which medication is commonly used to manage this condition?
questions.explanation: This 60-year-old male presents with classic Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms (LUTS) and a high post-void residual urine volume, which are diagnostic of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH). 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, such as finasteride and dutasteride, are commonly used for long-term management of BPH. These drugs inhibit the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), the androgen primarily responsible for prostatic growth. Reduction in DHT levels leads to gradual shrinkage of the prostate, thereby decreasing mechanical obstruction and improving urinary flow over time. Alpha-1 blockers (e.g., tamsulosin) are also frequently used, especially for rapid symptomatic relief, as they relax smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck but do not reduce prostate size. Calcium channel blockers (Option A), ACE inhibitors (Option C), and aldosterone antagonists (Option D) are antihypertensive agents and have no therapeutic role in BPH. Patients with a significantly increased post-void residual volume (>100 mL) are at risk of recurrent urinary tract infections, bladder stones, and renal impairment. Appropriate pharmacologic therapy can delay or prevent surgical interventions such as TURP. Counseling regarding adverse effects, including sexual dysfunction, is essential during treatment
questions.learning: This 60-year-old male presents with classic Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms (LUTS) and a high post-void residual urine volume, which are diagnostic of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 54-year-old man presents with intermittent flank pain, a sense of fullness, and hematuria. CT imaging of the abdomen and pelvis reveals a left renal lesion containing fat-density areas along with a neovascular mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presence of fat density (characterized by Hounsfield units typically between -20 and -100) within a renal mass on a CT scan is virtually pathognomonic for a Renal Angiomyolipoma (AML). AML is a benign triphasic tumor composed of dysplastic blood vessels (angio-), smooth muscle (-myo-), and adipose tissue (-lipoma). While Renal Cell Carcinoma (Option A) is the most common renal malignancy and can cause flank pain and hematuria, it very rarely contains visible macrofat. Renal oncocytoma (Option B) typically shows a central stellate scar and lacks fat density. A renal cyst (Option D) appears as a simple, fluid-filled, well-circumscribed lesion with water density, not fat or vascularity. AMLs are often associated with Tuberous Sclerosis. Given the specific radiological finding of fat density, which appears as black pockets on the CT image, Renal Angiomyolipoma is the most accurate diagnosis for this patient
questions.learning: The presence of fat density (characterized by Hounsfield units typically between -20 and -100) within a renal mass on a CT scan is virtually pathognomonic for a Renal Angiomyolipoma (AML).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The fallopian tube is lined by ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ciliated columnar epithelium

The lining epithelium of the fallopian tube is a single layer of ciliated columnar epithelium.

The ciliated epithelial cells are predominant in the distal part of the fallopian tube. There is an increase in the height and number of cilia in these cells during the estrogenic phase of the menstrual cycle.

Other cells in the fallopian tube epithelium include:

* Secretory or peg cells - maximally located in the proximal portion of the tube. These cells are active around the time of ovulation, and their secretions help in the capacitation of sperms.

* Intraepithelial lymphocytes - may present occasionally.

Pearl PF1615: Fallopian tube

Gross anatomy:

The fallopian tube is divided into the following parts:

* Intramural/Interstitial portion:

* Intrauterine

* The narrowest and shortest part

* Isthmus:

* The most common site for tubectomy

* Ampulla:

* The longest part

* The most common site for - fertilization and ectopic pregnancy

* Infundibulum:

* The widest part

Histology:

The ampulla, isthmus and infundibulum are extrauterine. They're covered by three layers:

* Mesosalpinx - It is the peritoneal layer. Also called serosa.

* Myosalpinx - It contains smooth muscle and has 2 layers:

* Inner circular

* Outer longitudinal

* Endosalpinx - It is the mucosal layer. It has the following features:

* Numerous branching folds, filling the entire lumen

* Basement membrane

* Ciliated, columnar epithelium

* Peg cells - non-ciliated epithelium. They help in the capacitation of sperms.

Pearl PF1699: Various Types of Epithelium, Their Location and Functions
questions.learning: Ciliated columnar epithelium — The lining epithelium of the fallopian tube is a single layer of ciliated columnar epithelium. The ciliated epithelial cells are predominant in the distal part of the fallopian tube.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: At what vertebral level does the part marked in the image lie in a normal anatomical position?
options: Disc space between L4 and L5
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tip of coccyx

In the right pelvic bone given above the marked structure is the ischial spine which lies approximately at the level of the fifth sacral vertebrae in a normal anatomical position. As the tip of the coccyx is the closest option relating to the spine , it can be the most appropriate answer.

The ischial spine is a bony prominence found on the ischium, one of the three bones that make up the hip bone. The ischial spine forms a part of the plane of least pelvic dimensions or narrow pelvic plane which comprises of :

• lower border of the symphysis pubis
• the tip of ischial spines
• fifth sacral vertebra

The interspinous distance is the distance between the tip of two ischial spines. ( Bispinous diameter = 10.5 cm or 4.5" )

The important events occurring at the narrowest plane in the pelvis :

• It corresponds roughly to the origin of levator ani muscles.
• The internal rotation of the fetal head occurs during labour at this plane.
• It marks the beginning of the forward curve of the pelvic axis
• This level of ischial spines indicates station ‘O’
• When the fetal head station is at ‘O’, the head is considered to be engaged.
• Deep transverse arrest occurs at this plane.
• The ischial spine can serve as a landmark in pudendal anaesthesia, as the pudendal nerve lies close to the ischial spine

The image given below highlights the interspinous distance seen through the pelvic inlet.
questions.learning: Tip of coccyx — In the right pelvic bone given above the marked structure is the ischial spine which lies approximately at the level of the fifth sacral vertebrae in a normal anatomical position.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old mother presents with pain in her left breast. Which of the following is the most likely cause of acute mastitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Crack in the nipple

Acute mastitis is caused by a local bacterial infection when the breast is most vulnerable due to cracks and fissures in the nipples.

Mastitis occurs due to a combination of factors such as inadequate milk drainage and the introduction of bacteria present on the skin. The cracks in the nipple serve as an entry point, thus resulting in infection. The most common organism causing acute mastitis is Staphylococcus aureus.

Acute bacterial mastitis typically occurs during the 1st month of breastfeeding (lactational breast abscess).

Staphylococcal acute mastitis typically results in localized abscesses. Signs and symptoms of this condition involve:

* Fever and malaise

* Localized pain and tenderness

* Redness and swelling of the affected breast

* Fluctuation test positive due to pus in the abscess. It is a late sign.

Management includes analgesia, continued expression from the breast, antibiotics such as amoxiclav, and repeated aspiration of pus. In case of aspiration and antibiotics failure, incision and drainage can be done.
questions.learning: Crack in the nipple Acute mastitis is caused by a local bacterial infection when the breast is most vulnerable due to cracks and fissures in the nipples.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The following image shows an uterine anomaly. This anomaly occurs due to which of the following developmental defects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Para mesonephric duct; partial fusion

The female reproductive tract develops from the Paramesonephric Duct, also known as the Müllerian duct.

These ducts form:

| Structure formed | Organ

| ---------------- | -----

| Fallopian tubes | From upper duct

| Uterus | Fusion of both ducts

| Cervix | From fused ducts

| Upper vagina | From fused ducts

Mechanism of the Anomaly

Two paramesonephric ducts develop

↓

They normally fuse in midline

↓

Uterus and cervix formed

If fusion is incomplete or partial: Müllerian duct anomaly develops

In this case: Partial fusion defect of paramesonephric ducts

Common uterine anomalies arise due to fusion or resorption defects-

| Defect | Resulting anomaly

| ------ | -----------------

| Complete non-fusion | Uterus didelphys

| Partial fusion | Bicornuate uterus

| Failure of septal resorption | Septate uterus

| Complete agenesis | MRKH syndrome

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Seminal vesicles and vas deferens would be bilaterally absent congenitally in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cystic fibrosis

Seminal vesicles and vas deferens would be bilaterally absent, congenitally in cystic fibrosis. This is known as the congenital bilateral absence of vas deference (CBAVD).

Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder that affects fluid secretion in the exocrine glands and in the epithelial lining. It is caused primarily due to a mutation in the CFTR gene, which codes for an anion channel in the apical membranes of epithelial cells. This leads to abnormally viscous secretions that obstruct organ passages, resulting in recurrent infections, pancreatic insufficiency, steatorrhea, malnutrition, hepatic cirrhosis, intestinal obstruction, and male infertility.

Infertility is due to azoospermia and CBAVD. In some patients, the bilateral absence of the vas deferens may be the only feature suggesting an underlying CFTR mutation.

On examination, a normal reproductive tract (including testis, and epididymis) is seen, with bilateral absence of vas deferens and atrophic or absent seminal vesicles. Semen analysis shows a low-volume (0.5 mL), acidic ejaculate that is devoid of fructose and seminal vesicle fluid. There may be associated renal agenesis in some patients.

Other options:

Option B: Klinefelter syndrome is a genetic disorder that results from a 47, XXY karyotype in phenotypically male patients. They present with gynecomastia, azoospermia, and infertility due to hyalinization of the seminiferous tubules and a small testis.

Option C: Kallmann syndrome is associated with a low or absent GnRH that is characterized by anosmia, hypogonadism, infertility, cryptorchidism, delayed pubertal maturation, and neurological abnormalities.

Option D: Kartagener syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder affecting ciliary motility; it is characterized by situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis. Male infertility may be present and is due to asthenospermia (immotile spermatozoa due to impaired sperm flagella function).
questions.learning: Cystic fibrosis Seminal vesicles and vas deferens would be bilaterally absent, congenitally in cystic fibrosis. This is known as the congenital bilateral absence of vas deference (CBAVD).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient after myocardial infarction, develops a broad QRS complex tachycardia. His BP is 120/70 mm Hg. ECG is given below. What is the best management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Amiodarone IV

The patient here complaining of chest pain, and palpitations and has ECG changes showing wide QRS complex tachycardia with absent p waves is likely to have acute ventricular tachycardia. Since the patient is stable and has an underlying coronary artery disease the drug of choice is intravenous amiodarone. Intravenous amiodarone is recommended by the AHA/ACC 2015 guidelines for the treatment of hemodynamically stable ventricular tachycardia.

Ventricular tachycardias can be defined as three or more pre-ventricular contractions at a rate >100/minute.

ECG changes include wide QRS complexes, absence of P waves, and ventriculoatrial dissociation. It can be broadly classified as sustained VT or non-sustained VT. Nonsustained VT has QRS complexes lasting <30 seconds while sustained VT lasts for >30 seconds. In monomorphic VT, all QRS complexes look the same. Polymorphic VT has QRS complexes varying in shape or direction in the same lead.

Most monomorphic VT have an underlying cardiac disease. Symptoms of ventricular tachycardia include palpitations, syncope, and shortness of breath.

In a hemodynamically stable patient, amiodarone, procainamide, and lidocaine can be used to treat the condition. In the presence of heart disease, intravenous amiodarone is the drug of choice. In hemodynamically unstable patients, electrical cardioversion is done. Further management depends on the underlying heart condition and frequency of VT. Frequent episodes warrant the use of antiarrhythmics or catheter ablation.

Torsades de Pointes is a type of polymorphic VT occurring with QT prolongation. It can progress to ventricular fibrillation which is treated with defibrillation. Recurrent episodes can be managed with intravenous magnesium sulfate.

Other causes of wide QRS complexes include supraventricular tachycardias with bundle branch block and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

Pearl PF1836: ECG patterns of various ventricular arrhythmias

Ventricular tachycardia

Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with QTc prolongation- Torsades de pointes

Ventricular flutter

Ventricular fibrillation
questions.learning: Amiodarone IV — The patient here complaining of chest pain, and palpitations and has ECG changes showing wide QRS complex tachycardia with absent p waves is likely to have acute ventricular tachycardia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with intermittent lower abdominal pain and occasional constipation, without rectal bleeding or weight loss. A barium enema study reveals multiple small, rounded outpouchings arising from the sigmoid colon. Based on these radiological findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The barium enema findings of multiple "outpouchings" from the colonic wall, particularly in the sigmoid region, are diagnostic of "Diverticulosis". These represent herniations of the mucosa and submucosa through the muscular layers of the colon at points of vascular entry. Colonic polyps (Option A) appear as "filling defects" within the barium column (protruding inward), not outpouchings (protruding outward). Ulcerative colitis (Option B) typically presents with mucosal blurring, ulcers, and eventually a "lead pipe" (narrowed, featureless) colon rather than discrete outpouchings. Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS, Option D) is a functional disorder that does not show structural abnormalities on a barium enema. Diverticulosis is common in older patients and is often related to a low-fiber diet. While often asymptomatic, it can lead to complications such as diverticulitis (infection) or lower gastrointestinal bleeding. Management focuses on a high-fiber diet to reduce colonic pressure and prevent further diverticula formation

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly man with a history of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery for obesity presents with episodes of dizziness, fatigue, and tremors occurring about two hours after eating a carbohydrate-rich meal. These postprandial symptoms are most likely caused by which underlying mechanism? 1. Hypoglycemia 2. Small volume of food intake 3. High osmotic load of food 4. Increased release of insulin 5. Increased release of glucagon
questions.explanation: The patient is experiencing Late Dumping Syndrome, a common complication after gastric bypass surgery. Unlike "Early" dumping, which occurs within 30 minutes due to osmotic shifts, Late Dumping occurs 1 to 3 hours after a meal. It is caused by the rapid transit of simple carbohydrates into the small intestine, triggering an exaggerated and rapid increase in insulin release (4) from the pancreas. This "overshoot" of insulin leads to reactive hypoglycemia (1), resulting in the characteristic tremors, dizziness, and fatigue. Option 3 (High osmotic load) is the primary cause of Early dumping syndrome. Option 2 (Small volume) and Option 5 (Glucagon) are not the drivers of this reactive metabolic state. Therefore, the specific timing and neuroglycopenic symptoms confirm that reactive hypoglycemia caused by hyperinsulinemia is the responsible mechanism. Management involves frequent, small, low-carbohydrate meals
questions.learning: The patient is experiencing Late Dumping Syndrome, a common complication after gastric bypass surgery. Unlike "Early" dumping, which occurs within 30 minutes due to osmotic shifts, Late Dumping occurs 1 to 3 hours after a meal.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: You are measuring a patient's blood pressure at a primary health center when the sphygmomanometer fell and broke and mercury was spilled onto the ground. How will you clean the mercury?
options: Collect it by using a card onto a sheet of paper and put the mercury into a jar
Collect it by sweeping it with a broom and throw it outside
Collect it by sweeping it and flush it in the toilet
Collect it by hand and then wash hands with water
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Collect it by using a card onto a sheet of paper and put the mercury into a jar

Mercury is cleaned by collecting it by using a card onto a sheet of paper and putting the mercury into a jar.

After a mercury spill, the following steps should be followed:

• Isolation of the spill and ventilation of the area
• Collection of items to clean the spill: zipper-top plastic bags, trash bags, gloves, paper towels, cardboard or squeegee, eye dropper, tape, flashlight, and powdered sulfur.
• Clean up the spill.
• After putting on the gloves, the glass pieces are picked and placed on a towel, rolled and disposed of into a zipper-top plastic bag, and finally sealed.
• The beads of mercury are cleaned by using cardboard or a squeegee. They are rolled onto a sheet of paper, disposed into the zipper bag, and sealed.
• Powdered sulfur may be used to absorb small beads that are not visible
• Looking for any missed spill using a flashlight
• Remove other mercury contaminated items and wipe off any mercury beads with a wet towel into a plastic trash bag
• Proper disposal of contaminated clean-up materials.
• Keep the area well ventilated for 24 hours, keep pets and children away from the area

The use of a vacuum cleaner or broom to clean the spill should be avoided. This will break the mercury into smaller droplets and spread it further. Mercury should not be poured down any drain. Do not use a washing machine to clean the clothes contaminated with mercury. This can contaminate the water and sewage. Mercury-contaminated shoes or clothing should not be worn.
questions.learning: Collect it by using a card onto a sheet of paper and put the mercury into a jar Mercury is cleaned by collecting it by using a card onto a sheet of paper and putting the mercury into a jar.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A neonate was diagnosed with meningitis. The organism showed resistance to bacitracin. What is the most likely cause for this neonate's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Streptococcus agalactiae

Streptococcus agalactiae is a group B streptococci that shows β-hemolysis on blood agar, is resistant to bacitracin, and gives a positive CAMP test.

S. agalactiae is a capsulated Gram-positive coccus occurring in chains. It causes meningitis in the neonatal period. Infection is commonly acquired from the maternal vagina during birth. There are two clinical types seen in neonates:

* Early-onset type (more common) presents within a week of birth as meningitis or septicemia and is often fatal.

* Late-onset type presents between the second to twelfth week of life commonly as septicemia.

The CAMP test (Christie, Atkins and Munch-Peterson) is used to identify group B β-hemolytic-streptococci based on their ability to form CAMP factor. This factor causes synergistic hemolysis with β-hemolysin formed by Staphylococcus aureus, when Streptococcus agalactiae is inoculated perpendicular to a streak of Staphylococcus aureus on blood agar. This produces the characteristic arrow-head zone of hemolysis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is not given in status epilepticus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ethosuximide

Status Epilepticus:

• Continuous seizure activity >5 minutes OR
• Recurrent seizures without regaining consciousness

It’s a neurological emergency → risk of:

• Neuronal injury
• Hypoxia
• Death

1. Immediate suppression (fastest acting)

→ Benzodiazepines (IV Lorazepam)

2. Stabilization (prevent recurrence)

→ Longer-acting anticonvulsants

3. Refractory phase

→ Anesthetics (propofol, midazolam infusion)

Ethosuximide Fails in SE

• Works on thalamic pacemaker activity
• SE involves diffuse cortical excitation
• Ethosuximide → ONLY absence seizures

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which is not a feature of 3rd nerve palsy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Abduction limitation

Oculomotor nerve (3rd nerve) palsy affects most extraocular muscles except lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV).

Typical features of 3rd nerve palsy:

• Ptosis → paralysis of levator palpebrae superioris
• Pupil dilatation (mydriasis) → loss of parasympathetic supply
• “Down and out” eye → unopposed action of lateral rectus and superior oblique
• Loss of adduction, elevation, and depression

Why D is correct (NOT a feature):

• Abduction is preserved because it is controlled by the lateral rectus (CN VI)
• Hence, no abduction limitation in isolated 3rd nerve palsy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are typical physical findings in pericardial effusion? 1. Raised JVP 2. Hypotension 3. Oliguria 4. Water hammer pulse Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Pericardial effusion is the accumulation of fluid within the pericardial sac. When the accumulation is large or rapid, it can cause cardiac tamponade, leading to impaired ventricular filling, reduced cardiac output, and hemodynamic compromise.

• Statement 1. Raised JVP: Correct. Raised JVP occurs due to impaired right atrial filling and elevated systemic venous pressure.
• Statement 2. Hypotension: Correct. Hypotension results from reduced ventricular filling and decreased cardiac output. It is one of Beck’s triad in cardiac tamponade.
• Statement 3. Oliguria: Correct. Oliguria develops due to reduced renal perfusion secondary to low cardiac output.
• Statement 4. Water hammer pulse: Incorrect. Water hammer pulse (collapsing pulse) is seen in aortic regurgitation, PDA, and other high stroke volume states—not in pericardial effusion or cardiac tamponade.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A man presents with sudden onset bilateral leg swelling, diarrhea, and difficulty breathing. He reports consuming mustard oil purchased from a local vendor prior to the onset of symptoms. A health inspector is investigating the cause of his condition. Which test is the most appropriate to detect the adulterant in the mustard oil?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Paper Chromatography Test

The clinical scenario is suggestive of epidemic dropsy. Paper chromatography test is used to identify the presence of toxic alkaloids from Argemone mexicana seeds that adulterate mustard oil.

Epidemic dropsy is caused by the toxic compound sanguinarine, which is present in argemone oil extracted from argemone seeds. It is commonly used as an adulterant in mustard oil.

Epidemic dropsy results in sudden onset of swelling of lower limbs, diarrhea, and breathlessness. Some patients may develop hypersecretory glaucoma. It can lead to death due to cardiac failure.

Adulteration with argemone oil can be detected by the following tests:

• Paper chromatography - most sensitive test
• Nitric acid test
questions.learning: Paper Chromatography Test — The clinical scenario is suggestive of epidemic dropsy. Paper chromatography test is used to identify the presence of toxic alkaloids from Argemone mexicana seeds that adulterate mustard oil.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents to the OPD with the visual field defect shown in the image. Based on this visual field pattern, what is the most likely site of the lesion?
questions.explanation: The visual field plot shows a classic Bitemporal Hemianopia, which is the loss of the temporal (outer) visual fields in both the right and left eyes. This specific pattern of vision loss is the hallmark of a lesion at the optic chiasm. In the chiasm, the nerve fibers from the nasal retinas (which carry information from the temporal visual fields) cross over to the contralateral side. A compressive lesion here, most commonly a pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, or meningioma, disrupts these decussating fibers while sparing the uncrossed temporal retinal fibers. A lesion of the optic tract (Option B) or optic radiations (Option D) would result in a contralateral homonymous hemianopia (loss of the same side of the visual field in both eyes). A lesion in the occipital cortex (Option C) typically causes a homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. Therefore, the unique "tunnel vision" or loss of peripheral vision on both sides is localizing specifically to the midline optic chiasma, necessitating neuroimaging of the sellar region
questions.learning: The visual field plot shows a classic Bitemporal Hemianopia, which is the loss of the temporal (outer) visual fields in both the right and left eyes. This specific pattern of vision loss is the hallmark of a lesion at the optic chiasm.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman presents with lower abdominal discomfort, and a post-operative image is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mature teratoma

The above image shows a tumor with hair, bone, and sebaceous material which points to the diagnosis of mature teratoma.

Teratomas are germ cell tumors. They contain embryonic tissues leading to the differentiation of cells along these pathways. There are three classes of teratomas:

* Mature (benign) teratomas (eg: Dermoid cyst)

* Immature (essentially malignant) teratomas (eg: solid teratoma)

* Monodermal tumors - eg: Struma ovarii

Mature cystic teratoma, also known as dermoid cysts are unilocular in structure and have a smooth surface. They usually are lined by squamous epithelium with hair follicles leading to the formation of sebaceous material and hair. Other structures like teeth, bone, cartilage, thyroid tissue, and mucous membranes can also be found.

Most patients are asymptomatic. Complications include:

* rupture of the cyst and peritoneal spilling (rare)

* torsion of the ovary

* symptoms due to mass size of teratoma

Treatment of mature teratomas involves excision in order to prevent complications. Otherwise, mature teratomas are generally innocent.

Other options:

Option A: Immature teratomas such as solid teratomas of the ovary are solid and trabeculated. They also contain cartilage, bone, hair, and sebaceous material. There is no structural order. They are generally malignant. Grossly, they have a smooth external surface and are solid on sectioning. There may be areas of necrosis or hemorrhage.

Option C: Granulosa cell tumors arise from the sex cords of the gonads. They are solid and generally produce estrogen. They can cause precocious puberty in children, hyperestrogenism in adults, and post-menopausal bleeding. They vary in appearance and range from microscopic to large, solid and cystic, encapsulated masses. If hormonally active, they may be yellow due to intracellular lipids.

Option D: Struma ovarii - highly specialized teratoma. I has only thyroid tissue. If  functioning, it  leads to hyperthyroidism.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient is started on lithium therapy. Which of the following side effects should the patient be asked to watch out for to monitor for toxicity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vertigo and Diarrhoea

Vertigo and diarrhoea are known side-effects of lithium therapy. Lithium therapy can cause side effects at both therapeutic and toxic levels.

Known significant side effects of lithium therapy include

• Polyuria-polydipsia
• Dry mouth
• Leukocytosis Headache
• Hand tremors
• Confusion
• Decreased memory
• Muscle weakness
• Hyperreflexia
• Muscle twitch
• Vertigo
• ECG changes
• Nausea & vomiting
• Diarrhoea

Other options:

No evidence of significant association with sore throat, fever or breathlessness has been documented with lithium therapy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden- onset, tearing chest pain radiating to the back, accompanied by breathlessness and nausea. CT imaging of the chest suggests an aortic dissection. What is the most appropriate management strategy for this patient?
questions.explanation: Aortic dissection is a critical emergency where a tear in the inner layer of the aorta allows blood to flow between the layers of the aortic wall. The classic presentation is "tearing" or "ripping" chest pain that radiates to the back. Management depends on the location. For Stanford Type A dissections (involving the ascending aorta), the risk of catastrophic rupture, aortic regurgitation, or coronary involvement is extremely high. The standard of care is immediate heart rate and blood pressure control, typically with intravenous Labetalol (an alpha and beta-blocker), to reduce the "shear stress" on the aortic wall. This is followed by "urgent surgical repair." Urgent surgery alone (Option B) without medical stabilization is dangerous. A "wait and watch" approach (Option C) is only considered for some stable Type B (descending) dissections. Blood transfusion (Option D) is not a primary treatment unless there is overt hemorrhage or rupture. Therefore, the combination of pharmacological control and surgical intervention is the life-saving protocol for suspected Type A aortic dissection
questions.learning: Aortic dissection is a critical emergency where a tear in the inner layer of the aorta allows blood to flow between the layers of the aortic wall. The classic presentation is "tearing" or "ripping" chest pain that radiates to the back.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient comes to you with fears of becoming pregnant and presents a history of unprotected sex five days ago. Which of the following emergency contraceptives can be used in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intra uterine contraceptive device (IUCD)

Since the patient had unprotected sex 5 days ago, an intrauterine contraceptive device(IUCD) can be used for emergency contraception in this case. It can be inserted within 5 days (120 hours) of coitus as a method of emergency contraception. All other methods of emergency contraception mentioned above need to be administered within 72 hours.

The administration of postcoital contraceptive agents that interfere with postovulatory events that can lead to pregnancy is known as the emergency contraception method. They are used to prevent pregnancy after unprotected intercourse.

IUCD (Intrauterine contraceptive device) prevents the implantation of a fertilized ovum. It does so by acting as a foreign body within the uterine cavity. This leads to increased contractility, tubal peristalsis, and promotes leukocytic infiltration in the endometrium so that the fertilized egg is unable to implant.

Emergency contraceptives, also known as postcoital contraceptives are used to prevent conception after unprotected intercourse. They are interceptives. Their main action is to make the endometrium unsuitable for implantation. They can also delay or inhibit ovulation, and prevent fertilization of the egg by sperm.

They include:

* RU 486 (Mifepristone): 25 mg single dose is effective in 99.1% as a postcoital drug.

* Prostaglandins

* Copper T

* Yuzpe method: Combined high-dose estrogen-progestin pills are used as post-coitus contraceptives.
questions.learning: Intra uterine contraceptive device (IUCD) Since the patient had unprotected sex 5 days ago, an intrauterine contraceptive device(IUCD) can be used for emergency contraception in this case.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Identify the communication method in which speakers present one after another on a specific health topic, followed by a summary from the chairperson, but without any discussion among the speakers.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Symposium

A symposium is a communication method in which multiple speakers present sequentially on different aspects of a single topic.

Each speaker delivers an individual presentation, and the session concludes with a summary by the chairperson, without interaction or discussion among the speakers.

| Feature | Description

| ------- | -----------

| Speakers | Multiple experts

| Presentation | Sequential

| Interaction | No discussion among speakers

| Role of chairperson | Summarizes at the end

| Method | Main Feature

| ------ | ------------

| Symposium | Sequential expert presentations

| Panel discussion | Experts discuss among themselves

| Seminar | Presentation + discussion

| Workshop | Practical skill training

In contrast, panel discussions involve interaction, seminars include audience participation, and workshops emphasize hands-on training.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis based on the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aberrant right subclavian artery

An aberrant right subclavian artery is an anatomical variant where the artery arises as the fourth branch of the aortic arch and courses posterior to the esophagus, often leading to dysphagia lusoria due to esophageal compression.

Signature Imaging Clues:

• Indentation on posterior wall of esophagus
• Vessel arising distally from aortic arch
• Courses behind the esophagus (retro-esophageal)

| Condition | Imaging Feature | Key Difference

| --------- | --------------- | --------------

| ARSA | Posterior esophageal indentation | Retro-esophageal vessel

| Right-sided aortic arch | Right arch shadow | No posterior compression

| Tracheal diverticulum | Air pouch near trachea | Not vascular

| Esophageal duplication | Cystic mass | No vascular flow

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A newborn male presents with urinary retention, lethargy, and a distended bladder. Antenatal ultrasonography revealed a characteristic “keyhole sign” along with a thickened bladder wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Posterior urethral valves (PUV) are congenital obstructing membranous folds in the male posterior urethra. The "keyhole sign" on antenatal ultrasound refers to a dilated bladder and a dilated posterior urethra, which is a classic finding for PUV. Postnatal symptoms include urinary retention, a palpable distended bladder, and lethargy. Hypospadias (Option A) involves an abnormal urethral opening on the ventral penis and does not cause high-grade internal obstruction. Vesicoureteral reflux (Option B) is the retrograde flow of urine; while it can occur secondary to PUV, it does not produce the "keyhole sign" independently. Neurogenic bladder (Option D) results from spinal or nerve defects and lacks the specific urethral membrane found in PUV. PUV is a leading cause of chronic kidney disease in male infants and requires urgent cystoscopic ablation
questions.learning: Posterior urethral valves (PUV) are congenital obstructing membranous folds in the male posterior urethra. The "keyhole sign" on antenatal ultrasound refers to a dilated bladder and a dilated posterior urethra, which is a classic finding for PUV.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old man with diabetes presents with progressively worsening pain in his calf. The pain predominantly affects the distal parts of the limb, such as the toes and feet, and is aggravated by movement and pressure. He reports that the pain intensifies when lying down or elevating the leg, but is relieved when he hangs the affected leg down, even preferring to sleep in a seated position for relief. Based on this presentation, what is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms are pathognomonic for Ischemic Rest Pain, a severe stage of peripheral arterial disease (PAD). Rest pain classically involves the distal foot and toes and is worsened by lying flat or elevating the limb, as gravity no longer assists the restricted arterial flow. The patient's preference to sleep in a seated position with the leg hanging down utilizes gravity to increase perfusion pressure, which provides characteristic relief. Sciatica (Option B) involves shooting pain down the back of the leg. Neurological claudication (Option C) is related to spinal stenosis and is relieved by leaning forward. Venous claudication (Option D) is worsened by standing or dependency (hanging the leg down) and relieved by elevation. Because this patient’s pain is specifically relieved by dependency and occurs at rest, it indicates critical limb ischemia. Therefore, "Rest pain" is the definitive clinical cause of his symptoms

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A long-term study found that individuals with high blood pressure (BP) during childhood continued to have high BP in adulthood, while those with low BP in childhood tended to maintain lower levels later in life. Which epidemiological concept does this pattern best represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tracking of blood pressure

The above phenomenon is best described as the "tracking" of blood pressure.

In this phenomenon, the blood pressure of individuals is followed up from early childhood into adulthood. The BP in individuals with low BP levels tend to remain low, and in those with high BP levels, they tend to remain high. This phenomenon of persistence of rank order of blood pressure has been described as "tracking". This is helpful in identifying children and adolescents who are at risk of developing hypertension in their future.

Other options:

Option A: The rule of halves depicts the disease burden of hypertension in the community. It states that only about half of the hypertensive subjects in the general population are aware of the condition. Only half of those aware are being treated and only half of those being treated are considered to be adequately treated.

A pictorial representation of the rule of halves in hypertension is shown below:

Option C: The cohort effect is a concept used in social science and epidemiology, particularly when studying changes in populations over time. It refers to the variations or trends in a particular characteristic or outcome that are observed in a group (cohort) due to their shared experiences and exposures during a specific time period.

Option D: Regression to the mean describes the statistical tendency of extreme values to move closer to the average upon repeated measurement
questions.learning: Tracking of blood pressure — The above phenomenon is best described as the "tracking" of blood pressure. In this phenomenon, the blood pressure of individuals is followed up from early childhood into adulthood.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A rapid test for hepatitis has sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%. In a screening camp where true prevalence is 1%, the most accurate statement is:
options: Negative predictive value will be high
Positive predictive value will be high
False negatives will exceed false positives
Likelihood ratio positive will be less than 1
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Negative predictive value will be high

In a population with low disease prevalence (1%), even tests with good sensitivity and specificity produce a high negative predictive value (NPV) and a low positive predictive value (PPV). This occurs because most individuals tested are disease-free, so negative results are usually true negatives. Therefore, NPV will be high, making the test useful for ruling out disease in screening settings.
questions.learning: Negative predictive value will be high — In a population with low disease prevalence (1%), even tests with good sensitivity and specificity produce a high negative predictive value (NPV) and a low positive predictive value (PPV).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are the prerequisites of outlet forceps delivery? 1. Bladder should be empty. 2. Membranes should be intact. 3. Cervix should be fully dilated. 4. Fetal skull has reached level of pelvic floor. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Outlet forceps delivery is performed when the fetal head has descended to the pelvic floor and delivery can be safely expedited. Certain prerequisites must be fulfilled before applying forceps.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Bladder should be empty. Correct. Reduces the risk of bladder injury and facilitates descent.
• 2. Membranes should be intact. Incorrect. Membranes must be ruptured before forceps application.
• 3. Cervix should be fully dilated. Correct. An incompletely dilated cervix is an absolute contraindication.
• 4. Fetal skull has reached the level of the pelvic floor. Correct. This is a defining feature of outlet forceps.
questions.learning: 1, 3 and 4 Outlet forceps delivery is performed when the fetal head has descended to the pelvic floor and delivery can be safely expedited. Certain prerequisites must be fulfilled before applying forceps.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy presents with mental retardation and an inability to walk. The fundoscopy image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tay-Sachs disease

Tay–Sachs disease is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by hexosaminidase A deficiency, leading to accumulation of GM2 ganglioside in neurons.

• Developmental delay / regression
• Hypotonia → inability to walk
• Exaggerated startle response
• Progressive neurodegeneration

Fundoscopy finding:

• Cherry red spot at macula with surrounding retinal pallor (due to ganglion cell accumulation)

Important distinction:

• Tay–Sachs → no hepatosplenomegaly
• Gaucher / Niemann–Pick → organomegaly present

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 48-year-old woman undergoes a minor pelvic surgery involving dissection along the lateral pelvic wall. During the procedure, a nerve that passes through a canal is inadvertently injured. Postoperatively, she has difficulty in adduction of thigh while walking, along with loss of sensation over the medial aspect of the thigh. Which nerve was most likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Obturator nerve

The obturator nerve (L2–L4) arises from the lumbar plexus and exits the pelvis through the obturator canal to supply the adductor muscles of the thigh and provide sensory innervation to the medial aspect of the thigh. It is at risk of injury during pelvic lymph node dissection, gynecologic surgery, and surgery along the lateral pelvic wall.

Why not the other options?

• A. Femoral nerve: Supplies the quadriceps (knee extension) and sensation over the anterior thigh and medial leg; injury causes difficulty climbing stairs and reduced patellar reflex, not isolated loss of thigh adduction.
• B. Sciatic nerve: Supplies the posterior thigh and most muscles below the knee; injury causes foot drop and weakness of knee flexion, not medial thigh sensory loss.
• D. Superior gluteal nerve: Supplies gluteus medius and minimus; injury causes a Trendelenburg gait due to hip abductor weakness.
questions.learning: Obturator nerve — The obturator nerve (L2–L4) arises from the lumbar plexus and exits the pelvis through the obturator canal to supply the adductor muscles of the thigh and provide sensory innervation to the medial aspect of the thigh.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Which of the following is not associated with G6PD deficiency?

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)
options: Equal incidence in males and females
Predisposes the patient to oxidative stress
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Equal incidence in males and females

G6PD Deficiency does not have an equal incidence in males and females. It is an X-linked recessive (XLR) disorder, hence males are more affected than females.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency causes congenital hemolytic anemia due to enzyme deficiency. G6PD is required to generate NADPH while oxidizing glucose-6-phosphate in the hexose monophosphate pathway (HMP). G6PD deficiency leads to reduced NADPH levels (option B) which then reduces the level of reduced glutathione. Reduced glutathione is required to protect the cells against oxidative stress to RBCs and hemolysis.

Clinically, most patients are asymptomatic. When exposed to triggers like fava beans, infections, drugs such as primaquine, chloroquine, sulfonamides/sulfones, dapsone, and nitrofurantoin patient develops:

• Episodic hemolysis, both intravascular and extravascular
• Hemolytic anaemia
• Hemoglobinemia
• Hemoglobinuria

Increased oxidative damage to RBCs leads to the formation of denatured precipitates known as Heinz bodies. These bodies can damage the RBC membrane leading to intravascular hemolysis. Additionally, when such RBCs pass through the splenic cords, macrophages pluck out these precipitates, giving them the characteristic appearance of bite cells.

The images below show the presence of Heinz bodies and bite cells.
questions.learning: Equal incidence in males and females G6PD Deficiency does not have an equal incidence in males and females. It is an X-linked recessive (XLR) disorder, hence males are more affected than females.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Mechanism of action of dicumarol?
options: Inhibits vitamin K dependant Clotting factors
questions.explanation: Dicumarol is a naturally occurring oral anticoagulant that belongs to the coumarin class, functionally identical to warfarin. Its mechanism of action is the inhibition of the enzyme Vitamin K epoxide reductase. This inhibition prevents the recycling of Vitamin K, which is a necessary cofactor for the post-translational gamma-carboxylation of several critical proteins. Specifically, it leads to the production of dysfunctional, vitamin K-dependent clotting factors: II (prothrombin), VII, IX, and X, as well as regulatory proteins C and S. Activating antithrombin III (Option A) is the mechanism of heparin. Inhibiting Factor Xa (Option D) is the mechanism of drugs like rivaroxaban. Inhibiting tissue plasminogen activator (Option C) would be pro-thrombotic rather than anticoagulant. Because dicumarol inhibits the synthesis of new factors rather than inactivating existing ones, its anticoagulant effect has a slow onset (delayed by several days). Monitoring is traditionally performed via the prothrombin time (PT) or INR to ensure therapeutic efficacy and safety
questions.learning: Dicumarol is a naturally occurring oral anticoagulant that belongs to the coumarin class, functionally identical to warfarin. Its mechanism of action is the inhibition of the enzyme Vitamin K epoxide reductase.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is characteristic of hypovolemic shock?
questions.explanation: Hypovolemic shock results from a significant loss of intravascular volume (blood or fluids), leading to reduced tissue perfusion. In response, the body activates the sympathetic nervous system to preserve perfusion to vital organs. This compensatory response causes marked peripheral vasoconstriction, leading to an increase in systemic vascular resistance (SVR)—the key hemodynamic change in hypovolemic shock. Because circulating volume is reduced, cardiac output is decreased (not increased), as both preload and stroke volume fall. Venous pressure, including central venous pressure (CVP), is also decreased due to reduced venous return. Additionally, mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO₂) is low, reflecting increased tissue oxygen extraction from a diminished blood supply. Clinically, patients present with tachycardia, hypotension, cold and clammy skin, delayed capillary refill, and oliguria. These signs reflect intense vasoconstriction and poor perfusion. Management focuses on rapid volume replacement using intravenous crystalloids or blood transfusion, depending on the cause, to restore preload, improve cardiac output, and reverse shock
questions.learning: Hypovolemic shock results from a significant loss of intravascular volume (blood or fluids), leading to reduced tissue perfusion. In response, the body activates the sympathetic nervous system to preserve perfusion to vital organs.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A new drug combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy for metastatic melanoma was prescribed by a radiotherapist. It prolongs the survival. Which of the following is true in this situation?
options: Incidence reduces and prevalence remains the same
Incidence remains the same and prevalence increases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Incidence remains the same and prevalence increases

By the new drug combination, the survival of the patient has increased, hence incidence remains the same while prevalence increases.

Incidence: Number of new cases in a defined population in a specified period of time.
Prevalence: Number of old and new cases at a given point of time over a period of time.

Options A, B, D: The treatment only prolongs the disease, it has nothing to do with the occurrence of cases thereby nothing to do with incidence.
questions.learning: Incidence remains the same and prevalence increases By the new drug combination, the survival of the patient has increased, hence incidence remains the same while prevalence increases.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident presents with a right upper limb nerve injury. On examination, the patient can flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.explanation: The ability to perform flexion at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and extension at the interphalangeal (IP) joints is primarily the function of the lumbrical muscles. The lumbricals are innervated by the median and ulnar nerves. If the patient can still perform these specific movements, it indicates that the median and ulnar nerves are largely intact. However, the radial nerve (Option D) is responsible for the extension of the MCP joints and the wrist. Radial nerve injury, common in humeral shaft fractures following road traffic accidents, leads to "wrist drop" and the inability to extend the MCP joints. The median nerve (Option A) primarily controls thumb opposition and finger flexion. The anterior interosseous nerve (Option B), a branch of the median, controls the "OK" sign (flexion of the thumb IP and index distal IP joints). The ulnar nerve (Option C) controls most of the intrinsic muscles of the hand. Therefore, the clinical preservation of lumbrical-mediated movements while experiencing upper limb trauma most likely points to a radial nerve injury
questions.learning: The ability to perform flexion at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and extension at the interphalangeal (IP) joints is primarily the function of the lumbrical muscles.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the name of the pediatric malignant tumor that commonly occurs in children and has a strong tendency to metastasize to the bone marrow?
questions.explanation: Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood, arising from primitive neural crest cells. It is notoriously aggressive and frequently metastasizes to the bone marrow (found in approximately 70% of Stage 4 cases). This spread is so characteristic that a bone marrow biopsy is a standard part of the initial staging workup. Wilms tumor (Option A) is a common pediatric kidney tumor but primarily metastasizes to the lungs rather than the bone marrow. Adrenal gland tumors (Option C) and Granulosa cell tumors (Option D) are less common in children and have different metastatic patterns . Clinically, bone marrow involvement in neuroblastoma may lead to anemia and thrombocytopenia. Small blue round cell tumors in a bone marrow aspirate should always raise suspicion for neuroblastoma. Therefore, due to its highly specific hematogenous spread to the marrow space, neuroblastoma is the correct answer
questions.learning: Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood, arising from primitive neural crest cells. It is notoriously aggressive and frequently metastasizes to the bone marrow (found in approximately 70% of Stage 4 cases).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the Nalgonda technique for defluoridation of water, which of the following chemicals are used? Select the best combination. 1. Gypsum 2. Lime 3. Charcoal 4. Alum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 & 4

The Nalgonda technique is a community-level method for Defluoridation of drinking water, developed in India.

It uses alum (aluminium sulphate) as a coagulant to precipitate fluoride and lime to aid floc formation and adjust pH.

The technique uses three main chemicals:

The process also involves rapid mixing, flocculation, sedimentation, and filtration, making it suitable for rural and semi-urban settings with high fluoride levels.

Steps in Nalgonda Technique

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text:
Match the following:

1. Eonism
A. Exposure of one’s genitals to an unsuspecting stranger

2. Exhibitionism
B. Sexual gratification by intercourse with dead bodies

3. Frotteurism
C. Sexual pleasure by wearing clothes of the opposite sex

4. Necrophilia
D. Sexual gratification by rubbing private parts against another person
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-C;2-A;3-D;4-B

The correct answer is option B: 1-C;2-A;3-D;4-B

1. Eonism
C. Sexual pleasure by wearing clothes of the opposite sex

2. Exhibitionism
A. Exposure of one’s genitals to an unsuspecting stranger

3. Frotteurism
D. Sexual gratification by rubbing private parts against another person

4. Necrophilia
B. Sexual gratification by intercourse with dead bodies

Paraphilias or perversions are sexual stimuli or acts that are deviations from normal sexual behaviors but are necessary for some people to experience arousal and orgasm.

Eonism (also known as transvestism) is a sexual perversion, where a person's whole personality is dominated by a desire to be identified as a member of the opposite sex. This is usually seen in males who obtain sexual pleasure by wearing female clothes. There is no hormonal/genital abnormality.

Exhibitionism is the urge to expose genitals to a stranger or unsuspecting person.

Frotteurism refers to the sexual gratification achieved by touching or rubbing against a non-consenting person. This behavior often occurs in busy and crowded places. It is predominantly described in men.

Necrophilia is an obsession with obtaining sexual gratification from dead bodies.

questions.text: A 30-year-old male patient presented to the casualty department with torticollis and dystonia. His attender reported that he had been diagnosed with schizophrenia and had recently started treatment with Haloperidol. What is the next best step to treat the patient's presenting symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Give Benzhexol

This patient on haloperidol developed extra-pyramidal symptoms of torticollis and dystonia. The next best step in his management to alleviate his symptoms would be to administer benzhexol, an anticholinergic medication

Benzhexol, also known as trihexiphenidylis an antimuscarinic agent. Drug-induced parkinsonism is a condition that is caused by certain drugs that have D2 antagonistic action like typical antipsychotics. Due to the decrease in dopaminergic activity, they result in an unbalanced cholinergic activity. Benzhexol acts by restoring the balance of the cholinergics in the striatal interneurons.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the surgical step shown in the image given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Capsulorrhexis

Capsulorrhexis is the step shown in the given image.

Capsulorrhexis is a method of anterior capsulotomy, where an opening is made in the anterior capsule of the lens. It is one of the steps involved in conventional extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE).

Anterior capsulotomy can be done by one of three methods - can opener's technique, linear capsulotomy or envelope technique, or continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis.

Continuous curvilinear capsulorrhexis (CCC), is considered to be superior to all the preexisting methods because when done correctly, it does not leave any edges or tears. Trypan blue dye can be used to stain the lens capsule for better visibility.

In ECCE, a portion of the anterior capsule of the lens is removed, allowing extraction of the lens nucleus and cortex. This leaves the remainder of the anterior capsule, the posterior capsule, and the zonular support intact. The intact lens nucleus is then removed from the eye through a limbal incision.

An anterior capsulotomy is followed by hydro dissection using a balanced salt solution. This helps to separate the corticonuclear mass from the capsule. Removal of lens nucleus and aspiration of the cortex is done using a two-way irrigation and aspiration cannula. An intraocular lens (IOL) is then implanted and the incision is then closed.

Some of the IOLs used are shown in the image below.
questions.learning: Capsulorrhexis Capsulorrhexis is the step shown in the given image. Capsulorrhexis is a method of anterior capsulotomy, where an opening is made in the anterior capsule of the lens.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with gradually worsening swelling around his wrist over the past 3 months. Based on the provided X-ray image, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays an eccentric, expansile, and multi-loculated lytic lesion in the epiphysis of the distal radius, classically described as having a "soap-bubble" appearance. Most significantly, the lesion extends right up to the subchondral bone (articular surface). These are the hallmark radiological findings for Osteoclastoma, also known as a Giant Cell Tumor (GCT) (Option C). GCT is typically seen in young adults (ages 20-40) and is locally aggressive. Ewing’s sarcoma (Option A) classically shows an "onion-skin" periosteal reaction in the diaphysis. Osteosarcoma (Option B) would show a "sunburst" appearance and Codman's triangle. Osteochondroma (Option D) appears as a bony growth on a stalk (exostosis) pointing away from the joint. Because the subarticular "soap-bubble" location is so characteristic, Osteoclastoma is the definitive diagnosis. Treatment involves surgical curettage and bone grafting or cementation to prevent joint collapse

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with a malar rash, recurrent oral ulcers, and polyarthralgia. She has no significant medical history and is not on any medications. Laboratory tests reveal thrombocytopenia and a positive anti–Smith antibody. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This young female patient presents with a multi-system clinical picture fulfilling multiple ACR diagnostic criteria for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). These include a malar rash (butterfly rash on cheeks), recurrent oral ulcers, arthritis (joint pain), and hematologic involvement (thrombocytopenia). The definitive diagnostic hallmark provided is the positive Anti-Sm (Anti-Smith) antibody, which is highly specific for SLE. Scleroderma (Option A) presents with skin thickening and Raynaud's. Sjogren's syndrome (Option B) is characterized by dry eyes and dry mouth. Rheumatoid arthritis (Option C) presents with chronic symmetric joint destruction but lacks the specific malar rash and Sm-antibodies. SLE is a systemic autoimmune disease that primarily affects young women. Therefore, the combination of clinical symptoms and the pathognomonic serological marker confirms SLE as the definitive diagnosis. Management involves corticosteroids and hydroxychloroquine to control flares and prevent organ damage
questions.learning: This young female patient presents with a multi-system clinical picture fulfilling multiple ACR diagnostic criteria for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text:
Which of the following statements are true regarding cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection?

1. Neonates who are asymptomatic at birth have a lesser risk of later sequelae.

2. 20-40% are symptomatic at birth.

3. In developing countries, the rate of transmission of CMV infection to the infant is more common from primary maternal infection than reactivation.

4. Diagnosis by urine specimen at 4 weeks of age
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 3

The true statements regarding CMV infection are statements 1 and 3.

Most CMV transmission occurs in the first trimester. The risk of transmission is high in the third trimester.

Only 10% (statement 2) of the infected babies are symptomatic. Asymptomatic neonates have lesser chances of having late sequelae (statement 1).

Congenital CMV infection can result from either primary or reactivation infection of the mother. The rate of transmission of infection to the fetus in a mother who has a primary infection is about 30% (statement 3) while in a mother with a non-primary infection, it is 1-2%. However, the total number of infants who have acquired an infection from a mother with a non-primary infection is 3-4 times more than infants who have acquired an infection from mothers with a primary infection.

The clinical manifestations include hepatosplenomegaly, petechial rashes, jaundice, chorioretinitis, and microcephaly. Neuroimaging shows intracranial periventricular calcifications. One of the long-term sequelae is sensorineural hearing loss.

The investigation of choice is PCR or viral culture. It should be done within the first three weeks of life (statement 4). After this period, it is difficult to distinguish between a congenital and an acquired infection. Since not all affected infants are viremic at birth, urine and/or saliva are more reliable samples than blood.

There is no definitive treatment for congenital CMV infection. Treatment with ganciclovir is indicated only in patients with progressive neurologic disease and deafness.

questions.learning: 1, 3 The true statements regarding CMV infection are statements 1 and 3. Most CMV transmission occurs in the first trimester.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 55-year-old man is diagnosed with left testicular carcinoma. Which of the following lymph nodes is the first to be involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Para-aortic lymph nodes

In a patient with testicular carcinoma, para-aortic lymph nodes are the first to be involved.

The lymphatic drainage of the testes is to the para-aortic lymph nodes near the origin of the gonadal vessels. The contralateral para-aortic lymph nodes are sometimes involved in tumor spread, but the inguinal lymph nodes are affected only if the scrotal skin is involved.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A woman presents with sudden onset of high- grade fever, hypotension, and a diffuse rash, with a history of prolonged tampon use. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of high fever (>38.8°C), hypotension, and a diffuse erythrodermic rash in the context of prolonged tampon use is diagnostic of Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS). This condition is most often caused by toxin-producing Staphylococcus aureus (specifically TSST-1), which acts as a superantigen to trigger massive T-cell activation and cytokine release. General septic shock (Option A) can cause fever and hypotension but lacks the specific diffuse rash and tampon association. Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (Option C) presents with pelvic pain and cervical motion tenderness rather than systemic shock and rash. Streptococcal pharyngitis (Option D) is a localized infection that doesn't match this severe systemic pattern. Treatment involves intensive supportive care with IV fluids and antistaphylococcal antibiotics
questions.learning: The clinical triad of high fever (>38.8°C), hypotension, and a diffuse erythrodermic rash in the context of prolonged tampon use is diagnostic of Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 65-year-old female patient with a history of chronic arthritis on treatment came with complaints of defective vision in both eyes. On examination, vision in RE = 6/12, LE = 6/18, IOP = 18 mmHg in both eyes, the anterior segment was normal, fundus examination and fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) findings given in the figure. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chloroquine toxicity

The given clinical viginette of female patient on treatment for chronic arthritis which is most likely the drug chloroquine given for rheumatoid arthritis, now presenting with decreased visual acuity, fundoscopy with a typical bull's eye sign and Fundus fluroscein angiography showing increased fluroscence in the macular area is suggestive of chloroquine toxicity.

Chloroquine and it's derivative hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) are antimalarial drugs which is also used to treat connective tissue disorders such as Rheumatoid arthritis, Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) and Discoid Lupus.

The maximum dose allowed for chloroquine is 6 mg/kg in 24 hours while for hydroxychloroquine it is 4.5 mg/kg. Hydroxychloroquine has a lower risk of ocular toxicity and hence is percived to be a safer drug but with weaker anti-inflammatory effect.

Manifestations of Chloroquine toxicity:

• Reversible on stopping the drug: difficulty in night vision, blurring of vision, diplopia, keratopathy
• Central and paracentral scotomas
• Earliest fundus findings: blunting of foveal reflex, irregularity in the macular pigmentation.
• Advanced stages: 'Bull's eye maculopathy' where the central irregular pigmentation may become surrounded by a concentric zone of hypopigmentation
• End-stage appearance includes bullseye maculopathy, pigmentary degeneration of retina and bone spicule formation, vascular attenuation, and optic atropy.

Screening should include a baseline examination for all patients before starting these drugs followed by annual screening starting after 5 years of use.

Pre-existing maculopathy is considered a contraindication to treatment with chloroquine and HCQ because underlying abnormalities may mask early toxicity.

Screening examinations include visual acuity testing, dilated fundus examination, spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) testing, and functional assessment with Humphrey test.

Various causes of Bull's eye maculopathy are:

1. Chloroquine and HCQ toxicity
2. Cone-Rod dystrophy
3. Advanced stargardt's disease
4. Clofazimine retinopathy
