questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with sinusitis, ulcerative lesions on the nasopharynx, nodular lesions with cavitations of the lung, and renal failure. Which of the following is the most useful investigation in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Test for ANCA

The given patient has the involvement of upper respiratory tract (chronic sinusitis, ulcerations on nasopharynx), lower respiratory tract (nodular lesions with lung cavitations), and kidneys (renal failure) which are suggestive of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's granulomatosis) and testing for cytoplasmic ANCA (c-ANCA) would be the most helpful investigation in this condition.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a granulomatous and necrotizing vasculitis of the small arteries and veins that mainly affects:

• Upper respiratory tract: chronic sinusitis, serous otitis media due to eustachian tube blockage, nasal septal perforation, and mucosal ulceration of the nasopharynx.
• Lower respiratory tract: presenting with cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and persistent pneumonitis. Lung involvement typically appears as multiple, bilateral nodular cavitary infiltrates.
• Kidneys: focal or segmental glomerulonephritis presenting with proteinuria, hematuria, and hypertension. If left untreated it can lead to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

Apart from these organs, it can also affect the eyes and skin. Skin lesions present as palpable purpura or subcutaneous nodules.

Lab investigations will show anemia, leucocytosis, elevated ESR, and high titers of cytoplasmic ANCA (c-ANCA) targetted against anti-proteinase-3 (anti-PR-3). The specificity of a positive PR-3 ANCA for Wegener's is very high, especially in the presence of active glomerulonephritis. Following treatment, PR-3 ANCA titers fall and subsequent rise in titers is predictive of relapse. Chest radiograph will show multiple, bilateral cavitating nodules and pulmonary infiltrates.

The diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis on biopsy. This finding is commonly seen in the tissues obtained from the lungs, upper airways, skin, and rarely in the kidneys.

The radiograph below shows cavitating nodules in a patient with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman comes with complaints of warty lesions on the vulva. On examination, multiple warty growths on the vulva and around the anal canal are seen. This condition is most likely seen in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Condyloma accuminata

Multiple warty growths on the vulva (shown below) and around the anal canal are suggestive of condyloma acuminata (genital warts). HPV 6 and 11 are associated with the development of condyloma acuminatum. They are sexually transmitted.

The verrucous growths may appear discrete or coalesce to form large cauliflower-like growths. Infections are often transient in young women but can persist and progress to cancer in older women and immunocompromised individuals. Histopathology will show koilocytes, perinuclear halo, multinucleation, and acanthosis.

Treatment options include podophyllin, trichloroacetic acid, and surgical removal. The use of podophyllin cream is contraindicated in the first trimester of pregnancy. Larger lesions can be removed with a diathermy loop or laser ablation. Cesarean section is advised for women with genital warts during early labor to prevent the risk of transmitting laryngeal papillomatosis to the newborn.

Option B: Molluscum contagiosum presents as a crop of small domed vesicles with central umbilication (shown below). It is caused by the pox virus and it spreads by close sexual or nonsexual contact and by autoinoculation.

Option C: Chancroid appears as small papules that develop into painful ulcerating pustules. They are associated with unilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. It is caused by H. ducreyi.

Option D: Herpes appears as multiple crops of vesicles and ulcers.
questions.learning: Condyloma accuminata Multiple warty growths on the vulva (shown below) and around the anal canal are suggestive of condyloma acuminata (genital warts).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: While evaluating a patient with anemia suspected to be hemolytic in origin—based on features like fatigue, pallor, and jaundice— which laboratory finding is directly indicative of hemolytic anemia?
options: All of the options given below
questions.explanation: The hallmark of hemolytic anemia is the premature destruction of red blood cells (hemolysis). When RBCs lyse, they release free hemoglobin into the plasma. Haptoglobin is a serum protein that binds to this free hemoglobin to prevent its oxidative damage and facilitate its clearance by the liver. Consequently, in cases of active hemolysis, haptoglobin is rapidly consumed, leading to its characteristic decrease or total absence in laboratory tests. Neutropenia (Option B) is a decrease in white blood cells and is not a feature of hemolysis. Reticulocytopenia (Option C) describes an inadequate bone marrow response, whereas hemolytic anemia characteristically shows reticulocytosis as the healthy marrow attempts to compensate for the cell loss. Other supportive findings include elevated indirect bilirubin (causing jaundice) and increased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). Decreased haptoglobin is one of the most specific markers for confirming that anemia is due to increased red cell destruction rather than impaired production or blood loss
questions.learning: The hallmark of hemolytic anemia is the premature destruction of red blood cells (hemolysis). When RBCs lyse, they release free hemoglobin into the plasma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which medication has been shown to reduce mortality in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)?
questions.explanation: In the management of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), the primary therapeutic goal is to inhibit the neurohormonal pathways that drive disease progression. Beta-blockers, specifically Metoprolol succinate, Bisoprolol, and Carvedilol, are cornerstone therapies proven in large clinical trials to reduce mortality and hospitalizations. These drugs work by counteracting the chronic, deleterious effects of the sympathetic nervous system on the failing heart. Furosemide (Option B) and Torsemide (Option C) are loop diuretics; while they are essential for managing fluid overload and improving symptoms of congestion, they have never been shown to provide a mortality benefit. Prazosin (Option D) is an alpha-1 blocker used primarily for hypertension or BPH; it is not a standard treatment for heart failure and can occasionally worsen symptoms. Therefore, metoprolol (in its extended-release form) is the correct choice for a drug that extends life in HFrEF. It is typically initiated at a low dose once the patient is clinically stable and gradually up-titrated
questions.learning: In the management of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), the primary therapeutic goal is to inhibit the neurohormonal pathways that drive disease progression.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text:
A 60-year-old patient who is a known case of hypertension and diabetes underwent PCI stent placement for NSTEMI last year. He is currently on aspirin, metoprolol and atorvastatin. He comes for a follow-up, and his lipid profile is as follows- Total cholesterol 252mg/dl LDL: 156mg/dl, triglyceride 158mg/dl and HDL- 40 mg/dl. Which drugs can be added based on his lipid profile?

1. Ezetemibe

2. Evolocumab

3. Gemfibrozil

4. Bemepedoic acid
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 4

1,2 and 4 can be added based on his lipid profile.

A patient with hypertension and diabetes who underwent PCI stent placement for NSTEMI has atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). The treatment goal in patients with ASCVD is to decrease LDL levels.

Ezetemibe, Evolocumab, Bemepedoic acid decrease LDL. Gemfibrozil mainly decreases triglycerides and not LDL.

1. Evolocumab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits PCSK-9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin). Inhibition of PCSK-9 prevents the degradation of LDL receptors and thus increases LDL-cholesterol clearance by the liver. They are used in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) to decrease LDL levels.

2. Ezetimibe inhibits cholesterol absorption by enterocytes in the small intestine. It lowers the total and LDL-C levels.

3. Gemfibrozil belongs to the fibrate group of drugs that binds to peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARα), which stimulate fatty acid oxidation and thereby reduce triglyceride levels mainly.

4. Bempedoic acid inhibits adenosine triphosphate-citrate lyase (ACL) and results in decreased LDL in patients not responding to statin therapy.

Note - Ezetimibe, colestipol, bempedoic acid and PCSK-9 inhibitors like alirocumab have been proven to reduce atherosclerosis risk when added to statins, whereas the fibrate group of drugs and niacin show no significant effect in addition to statins.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 1,2 and 4 can be added based on his lipid profile. A patient with hypertension and diabetes who underwent PCI stent placement for NSTEMI has atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) dressing are correct? 1. Reduces bacterial load 2. Maximum pressure is -125mm of Hg 3. Promotes granulation tissue 4. Reduces size of wound
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3 and 4

All statements about Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) dressing are correct.

| Statement | Explanation

| --------- | -----------

| Reduces bacterial load | Continuous suction removes exudate, debris, and bacteria, lowering infection risk.

| Maximum pressure −125 mmHg | Standard optimal negative pressure used in VAC therapy is around −125 mmHg.

| Promotes granulation tissue | Negative pressure increases blood flow and angiogenesis, stimulating granulation tissue formation.

| Reduces size of wound | VAC causes macrodeformation, pulling wound edges together and decreasing wound size.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following processes is mediated by CRISPR CAS-9 technology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gene editing

CRISPR CAS-9 technology mediates the process of gene editing.

CRISPR is Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats

* CRISPR-Cas9 is a genome editing tool and this system enables select bacteria to respond to and eliminate invading genetic material.

* CRISPRs are transcribed into an RNA sequence that directs the Cas9 to a sequence, leading to its cleavage.

* Gene editing uses an artificial guide RNA that binds Cas9 and is complementary to a DNA sequence of interest and Cas9 induces the break of double-stranded DNA.

One of the first successful diseases used on an experimental basis is sickle cell anemia.

Other gene editing tools are:

* Zinc-finger nucleases (ZNFs)

* Transcription-Activator Like Effector Nucleases (TALEN)

* Meganucleases

The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020 was awarded jointly to Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer A. Doudna "for the development of the CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing system, which has for the first time enabled scientists to make precise changes in the long stretches of DNA.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Arrange the following steps of Karyotyping in the correct order :

1. Collect cells by peripheral vein using a heparin syringe.
2. Culture in phytohaemoagglutinin.
3. Incubation at 37 degrees C for 3 days.
4. Harvest with colchicine.
5. Routine staining with Giemsa
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5

The correct order of steps of Karyotyping is as follows:

1. Collect cells by peripheral vein using a heparin syringe.
2. Culture in phytohaemoagglutinin.
3. Incubation at 37 degrees C for 3 days.
4. Harvest with colchicine.
5. Routine staining with Giemsa

Karyotyping is the process by which chromosomes are isolated, stained, and examined to find chromosomal anomalies. It is used in prenatal diagnosis, investigation of repeat pregnancy loss, investigation of children and adults suspected of having a chromosomal disorder, and subtyping of lymphomas and leukemias for the purpose of exact diagnosis, giving a prognosis, and treatment.

Various techniques are used in karyotyping to study chromosomes. Staining with various compounds produces various results and helps us to understand the chromosomes better.

Common techniques used are:

• Q banding - fluorescence staining with quinacrine mustard
• G banding - Giemsa staining after partial denaturation of chromatin
• R banding - reverse Giemsa staining. In this, the light and dark areas are reversed
• C banding - staining of heterochromatin with silver salts
• T banding - staining the telomeres of chromosomes

The karyotyping of a normal human male is given below.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 The correct order of steps of Karyotyping is as follows: 1. Collect cells by peripheral vein using a heparin syringe.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A researcher engineers a cell line lacking functional signal recognition particle (SRP). Which immediate consequence on protein localization would be expected for proteins normally destined for secretion?
options: Proteins would be correctly translocated into the RER lumen via an SRP-independent backup pathway
Proteins would accumulate in the cytosol due to failure of ribosome-RER targeting
Proteins would be retained in the Golgi due to failure of COPII vesicle formation
Proteins would be degraded by lysosomal enzymes due to failure of mannose-6-phosphate tagging
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Proteins would accumulate in the cytosol due to failure of ribosome-RER targeting

SRP traffics the polypeptide-ribosome complex from cytosol to RER. Absent or dysfunctional SRP → ribosome-mRNA-polypeptide complex never reaches RER → translation either continues in cytosol (for proteins lacking proper insertion) or the protein accumulates untranslocated, mislocalized in the cytosol rather than entering the secretory pathway.

| Component | Function | If SRP absent

| --------- | -------- | -------------

| SRP | Targets polypeptide-ribosome complex to RER | Fails — no targeting

| RER | Site of secretory protein synthesis | Bypassed

| Result | Normal secretory pathway entry | Cytosolic protein accumulation

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female presents with a painless, rapidly growing lump in her left breast that she noticed over the past few months. On examination, the lump is well-defined, mobile, and firm in consistency. A breast ultrasound reveals a solid mass, and a core needle biopsy is performed. Histopathological examination shows a leaf-like pattern with an overgrowth of the stromal component and ductal structures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phyllodes tumor

The histopathology of the biopsy of the lump shows increased stromal cellularity, overgrowth, and typical leaflike architecture which is suggestive of phyllodes tumor.

Phyllodes tumor is also known as cystosarcoma phyllodes, presents as a large tumor with an unevenly bosselated surface. This tumour does not infiltrate the skin though the overlying skin becomes thin and tense due to swelling. Nipple retraction is not seen in this condition.

Phyllodes tumors usually occur in women over the age of 40 years but can appear in younger women. They are mostly benign even though it is also called as cystosarcoma phyllodes or as serocystic disease of Brodie. They are usually mobile over the chest wall despite their large size.

Histologically, there is a wide variation with some of low malignant potential and others having a higher mitotic index.

* They are fibroepithelial tumours that arise from the intralobular stroma.

* It can be benign, borderline or malignant.

* Phyllodes tumor can be differentiated from intracanalicular fibroadenoma by its subepithelial or periepithelial accentuation of stromal cellularity.

* Most phyllodes tumor are of low grade. Recurrence rate is high in intermediate and high grade tumors.

* Increased stromal cellularity, stromal overgrowth (absence of epithelial elements), nuclear atypia, increased mitosis(>10 per 10HPF) suggests the diagnosis of malignant phyllodes tumour.

* Gain in chromosome 1q is the most frequent clonal acquired chromosomal changes seen in Phyllodes tumor. HOXB13 overexpression is associated with more aggressive clinical behaviour.

Microscopy reveals the presence of nodules of proliferating stroma covered by epithelium (leaf-like architecture).

Note: "Phyllodes" means "leaf like" in Greek.

Treatment of phyllodes tumor:

* Benign type- Enucleation or wide local excision

* Massive tumors, recurrent tumors and malignant type- Mastectomy

* Axillary dissection is not done if malignant transformation occurs because the lymphatic spread is rare.

Other Options:

Option B: Galactocele: A galactocele is a milk-filled cavity in the breast of a woman who is usually lactating. It can be caused due to lactation problems, prolactin stimulation by drugs, or duct obstruction. It presents as a palpable, round, well-circumscribed, and freely mobile mass with no fever, pain, or inflammation. It is usually subareolar and unilateral.

Option C: Paget's Disease: Presents as a chronic, eczematous eruption of the nipple which may progress to ulceration. In the majority of patients, there is also an underlying breast lump. Histology shows the presence of large, pale, vacuolated cells (Paget cells) with round or oval nuclei in the rete pegs of the epithelium.

Option D: Fibroadenoma is a form of aberrations of normal development and involution of the breast (ANDI), and it is the most common cause of a breast lump in women aged 15–25 years. It arises from hyperplasia of a single lobule and presents as a well-circumscribed, smooth or lobular, firm, non-tender, freely mobile mass (mouse in the breast). The histopathology shows the proliferation of intralobular stroma, and the epithelium may be surrounded by stroma (pericanalicular pattern) or compressed and distorted (intracanalicular pattern). The histopathology image is given below:
questions.learning: Phyllodes tumor — The histopathology of the biopsy of the lump shows increased stromal cellularity, overgrowth, and typical leaflike architecture which is suggestive of phyllodes tumor.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 23-year-old female with 6 years of infertility, has a BMI of 33 and facial hair. Investigations reveal she has (PCOS) and spills from bilateral tubes. She and her husband are trying to conceive, what would be the best plan of management for this lady?
options: Weight loss + Metformin + induction of ovulation with urinary gonadotrophins
Weight loss + folic acid, Try for spontaneous induction, if failed move to induction of ovulation
Weight loss + Metformin + Induction of ovulation with clomiphene
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Weight loss + folic acid, Try for spontaneous induction, if failed move to induction of ovulation

In the given clinical scenario the most appropriate management would be weight loss + folic acid, try for spontaneous induction, if failed move to induction of ovulation. In obese PCOS patients, even modest weight loss (5% of body weight) can help in the restoration of ovulatory cycles in some cases. Hence spontaneous induction is tried. Folic acid is normally administered as prophylaxis before conception to prevent neural tube defects.

Polycystic ovarian syndrome

Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS)/ Polycystic ovarian disease (PCOD)/ Stein-Leventhal syndrome is a multisystem disorder. It involves metabolic and endocrine dysfunctions that commonly occur among women in the reproductive age group. It has multifactorial causation, such as lifestyle changes, stress, diet, obesity, and hyperinsulinemic states.

Important clinical features of PCOS are Menstrual abnormalities (70%) - oligomenorrhea, amenorrhea, obesity, hirsutism, acne, and alopecia due to hyperandrogenism, acanthosis nigricans due to insulin resistance, and infertility.

Rotterdam criterion is used to diagnose PCOS. The presence of any two of the three components of this criteria establishes the diagnosis of PCOS.

•  Oligo/ amenorrhoea, anovulation, infertility
• Hirsutism/ acne
• Ultrasound findings-

•

Enlarged ovaries with ovarian volume will be more than 10 mL

•

12 or more small follicles each of 2-9 mm in size placed peripherally.

Investigations

• Hormonal studies
• USG is diagnostic of PCOS - it shows enlarged ovaries with multiple follicles in the periphery. It also rules out other pathologies like ovarian tumors, endometrial hyperplasia.
• Laparoscopy (therapeutic). It reveals bilateral enlarged ovarian cysts.

The ultrasound image below shows an enlarged ovary with multiple follicles in the periphery.

Management of PCOD is individualized. Weight reduction and lifestyle changes are the first-line therapy for PCOD. Oral contraceptive pills (OCP), preferably fourth-generation pills with 30 mcg E2 and 2-3 mg drospirenone are used to treat menstrual abnormalities. Hirsutism and acne are managed with OCP with cyproterone acetate and topical agents such as epiornithine, clindamycin lotion 1%, erythromycin gel 2%, and isotretinoin.

Patients with PCOD are more prone to developing insulin resistance which can be controlled with metformin(Option A, C and D) and acarbose. Patients presenting with infertility are treated by inducing ovulation using clomiphene as a first-line drug, along with dexamethasone and letrozole.

Surgical management includes laparoscopic ovarian drilling or puncture of not more than four cysts in each ovary.

Note:

PCOS in association with diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and cardiovascular disease presenting in reproductive age group is known as "X syndrome".
questions.learning: Weight loss + folic acid, Try for spontaneous induction, if failed move to induction of ovulation In the given clinical scenario the most appropriate management would be weight loss + folic acid, try for spontaneous induction, if failed move to induction…

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
Which of the following is true?

1. BRCA1 is an oncogene.
2. HER2neu is amplified only in a fraction of breast cancer.
3. EGFR(+) is seen in non-small cell lung cancer.
4. N-MYC is a tumour suppressor gene.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2, 3

Of the given statements, 2 and 3 are true. BRCA1 is a tumor suppressor gene and MYC is a proto-oncogene.

BRCA1 is a tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 17q21 and its function is to repair the double-stranded breaks in DNA. It is associated with familial breast and ovarian carcinoma. BRCA1-associated breast cancers are commonly poorly differentiated.

All breast cancers are separated into 3 major groups based on the expression of two proteins, ER and HER2 (also known as ERBB2). HER2 cancers are defined as cancers overexpressing HER2 and can be either ER-positive or ER-negative. Thus HER2neu is expressed only in a fraction of people with breast cancer.

EGF-receptor family has two proto-oncogenes: ERBB1 that codes for EGFR and ERBB2 that codes for HER. Mutation in EGFR results in adenocarcinoma of the lung, which is one of the main subtypes of non-small cell lung carcinoma.

MYC is a proto-oncogene, that is expressed in all eukaryotic cells and belongs to the immediate-early response genes, which are rapidly induced by RAS/MAPK signaling following growth factor stimulation of quiescent cells. Normally, MYC protein concentration are tightly controlled at the level of transcription, translation and protein stability. The mechanisms by which MYC promotes neoplastic cell growth may be follows:

• MYC activates the expression of many genes like D cyclins, that are involved in cell cycle progression
• MYC regulates the expression of telomerase
• MYC is one of the transcriptional factors that can act together to reprogram somatic cells into pluripotent stem cells

MYC gene is deregulated in a number of cancers such as Burkitt lymphoma, breast, colon, lung and other cancers. The functionally identical NMYC and LMYC genes are also amplified in neuroblastomas and small cell cancers of the lung, respectively.
questions.learning: 2, 3 Of the given statements, 2 and 3 are true. BRCA1 is a tumor suppressor gene and MYC is a proto-oncogene.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most commonly affected nerve after parotid surgery?
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) is the most commonly affected nerve during parotid surgery. This is because it passes directly through the parotid gland, dividing it into superficial and deep lobes. Within the gland, it forms a complex branching pattern (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical branches), making it highly vulnerable during surgical dissection. Even with careful identification and preservation, temporary or permanent facial weakness/paralysis may occur, affecting facial expressions. Hence, it is the most clinically significant and most commonly injured nerve in parotidectomy. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Auriculotemporal nerve: It lies near the gland and may be involved in Frey’s syndrome (gustatory sweating), but it is less commonly injured than the facial nerve. (C) Glossopharyngeal nerve: Located deeper and away from the parotid gland, so it is rarely affected. (D) Greater auricular nerve: It may be sacrificed during surgery causing sensory loss over the ear, but it is less commonly affected compared to the facial nerve, which is the primary nerve at risk
questions.learning: The facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) is the most commonly affected nerve during parotid surgery. This is because it passes directly through the parotid gland, dividing it into superficial and deep lobes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An infant presents with hypotonia and seizures. It was confirmed to be cerebrohepatorenal syndrome. Which of the following is accumulated in the brain in cerebrohepatorenal syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Long chain fatty acid

Cerebrohepatorenal syndrome or Zellweger's syndrome is characterized by the accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acid, abnormalities of synthesis of bile acids and a marked reduction of plasmalogens.

It occurs in individuals with a rare inherited absence of peroxisomes. It is due to mutations in genes encoding certain proteins called peroxins (involved in various steps of peroxisome biogenesis) in all tissues. They accumulate C26-C38 polyenoic acids in brain tissues and also exhibit a generalized loss of peroxisomal functions. It causes severe neurological symptoms and most patients die in the first year of life.
questions.learning: Long chain fatty acid Cerebrohepatorenal syndrome or Zellweger's syndrome is characterized by the accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acid, abnormalities of synthesis of bile acids and a marked reduction of plasmalogens.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 52-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presents with fever, cough, and haemoptysis for the last four days. On examination, he is tachypneic with reduced breath sounds on the right side. A chest CT scan reveals a nodular lesion with a halo sign in the right upper lobe. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line antifungal agent in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Voriconazole

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, which is treated with voriconazole.

Invasive aspergillosis occurs due to infection with Aspergillus species. Most cases of invasive aspergillosis involve the lungs. The clinical features include fever, cough, which may be productive, chest discomfort, hemoptysis, and shortness of breath. It is often seen in immunocompromised or debilitated people due to prolonged treatment with antibiotics, steroids, and cytotoxics. Other manifestations of Aspergillus species are allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, aspergilloma, and superficial infections of the eye, external ear, and nasal sinuses.

Diagnosis of invasive aspergillosis is made when the following findings are observed:

* A positive culture from the affected organ

* Aspergillus antigen detection of galactomannan

* Narrow, septate hyphae with branching at 45o and conidiophores

* Halo sign on CT scan

The image below shows septate hyphae with 45o branching and conidiophores:

The image below shows the halo sign on the CT scan:

Other options:

Option A: Griseofulvin is an oral antifungal used for dermatophyte infections, including onychomycosis.

Option C: Amphotericin B is the drug of choice for mucormycosis and is the gold standard for induction treatment for cryptococcal meningitis when used in combination with 5-flucytosine. It can be used as a secondary treatment for invasive aspergillosis.

Option D: Fluconazole is the drug of choice for the treatment of cryptococcosis without CNS involvement.

Pearl PF0822: Classification of fungus based on morphology

Fungi are classified into 4 types based on their morphology:

* Yeast

* Yeast-like

* Molds

* Dimorphic fungi

Yeast:

* Unicellular fungi

* Reproduces by budding

* Oval to round forms

* Example: Cryptococcus, Saccharomyces.

Yeast like:

* Unicellular fungi

* Reproduces by budding or binary fission

* Spherical or oval forms

* Pseudohyphae may be seen.

* Example: Candida, Malassezia furfur.

Molds/filamentous fungi:

* Have hyphae which may be septate or aseptate

* Aseptate or coenocytic hyphae – Rhizopus, mucor, Lichtheimia.

* Septate hyphae – Penicillium, Dermatophytes, Aspergillus, fusarium.

Dimorphic fungi

* Filamentous forms in the culture at 220C – 250C and in the environment.

* Yeast form in the culture at 370C and in tissues.

* Examples – Histoplasma capsulatum, Blastomyces dermatitidis, Coccidioides immitis, Paracoccidioides brasiliensis, Talaromyces marneffei, Sporothrix schenckii.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient involved in a severe road traffic accident is declared dead on arrival at the emergency department. Within minutes, the examining doctor observes marked stiffness of the neck, upper limbs, and lower limbs, with no preceding phase of muscle relaxation. This immediate onset of rigidity is noted during the initial examination. What is the most likely explanation for this finding?
questions.explanation: Cadaveric spasm, also known as instantaneous rigor, is a rare form of post-mortem stiffening that occurs at the exact moment of death. It bypasses the stage of primary muscular relaxation that normally precedes rigor mortis. It is typically seen in deaths involving intense physical emotion, extreme nervous tension, or violent struggle (such as a severe road accident). In this condition, the muscles that were in a state of contraction at the time of death remain rigid. Rigor mortis (Option A) typically takes 2 to 3 hours to begin and 12 hours to become fully established. Heat stiffness (Option B) occurs due to coagulation of muscle proteins at high temperatures (e.g., in fires). Cold stiffness (Option D) occurs in freezing temperatures due to the solidification of body fats. Because the rigidity was "instantaneous" and "without preceding relaxation" following a violent event, Cadaveric spasm is the most accurate forensic diagnosis

questions.text: An unvaccinated child from a migrant worker's family presents with fever, sore throat, a characteristic red blotchy skin rash, and a Bitot's spot in the right eye. What would be the appropriate management in this situation?
options: Isolate in the institution along with Vitamin A treatment
Home isolation of the child along with Vitamin A supplementation
Give MR vaccine, isolate the child and vitamin A treatment
Only Vitamin A supplement, no action needed for the rash
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Isolate in the institution along with Vitamin A treatment

The given clinical scenario of an unvaccinated child from a migrant worker's family presenting with fever, sore throat, a characteristic red blotchy skin rash which suggests measles, and a Bitot's spot in the right eye suggests deficiency of VItamin A. The appropriate management in this situation would be to isolate in the institution along with vitamin A treatment.

Vitamin A deficiency arises primarily due to inadequate amounts of vitamin A in the diet. It can present as night blindness, conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots, and keratomalacia. In later stages, it can lead to xerophthalmia. It also increases the risk of developing measles, diarrhea, and dysentery. Hence, vitamin A therapy is indicated in all patients with measles.

Treatment of Vitamin A deficiency in measles:

Age
< 6 months
6-12 months
> 1 year

Dose

50,000 IU P.O for 2 doses

100,000 IU P.O for 2 doses

200,000 IU P.O for 2 doses

Vitamin A routine supplementation dosage schedule: A total dose of 17 lakh IU is given as per the following schedule:

* 100,000 IU is given with measles at 9 months.

* 200,000 IU is given with a DPT booster at 15–18 months.

* 200,000 IU is given every 6 months (till 5 years of age).

Other options :

Option B : Home isolation of the child along with Vitamin A supplementation is not enough as Measles is a highly contagious and potentially life-threatening illness, especially for young children, pregnant women, and people with weakened immune systems.  We need to isolate the patient in institution because Measles can lead to serious complications, such as pneumonia, bronchitis, laryngitis, and encephalitis .

Option C : Administeration of MR vaccine has no role in treatment once the symptoms have appeared.

Option D : Treatment with only Vitamin A supplementation is not enough as Measles has a SAR of >90% and hence Isolation of the patient in institution is necessary to prevent its spread and complications.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 25-year-old man undergoes an elective splenectomy for hereditary spherocytosis. While ligating the splenic vessels, the surgeon preserves an artery to maintain the blood supply to the stomach. Which artery is it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Short gastric artery

During splenectomy, the splenic artery and vein are ligated. The short gastric arteries, which arise from the terminal part of the splenic artery, supply the fundus of the stomach. Care must be taken to preserve them whenever possible to prevent ischemia or necrosis of the gastric fundus, especially if collateral blood supply is limited.

Why not the other options?

• A. Splenic artery: Main artery to the spleen; it is ligated during splenectomy.
• B. Left gastroepiploic artery: Also arises from the splenic artery and supplies the greater curvature, but preservation of the short gastric arteries is specifically important for the gastric fundus.
• C. Left gastric artery: Arises from the celiac trunk and supplies the lesser curvature; it is not the vessel encountered at the splenic hilum.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following correctly represents “late expanding”, i.e. the third stage in the demographic cycle?
options: High birthrates and high death rates
Decline in death rates and decline in birthrates
Decline in death rates and rising birthrates
Low death rates and low birthrates
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decline in death rates and decline in birthrates

The demographic cycle (demographic transition) is classically divided into four stages:

1. High stationary: High birth rate + high death rate
2. Early expanding: High birth rate + declining death rate
3. Late expanding: Declining birth rate + low/declining death rate
4. Low stationary: Low birth rate + low death rate

Therefore, the third stage (late expanding) is characterized by declining death rates and declining birth rates.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Serial monitoring of serum beta hCG is required for which of the following conditions?
options: Pregnancy associated with Neural tube defects
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Molar Pregnancy

Serial monitoring of serum Beta hCG testing is done for a molar pregnancy.

Follow-up after the termination of molar pregnancy is done with serum β hCG levels. During the follow-up period, pregnancy must be avoided as it might interfere with the β hCG levels. The initial β-hCG level is obtained 48 hours after evacuation and used as a baseline. It is measured weekly till it becomes negative, and three consecutive normal values are obtained.

All patients should be followed-up for 2 years because choriocarcinoma if it occurs, develops within this period of the evacuation of the mole. Commonly, the circulating levels of βhCG decrease or becomes negative within 4 to 8 weeks post-evacuation. Once negative, the patient is usually followed up monthly for 6 months, then 3 monthly in the first year, and 6 monthly in the second year.

After beta HCG levels have become normal, subsequent conception must be avoided for one year(preferably 2 years). Pregnancy should also be avoided for 1 year after the stoppage of chemotherapy because of the teratogenic effect of drugs.

Other options:

Options A and B: Downs syndrome and Pregnancy associated with Neural tube defects require Maternal serum AFP testing.

Option D: Rh-negative pregnancy requires Coombs antibody testing.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which amongst the following can be used to treat kesari dal toxicity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin C

Vitamin C in doses of 500-1000 mg can be used for the prevention and treatment of lathyrism (kesari dal toxicity).

Lathyrism is a paralyzing disease of humans and animals. It is due to the consumption of khesari dal or Lathyrus sativus. When the husk is removed, it looks similar to red gram or Bengal gram. It is mostly consumed by poor agricultural laborers because it is relatively cheap. Lathyrism is more prevalent in parts of Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha, and Bihar. The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act in India has banned Lathyrus sativus in all forms (whole/ split/ flour).

In humans, it is referred to as neurolathyrism because it affects the nervous system. It is characterized by gradually developing spastic paralysis of the lower limbs. Beta-oxalyl amino alanine (BOAA) is the toxic compound causing this disease. It is water-soluble and can be removed by the following methods:

* Soaking pulses in hot water and discarding the water

* Overnight soaking in lime water, followed by boiling

* Parboiling - for large-scale detoxification
questions.learning: Vitamin C Vitamin C in doses of 500-1000 mg can be used for the prevention and treatment of lathyrism (kesari dal toxicity). Lathyrism is a paralyzing disease of humans and animals.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statement is false about the Ayushman Bharat-National Health Protection Mission?
options: Setting up of Health and Wellness centres
Health insurance coverage upto Rs 10 lakh per family per year
Treatment to all preexisting diseases are covered
Age appropriate health promotion at schools
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Health insurance coverage upto Rs 10 lakh per family per year

The health insurance coverage under Ayushman Bharat-National Health Protection Mission is upto 5 lakh per family per year

The primary aim of the Ayushman Bharat-National Health Protection Mission is to build a comprehensive need-based health care service.

Components: The target of the two initiatives mentioned below is to build a New India 2022.

* Creation of 1,50,000 Health and Wellness Centres- These centers will provide Comprehensive Primary Health Care (CPHC), covering both maternal and child health services and non-communicable diseases, including free essential drugs and diagnostic services.

* The second component is the National Health Protection Mission (NHPM) which provides health protection coverage to poor and vulnerable families. The Health and Wellness Centres will play a critical role in creating awareness about AB-NHPM, screening for non-communicable diseases, and follow-up of hospitalization cases among others.

* School health programs including age-appropriate health promotion, screening, supplementation of iron and folic acid tablets, health administration via health centres.

Benefits:

* The government provides health insurance coverage of up to Rs. 5,00,000 per family per year.

* All families listed in the SECC database as per the defined criteria will be covered. No cap on family size and age of members.

* Priority to a girl child, women, and senior citizens.

* Free treatment is available at all public and empaneled private hospitals in times of need.

* Covers secondary and tertiary care hospitalization.

* 1,350 medical packages covering surgery, medical and daycare treatments, cost of medicines, and diagnostics.

* All pre-existing diseases are covered. Hospitals cannot deny treatment.

* Cashless and paperless access to quality health care services.

* Hospitals will not be allowed to charge any additional money from beneficiaries for the treatment.

* Can reach out for information, assistance, complaints, and grievances to a 24X7 helpline number - 14555

questions.text: A 55-year-old woman presents with bleeding after menopause. What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic investigation to evaluate the cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation: A 55-year-old woman with postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) must always be evaluated for endometrial carcinoma. In exam settings, the most appropriate initial diagnostic investigation is considered to be an endometrial biopsy, because it provides definitive histopathological diagnosis. Endometrial biopsy is: 1. Minimally invasive 2. Can be done as an outpatient procedure 3. Highly effective in detecting endometrial hyperplasia or malignancy Although transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) is often used as a first step in clinical practice to measure endometrial thickness, it is only a screening tool. A thickness >4–5 mm requires biopsy confirmation. Therefore, in exams where ruling out cancer is emphasized, biopsy is preferred as the initial definitive test. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Ultrasound → Screening tool, not diagnostic (C) Fractional curettage → More invasive, used if biopsy inconclusive (D) CA-125 → Not suitable for diagnosis of PMB

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida woman at 12 weeks of gestation comes to the antenatal clinic for nutritional advice. Which of the following will you recommend?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Additional 300kcal in 2nd trimester

For a pregnant woman, an additional 300kcal in the 2nd trimester is recommended.

According to Williams Obstetrics, in the first trimester, energy requirements are generally the same as non-pregnant women. In the second trimester, it increases by 340 kcal and in the third, it increases by 452 kcal per day. According to ICMR (Indian Council of Medical Research), an additional intake of 300 Kcal during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy is recommended. Therefore, option A would be a better answer in this case.

Pregnancy is a period where a mother will require additional nutritional requirements to support the healthy growth and development of the fetus. According to the National Institute of Nutrition,

• Protein intake should increase by 23g per day compared to non-pregnant women
• Fat intake should be 30g per day
• Calcium intake should be 1200mg per day
• Iron intake should be 35mg per day

During lactation, ICMR recommends increasing 550 Kcal during the first six months of lactation and 400 Kcal during 7- 12 months of lactation.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An 8-year-old child has difficulty walking and getting up from a squatting position. A muscle biopsy was done and is as shown in the image. Which of the following is true about this condition?
options: It is a mitochondrial storage disorder
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Death occurs in 3rd decade

The clinical scenario and the muscle biopsy showing fatty replacement of muscle fibers are suggestive of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). Death in DMD occurs in the late teens and 20s (3rd decade).

DMD is the most common hereditary neuromuscular disease. It is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern. It is caused by a mutation in the dystrophin gene on chromosome Xp21.

Normally, the dystrophin gene codes for the large protein dystrophin. Dystrophin protein forms a rod that connects the actin filaments to the transmembrane protein dystroglycan in the muscle cell membrane. This dystrophin-glycoprotein complex thereby provides strength to the muscle and connects them to the extracellular environment.

The image given below shows the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex.

Clinical features of DMD:

• Progressive weakness, developmental delay, and intellectual impairment
• In toddlers- delayed walking, falling, toe walking, and trouble running or walking upstairs
• Calf muscular pseudohypertrophy

The image given below shows pseudohypertrophy of the calf muscles.

• Gower's sign: Patient has to use their hands and arms to walk up their own body from squatting position due to the lack of hip and thigh muscle strength due to the weakness of proximal muscles, especially of the lower limbs.

• Trendelenburg gait/hip waddle
• The patient is unable to walk by the age of 12 years and death occurs by late 20 years of age, mostly due to respiratory failure during sleep.

The complications of DMD include contractures, scoliosis, dilated cardiomyopathy, and malignant hyperthermia after anesthesia.

Diagnosis of DMD:

• Elevated serum creatine kinase levels
• Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis for the dystrophin gene
• If PCR is normal, but clinical suspicion is high, muscle biopsy (fatty replacement of muscle fibers) with dystrophin immunocytochemistry (absence of the normal sarcolemmal staining) is done.

Treatment of DMD includes glucocorticoids (prednisone or deflazacort), and multidisciplinary management. Eteplirsen and casimersen are the two new FDA-approved drugs for the treatment of DMD.

Note- The FDA has approved Vamorolone, a novel corticosteroid for the treatment of DMD. The drug offers enhanced anti-inflammatory properties and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism as well. It is potentially a safer and more effective alternative to glucocorticoids.
questions.learning: Death occurs in 3rd decade — The clinical scenario and the muscle biopsy showing fatty replacement of muscle fibers are suggestive of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: How muscle spindle able to detect the length while muscle is contracting?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nuclear bag fibers

The muscle spindle is a proprioceptive receptor that detects muscle length and the rate of change in length (stretch reflex).

Muscle spindles contain intrafusal fibers of two types:

• Nuclear bag fibers → detect dynamic changes in muscle length, especially during active contraction or rapid stretch.
• Nuclear chain fibers → detect static muscle length.

Mechanism during contraction:

• Gamma motor neurons stimulate intrafusal fibers to maintain spindle sensitivity while the muscle shortens.
• Nuclear bag fibers help the spindle continue sensing changes in muscle length even during contraction.

Other receptors:

• Golgi tendon organ senses muscle tension, not muscle length.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with recurrent sinusitis and repeated lung infections. Genetic testing shows a mutation in the CFTR gene. Which test is considered the gold standard to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sweat chloride test

The clinical scenario of a child with recurrent sinusitis and lung infections along with a mutation in the CFTR gene is highly suggestive of cystic fibrosis. Sweat chloride test is the gold standard investigation for the confirmation of the cystic fibrosis.

Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the lungs, digestive system, and other organs. It is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, which leads to the production of thick and sticky mucus. The CFTR gene is on chromosome 7q. The most common CFTR mutation is F508 deletion. Features of CF include:

* Respiratory: Chronic cough, recurrent lung infections, bronchiectasis, and nasal polyps (Option A).

* Gastrointestinal: Pancreatic insufficiency, malabsorption, meconium ileus (Option C), and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies which cause bleeding diathesis (Option D).

* Sweat gland: Elevated sweat chloride levels.

* Reproductive: Infertility in males (due to absent vas deferens) and reduced fertility in females.

* Others: CF-related diabetes (CFRD), osteoporosis, and liver disease.

Diagnostic tests:
1. Immunoreactive trypsinogen for newborn screening of cystic fibrosis.
2. Sweat chloride test: Increased chloride concentration >60 mEq/L is diagnostic.
3. Genetic testing for CFTR gene mutations is the gold standard and should be done for all cases.
4. Nasal transepithelial potential difference can be estimated in equivocal cases.

The diagnosis is confirmed if both of the following criteria are met:

1. Presence of

* Clinical symptoms affecting at least one organ system (respiratory, gastrointestinal, or genitourinary) or

* Positive newborn screening or

* A sibling with cystic fibrosis.

2. Evidence of dysfunction of the CFTR gene by

* Two positive sweat chloride test results were obtained on separate days or

* Identification of two CFTR mutations by genetic testing or

* An abnormal measurement of nasal potential difference.

Cystic fibrosis requires a multidisciplinary approach to management. The correction of the defect can be done via lumacaftor, which corrects the misfolding and reverts the mutation defect, or ivacaftor, which potentiates CFTR channel opening and stimulates ion transport. End-stage pulmonary failure requires lung transplantation.

Note: Cholestasis is seen in CF. However, this is not due to biliary atresia, which is a congenital obstruction of the biliary tree.
questions.learning: Sweat chloride test — The clinical scenario of a child with recurrent sinusitis and lung infections along with a mutation in the CFTR gene is highly suggestive of cystic fibrosis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A surgeon inadvertently injured the middle trunk of the brachial plexus while removing a Pancoast tumor. Which of the following nerve functions can be impaired?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Thoracodorsal nerve

The middle trunk of the brachial plexus is formed by the anterior ramus of C7. Knowledge of which nerves ultimately carry C7 fibers helps predict deficits when this trunk is injured (e.g., during surgery for a Pancoast tumor at the lung apex).

The thoracodorsal nerve arises from the posterior cord and carries fibers from C6–C8 (especially C7). Therefore, injury to the middle trunk (C7) can impair the thoracodorsal nerve, affecting the latissimus dorsi muscle.

Function affected: Latissimus dorsi

• Extension of the arm
• Adduction of the arm
• Medial rotation of the arm

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

• Medial pectoral nerve → arises from the medial cord (C8–T1).
• Nerve to subclavius → arises from the upper trunk (C5–C6).
• Suprascapular nerve → also arises from the upper trunk (C5–C6).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A posterior staphyloma was observed on indirect ophthalmoscopy. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A posterior staphyloma is an ectasia (outpouching) of the posterior sclera. It is most commonly seen in pathological or high myopia. Progressive elongation of the globe in myopia leads to mechanical stretching and thinning of the posterior pole, resulting in this structural deformity. Hypermetropia (Option B) involves a shorter axial length and is not associated with scleral ectasia. Primary open-angle glaucoma (Option C) causes optic nerve cupping but not global scleral thinning. Retinitis pigmentosa (Option D) is characterized by "bone-spicule" pigmentation and vessel attenuation, not staphylomas. Therefore, posterior staphyloma is a hallmark diagnostic feature of degenerative high axial myopia
questions.learning: A posterior staphyloma is an ectasia (outpouching) of the posterior sclera. It is most commonly seen in pathological or high myopia.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following prevents gastrointestinal absorption of thallium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prussian blue

Thallium poisoning is a rare but potentially fatal heavy metal intoxication. Prussian blue (ferric hexacyanoferrate) is the antidote of choice because it binds thallium in the gastrointestinal tract, interrupting its enterohepatic circulation and preventing further gastrointestinal absorption and reabsorption, thereby enhancing fecal elimination.

Why not the other options?

• A. Calcium carbonate: Used as an antacid and phosphate binder; it has no role in thallium poisoning.
• C. Penicillamine: Chelating agent used for Wilson’s disease, copper poisoning, cystinuria, and occasionally lead poisoning, but not for thallium.
• D. Potassium permanganate: Previously used as a gastric oxidizing agent in certain poisonings but has no role in preventing thallium absorption.
questions.learning: Prussian blue Thallium poisoning is a rare but potentially fatal heavy metal intoxication. Prussian blue (ferric hexacyanoferrate) is the antidote of choice because it binds thallium in the gastrointestinal tract, interrupting its enterohepatic circulation…

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the condition based on the non-contrast CT scan of a patient given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hydatid cyst

The given CT image shows a cyst in the liver with the serpent sign and areas of calcification, which are suggestive of hydatid disease.

Hydatid disease or echinococcosis is a zoonotic infection caused by the Echinococcus species of flatworms. Its life cycle consists of dogs as definitive hosts and humans as accidental intermediate hosts.

Primary hydatid cysts most commonly occur in the liver. Most patients are asymptomatic but when symptomatic, the patient presents with hepatomegaly, pain, and obstructive jaundice.

The first/initial imaging test is USG, and CT scan can be used to diagnose the condition. CT scan shows the presence of a space-occupying lesion with a smooth outline and septa. CT scan has an accuracy of 98% in the detection of hydatid cysts and high sensitivity to the detection of daughter cysts and extra-hepatic cysts.

On CT imaging, serpent sign is seen as wavy membranes within the cyst:

The USG of an active hydatid cyst shows multiple septations and a rosette or honeycomb appearance:

The ball of wool sign is seen on USG when the contents settle in the dependent portion of the cyst, as seen below:

On USG, the water-lily sign is seen in hydatid infections when there is detachment of the endocyst membrane, which results in floating membranes within the pericyst that mimic the appearance of a water lily.

The image below shows the structures present within a cyst.

Other options:

Option A: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is diagnosed with contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) or MRI. On a non-contrast CT, it appears as a low-attenuated lesion with occasional calcification. On CECT, HCC lesions show enhancement in the arterial phase and washout in the portal phase.

The following image shows the triphasic CECT of HCC:

Option B: Focal nodular hyperplasia is a benign solid lesion in the liver. Histologically, it is composed of normal liver elements, but the biliary elements are not connected to the normal biliary tree. On CECT, they exhibit homogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase of IV contrast.

The image below shows late arterial and portal venous phase CECT of focal nodular hyperplasia:

Option C: Liver abscess may be caused by various infections. It begins as a local inflammatory reaction and later develops liquefactive necrosis in the center, with an inflammatory margin.

On a non-contrast CT, it appears as an ill-defined lesion with low attenuation, as seen in the image below:

The given image shows a liver abscess with rim enhancement on CECT.
questions.learning: Hydatid cyst — The given CT image shows a cyst in the liver with the serpent sign and areas of calcification, which are suggestive of hydatid disease. Hydatid disease or echinococcosis is a zoonotic infection caused by the Echinococcus species of flatworms.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old man presents with a lesion on his left ear that has gradually increased in size over the past three months. He has a history of chronic smoking with a 20-pack-year history. His vital signs are within normal limits, and the rest of his physical examination reveals no abnormalities. Histopathological evaluation of the lesion shows keratin pearls. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Squamous cell carcinoma

The image shows a picture of cutaneous horn and it is associated with squamous cell carcinoma.

Cutaneous horn: Cutaneous horns are hard conical projections from the skin, made of compact keratin. They arise from benign, premalignant, or malignant skin lesions. Approximately 9% showed SCC pathological features at the base.

SCC is the second most common skin cancer. The primary risk factor and driving force for the development of this common cancer is UV exposure(ex: gardener), previous chronic wounds, or chemical carcinogens

Variants :

* Bowen's disease

* Erythroplasia of Queyrat

SCC initially presents as smooth nodular, verrucous, papillomatous lesions. All these lesions later ulcerate and have a characteristic everted edge and are surrounded by inflamed, indurated skin.

Keratin pearls are seen on histopathologic evaluation.

Treatment : Surgical excision is the treatment of choice. Other modalities include cautery ablation, cryotherapy, drug therapy including imiquimod, Moh’s microsurgery and Radiation therapy.

Differential:

Basal cell carcinoma

It presents as a small, slowly growing pearly nodule, often with tortuous telangiectatic vessels on its surface, rolled borders, and a central crust (nodular BCC). The occasional presence of melanin in this variant of nodular BCC (pigmented BCC) may lead to confusion with melanoma.

Most common site is the inner canthus of the eye.

Different edges of ulcers are seen as:
questions.learning: Squamous cell carcinoma — The image shows a picture of cutaneous horn and it is associated with squamous cell carcinoma. Cutaneous horn: Cutaneous horns are hard conical projections from the skin, made of compact keratin.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 32-year-old man with a psychiatric illness was started on medication 3 weeks ago. He now develops resting tremor of both hands. Which class of drugs is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Typical antipsychotics

The patient has developed a resting tremor a few weeks after starting antipsychotic therapy, which is characteristic of drug-induced parkinsonism, an extrapyramidal side effect (EPS) caused by dopamine (D₂) receptor blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway. Typical (first-generation) antipsychotics, especially high-potency agents such as haloperidol and fluphenazine, are the most common cause.

Why not the other options?

• B. SSRIs: May cause a fine postural or action tremor, but they are not a common cause of parkinsonism.
• C. Atypical antipsychotics: Can also cause EPS, but the risk is much lower than with typical antipsychotics (except risperidone and high dose paliperidone).
• D. Benzodiazepines: Cause sedation, ataxia, and dependence, but do not cause resting tremor or parkinsonism.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following take part in the formation of the wrist joint, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Distal end of ulna

The distal end of the ulna does not take part in the formation of the radiocarpal joint.

The radiocarpal joint (Wrist joint) is a synovial, biaxial, and ellipsoid joint formed by the articulation of:

• The distal end of the radius
• Articular disc of the triangular fibrocartilage
• Scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum

In the neutral position of the wrist, only the scaphoid and lunate are in contact with the radius and articular disc; the triquetrum comes into apposition with the disc only in full adduction of the wrist joint.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most common cause of proptosis in middle aged individuals?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thyroid eye disease

The most common cause of proptosis in middle age is thyroid eye disease.

Graves ophthalmopathy is one of the most serious ocular manifestations of Graves disease. Between the ages of 25 and 50, it's the leading cause of unilateral and bilateral proptosis in adults. Proptosis, eyelid retraction, restricted myopathy, and perhaps compressive optic neuropathy are clinical manifestations that could potentially be used for diagnosis.

The mechanism proposed for this is the acute precipitation of a hypothyroid state which leads to an increase in TSH secretion. This leads to stimulation of the retro-orbital fibroblasts and adipocytes which have the receptor for TSH.

An abnormal protrusion of the globe is called proptosis. Exophthalmometry measures protrusion of the apex of the cornea from the outer orbital margin (with the eyes looking straight ahead). An absolute protrusion of >20 mm or a difference of >2 mm between the two eyes is labelled as proptosis.

Option A: Cavernous hemangioma is the most common primary benign orbital tumor in adults. They are composed of large, dilated vascular channels; are more infiltrative; frequently involve deep structures; and do not spontaneously regress. On histologic examination, the mass is sharply delineated but unencapsulated with large, cavernous blood-filled vascular spaces, separated by connective tissue stroma.

Option B: The type of proptosis seen in orbital varix is non-pulsatile, intermittent, and reducible proptosis. On activities such as forward bending or lowering of the head, turning the head forcefully, hyperextension of the neck, and coughing, the varices fill up, causing proptosis, and then, they regress on shifting to a non-dependent position.

Option D: Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy in children. It is associated with mutations in the RB1 gene at chromosome 13q14.  White pupillary reflex or leukocoria is the most common presenting feature, followed by a squint which is usually convergent. Histopathology of the tumor shows small round cells with large nuclei. Microscopic features includes Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes(highly specific of retinoblastoma), Homer-Wright rosettes, pseudorosettes, and fleurettes formation. Areas of necrosis and calcification can also be seen.
questions.learning: Thyroid eye disease — The most common cause of proptosis in middle age is thyroid eye disease. Graves ophthalmopathy is one of the most serious ocular manifestations of Graves disease.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A man was brought in by the police, accused of sexual assault. The police claim that he is 19 years old, whereas his school certificate mentions 17 years, with signs of overwriting. Which of the following X-rays would be the best investigation for his age determination?
options: Medial end of clavicle, elbow, and sacrum
Medial end of clavicle, wrist, and pelvis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Medial end of clavicle, wrist, and pelvis

When age is disputed (around 17–19 years), radiological age estimation using multiple ossification centers is the most reliable approach.

Use a combination of X-rays of different skeletal sites to assess epiphyseal fusion and narrow the age range.

Best combination (as in answer):

•

Medial end of clavicle + Wrist + Pelvis

Key fusion points

• Medial end of clavicle

• Appears: 18–19 yrs
• Fuses: 20–21 yrs
• Most important for ≥18 yrs

• Wrist (distal radius & ulna)

• Fusion: 16–19 yrs
• Helps confirm near 19 yrs

• Pelvis (iliac crest, ischial tuberosity)

• Fusion: 20–21 yrs
• If not fused → <20 yrs

Not useful for 18 yrs

• Elbow → fused by \~16 yrs
• Shoulder → fused by 17–18 yrs
• Skull sutures → fuse late (40+ yrs)
• Sternum → fuse 25–60 yrs

Final takeaway: ESHA ki Wrist (watch the FMT video if you dont what that means :)
questions.learning: Medial end of clavicle, wrist, and pelvis When age is disputed (around 17–19 years), radiological age estimation using multiple ossification centers is the most reliable approach.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 55 year old female complains of lower backache. The radiographic image of her lumbosacral spine is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Osteoporosis

The radiographic image of an elderly female's lumbosacral spine shows ballooning of disc spaces, resulting in the characteristic biconcave appearance of vertebral bodies known as the 'codfish' appearance, typically seen in osteoporosis.

Osteoporosis is a common metabolic bone disease characterised by a diffuse reduction in bone density due to a decrease in bone mass.

Risk factors for osteoporosis include:

• Increasing age
• Female sex
• Alcohol
• Smoking
• Previous history of fragility fractures
• Family history of hip fracture
• Low body mass index- less than 18.5 kg/m2
• Excessive usage of glucocorticoids

Osteoporosis presents with fractures that occur without any trauma or as a result of low-impact trauma. The commonly associated fractures are fractures of the distal part of the radius (Colle's fracture), fractures of the hip, and fractures of the vertebrae. In severe cases, the fracture of vertebrae can cause kyphosis.

Radiological findings:

• A decreased vertical height of the vertebra due to collapse
• Ground glass appearance - especially in bones like pelvis
• Codfish appearance - it occurs due to bulging of the disc into the adjacent vertebral bodies so that it becomes biconcave.

DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) is the investigation of choice for the diagnosis of osteoporosis. T-score less than -2.5 in the lumbar spine, femoral neck, or total hip indicates osteoporosis.
questions.learning: Osteoporosis — The radiographic image of an elderly female's lumbosacral spine shows ballooning of disc spaces, resulting in the characteristic biconcave appearance of vertebral bodies known as the 'codfish' appearance, typically seen in osteoporosis.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient stopped alcohol consumption for 3 days and presented with irritability, disorientation, paranoid delusions, agitation, visual hallucinations, and altered sensorium. What is the likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Delirium tremens

The given clinical scenario of a patient who has not consumed alcohol for the past 3 days with disorientation, paranoid delusions, visual hallucinations, and altered sensorium is suggestive of delirium tremens.

Delirium tremens is a medical emergency that occurs during alcohol withdrawal. It is an acute condition and usually develops within 72 hours after the last drink. It has symptoms of both delirium and alcohol withdrawal. The clinical features of delirium tremens are:

* Altered sensorium with disorientation

* Perceptual distortions, most frequently tactile or visual hallucinations

* Autonomic hyperactivity with tachycardia, fever, anxiety, insomnia, hypertension. And sweating

* Fluctuating levels of psychomotor activity, ranging from agitation to lethargy

* Altered sleep-wake cycle

Other options:

Option B - Wernicke’s encephalopathy (alcoholic encephalopathy) is associated with thiamine deficiency. Alcohol abuse may lead to thiamine deficiency because of poor nutritional habits, or malabsorption. It is an acute neurological disorder characterized by:

* Global confusion

* Ocular abnormalities like horizontal nystagmus, gaze palsy, anisocoria, and sluggish pupillary reflex

* Ataxia - mainly affecting the gait

* Vestibular dysfunction

It may resolve with thiamine therapy or progress to Korsakoff's syndrome.

Option C - Korsakoff’s psychosis can follow Wernicke’s encephalopathy due to thiamine deficiency. It is a chronic amnestic syndrome that is characterized by the following clinical symptoms in an intact and responsive patient:

* Impaired mental syndrome, especially recent memory

* Anterograde amnesia

* Confabulation

Option D - Alcohol-induced psychosis is characterized by the development of auditory hallucinations or paranoid delusions in the context of a heavy drinking or alcohol withdrawal. These patients have a clear sensorium, unlike the patients having delirium tremens.

Note: Tremulousness is the first alcohol withdrawal symptom.

Pearl PF1275: Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome

Manifestation

Symptoms/signs

Onset since last drink (hours)

Tremulousness

Continuous tremor of > 8 Hz (or) Bursts of tremor activity < 8 Hz

6–8

Alcoholic hallucinosis/

Psychotic and perceptual symptoms

Visual, auditory or tactile; intact orientation; stable vital signs.

8-12

Seizures (rum fits)

Single or multiple generalized tonic-clonic

12–24

Delirium tremens

Confusion, agitation, fever, tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, impaired orientation

< 72
questions.learning: Delirium tremens — The given clinical scenario of a patient who has not consumed alcohol for the past 3 days with disorientation, paranoid delusions, visual hallucinations, and altered sensorium is suggestive of delirium tremens.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with hypertension is being treated with thiazide diuretics and now complains of fatigue. Laboratory evaluation reveals hypokalemia. Which of the following drugs can be used to prevent potassium loss in this patient?
questions.explanation: Thiazide diuretics are a common cause of hypokalemia (low potassium) because they increase the delivery of sodium to the distal tubule, which triggers the secretion of potassium into the urine. To prevent potassium loss while maintaining diuresis, a potassium-sparing diuretic can be added. Amiloride works by directly blocking the Epithelial Sodium Channels (ENaC) in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct, which reduces the driving force for potassium secretion. Furosemide (Option A) is a loop diuretic that causes even more profound potassium loss than thiazides. Acetazolamide (Option C) works in the proximal tubule and also leads to hypokalemia. Indapamide (Option D) is a thiazide-like diuretic that, similar to thiazides, causes potassium depletion. Amiloride is often used in combination with thiazides (e.g., Co-amilozide) to help maintain serum potassium levels within the normal range, preventing the fatigue and arrhythmias associated with hypokalemia
questions.learning: Thiazide diuretics are a common cause of hypokalemia (low potassium) because they increase the delivery of sodium to the distal tubule, which triggers the secretion of potassium into the urine.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which statement is incorrect regarding a child presenting with abdominal pain and bloating after consuming a milk-containing product?
options: He is likely to have a deficiency of the enzyme lactase
Steatorrhea is likely to be associated.
Skim milk will make his symptoms worse than whole milk.
Hydrogen Breath test is a sensitive test to diagnose the condition.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Steatorrhea is likely to be associated.

This child most likely has lactose intolerance, a condition caused by lactase deficiency in the brush border of the small intestine. Undigested lactose reaches the colon, where it is fermented by bacteria, producing gas and osmotic diarrhea.

Steatorrhea (fatty, greasy stools) is not a feature of isolated lactose intolerance because fat digestion and absorption remain normal. Steatorrhea suggests a disorder causing fat malabsorption, such as celiac disease, pancreatic insufficiency, or giardiasis.

Explanation of Other Options:

A. He is likely to have a deficiency of the enzyme lactase

• Lactase deficiency is the underlying cause of lactose intolerance.

C. Skim milk will make his symptoms worse than whole milk

• Skim milk contains the same amount of lactose as whole milk but lacks fat, which normally delays gastric emptying.
• Therefore, lactose reaches the intestine more rapidly, potentially worsening symptoms.

D. Hydrogen Breath Test is a sensitive test to diagnose the condition

• It is the preferred non-invasive test.
• Undigested lactose is fermented by colonic bacteria, producing hydrogen that is detected in expired air.
questions.learning: Steatorrhea is likely to be associated. This child most likely has lactose intolerance, a condition caused by lactase deficiency in the brush border of the small intestine.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to IMNCI, a 6-month-old child is said to have pneumonia if the child has fast breathing with a respiratory rate more than:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 50

Three key clinical signs are used to assess a sick child with cough or difficult breathing:

• Respiratory rate (RR): distinguishes children who have pneumonia from those who do not. Children are classified as pneumonia if:

• > 50/min RR for infants 2 months to 12 months
• > 40/min RR for children 12 months to 5 years of age

• Lower chest wall indrawing indicates severe pneumonia
• Stridor indicates those with severe pneumonia requiring hospital admission.

The following image gives the IMNCI classification for cough/difficulty in breathing in children.

Signs of severe pneumonia are :

• Not able to drink
• Persistent vomiting
• Convulsions
• Lethargic or unconscious
• Stridor in a calm child
• Severe malnutrition
questions.learning: 50 Three key clinical signs are used to assess a sick child with cough or difficult breathing: • Respiratory rate (RR): distinguishes children who have pneumonia from those who do not.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman is a sedentary worker. She is a lactating mother with a 3-month-old child. Which one among the following is the best approximation of her energy requirement in terms of kilocalories per day?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2500 kcal/day

Lactation substantially increases a woman’s energy requirements to support breast milk production. According to the ICMR/NIN Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDA), a sedentary lactating woman during the first 6 months postpartum requires approximately 2500 kcal/day.

• A. 1500 kcal/day ✗: Grossly inadequate for a lactating mother.
• B. 2250 kcal/day ✗: Lower than the recommended energy requirement during early lactation.
• C. 2500 kcal/day ✓: Appropriate energy requirement for a sedentary woman with a 3-month-old infant.
• D. 2830 kcal/day ✗: Higher than the recommended intake for a sedentary lactating woman.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presented with complaints of itching and discharges on flexure aspect of elbow and the lesions were red as shown below. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Atopic dermatitis

The presence of diffuse, erythematous, itchy plaques on the flexural aspects of the elbow of a child is suggestive of atopic dermatitis.

Atopic dermatitis is the cutaneous manifestation of atopy, characterized by a family history of asthma, allergic rhinitis, or eczema.

There is a clear genetic predisposition. A characteristic defect is an impaired epidermal barrier. In many patients a mutation in the gene encoding filaggrin (a structural protein in the stratum granulosum) is responsible.

Patients may display many immunoregulatory abnormalities, including increased IgE synthesis, increased serum IgE levels, and delayed-type hypersensitivity reactions.

The disease progresses in three phases: Infantile, childhood, and adult.

In infants, the lesions of atopic eczema most frequently start on the face but may occur anywhere on the skin surface. Often, the napkin area is relatively spared. When the child begins to crawl, the exposed surfaces, especially the extensor aspect of the knees and elbows are most involved. The lesions consist of erythema and discrete or confluent oedematous papules. The papules are intensely itchy and may become exudative and crusted as a result of rubbing. Secondary infection and lymphadenopathy are common.

From 18 to 24 months onwards (childhood phase), the sites most characteristically involved are the elbow and knee flexures, a mixture of erythema, crusting, excoriation, hyper and hypopigmentation, and warty lichenification may be seen depending on the skin type on the sides of the neck, wrists, and ankles. The sides of the neck may show reticulate pigmentation, sometimes referred to as an atopic dirty neck. The erythematous and oedematous papules tend to be replaced by lichenification.

The picture in adults is essentially similar to that in later childhood, with lichenification, especially of the flexures and hands.
questions.learning: Atopic dermatitis — The presence of diffuse, erythematous, itchy plaques on the flexural aspects of the elbow of a child is suggestive of atopic dermatitis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The tip of the uncinate is attached superiorly to which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Middle turbinate

The uncinate process is a key structure in the lateral nasal wall that forms part of the osteomeatal complex, and its superior attachment is most commonly to the middle turbinate.

·         The uncinate process is a thin, curved bone of the ethmoid

·         It helps form the medial wall of the infundibulum (drainage pathway of frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses)

·         Superior attachment variations exist (middle turbinate, lamina papyracea, skull base),

but:

o    Most common attachment = middle turbinate

Clinical significance:

·         Determines the drainage pathway of frontal sinus

·         Important landmark in FESS (Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery)

Why not other options:

·         Middle meatus: Space, not an attachment site

·         Inferior turbinate: Not related to uncinate attachment

·         Ethmoid bulla: Lies posterior to uncinate, not a superior attachment
