questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A person who had dinner at 8 pm the previous night, tested his blood glucose levels at 7 am the next morning. What is the source of blood glucose in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hepatic glycogenolysis

The source of blood glucose in a person fasting overnight for 11 hours (8 pm to 7 am) is hepatic glycogenolysis.

First stage of fasting: The fasting state begins two to four hours after the absorptive/well-fed state. In early fasting i.e; 4-18 hours after the well-fed state, the blood glucose level is maintained by hepatic glycogenolysis. The glycogen stores are sufficient for around 18 hours after a meal following which they start to deplete. So the source of blood glucose in a person fasting for 11 hours will be liver glycogenolysis.
Second stage of fasting: Gluconeogenesis begins 4–6 hours after the last meal but becomes fully active only after stores of liver glycogen are depleted (after 18 hours). They can serve as a source of glucose for up to 2 days.

Substrates for gluconeogenesis are:

• Glucogenic amino acids ( mainly alanine) from the muscle and
• Glycerol from adipose tissue

During fasting, the glucogenic amino acids are transported to the liver, transaminated into pyruvate, and converted to glucose.

Third stage of fasting:

• Lipolysis occurs in the adipose tissue due to the activity of hormone-sensitive lipase, stimulated by increased glucagon:insulin ratio.
• Free fatty acids are the source of energy in this stage and not glucose. Triacylglycerols will be hydrolyzed to fatty acids and glycerol.
• Beta oxidation of fatty acids takes place which provides acetyl CoA.
• In prolonged starvation (>3 days), acetyl CoA is converted to ketone bodies in the liver which will act as the main fuel source for skeletal and heart muscle and can meet up to 20% of the brain’s energy needs.

Final stage of fasting: After several weeks of starvation, ketone body synthesis will not take place due to depleted triacylglycerol stores. Proteins remain the only source of fuel. Protein degradation increases, and death results from a loss of heart, liver, or kidney function.

Role of insulin and glucagon:

When blood glucose falls during fasting, there is increased secretion of glucagon and decreased release of insulin. Hence glucagon:insulin ratio is increased.

Effects of increased glucagon:insulin ratio on enzymes of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis:

1. It activates glycogen phosphorylase, the key enzyme of glycogenolysis, and deactivates glycogen synthase. This causes a rapid mobilization of liver glycogen stores to be utilized as fuel.
2. It favors the synthesis of glucose-6-phosphatase which converts glucose-6-phosphate to glucose. The resulting glucose is used by red blood cells (lack mitochondria) and the brain as they are largely dependant on glucose in the fasting state.
3. Phosphoenol pyruvate carboxykinase and fructose-1, 6-bisphosphatase are induced, leading to increased gluconeogenesis.

Metabolic process
Fasting state
Fed state

Glucagon: insulin
Increased
Decreased

Gluconeogenesis
Increased
Decreased

Glycogenolysis
Increased
Decreased

Ketogenesis
Increased
Decreased

Glycogen storage
Decreased
Increased

Other options:

Option C: Muscle glycogen cannot contribute directly to plasma glucose, since muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase. So glycogen cannot be converted to glucose to be used as fuel during starvation.

Option D: In the well-fed state/ absorptive state of two to four hours after a meal, dietary glucose is the main source of fuel.

The below image shows steps of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most appropriate immediate management for a 25-year-old man involved in a road traffic accident who has a respiratory rate of 25/min, blood pressure of 80/45 mmHg, and hyper-resonance on the left side of the chest?
options: Wide bore needle insertion in the right 5th ICS
Wide bore needle insertion in the left 5th ICS followed by an intercostal drain
questions.explanation: The patient exhibits the life-threatening triad of a Tension Pneumothorax: respiratory distress (RR 25), obstructive shock (BP 80/45 mmHg), and hyper-resonance on the affected side . Tension pneumothorax occurs when a one-way valve allows air into the pleural space but not out, causing mediastinal shift and compromising venous return to the heart. Immediate decompression is mandatory. Modern ATLS guidelines recommend needle decompression at the 5th intercostal space (ICS) at the anterior axillary line, which must be immediately followed by the insertion of an intercostal chest tube. Option A is incorrect as the clinical findings are on the left side. Option C is inappropriate as the pathology involves air, not fluid. Option D is incorrect as the condition is fatal if not treated immediately. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; treatment must never be delayed for radiographic confirmation
questions.learning: The patient exhibits the life-threatening triad of a Tension Pneumothorax: respiratory distress (RR 25), obstructive shock (BP 80/45 mmHg), and hyper-resonance on the affected side .

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following vitamin deficiencies is seen in rickets?
questions.explanation: Rickets is a childhood skeletal disorder characterized by soft, weak bones, typically caused by a profound and prolonged deficiency of Vitamin D. Vitamin D is essential for the absorption of calcium and phosphorus from the gut; without it, these minerals cannot be properly deposited into the growing bone (mineralization). Vitamin A deficiency (Option A) leads to night blindness and xerophthalmia. Vitamin B (Option B) is a complex of many vitamins, whose deficiencies cause various diseases like beriberi (B1) or pellagra (B3). Vitamin C deficiency (Option C) causes scurvy, which affects collagen synthesis and leads to bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Children with rickets often present with "bow-legs," "knock-knees," and a "rachitic rosary" (swelling of the rib-cartilage junctions). Prevention involves adequate sunlight exposure and Vitamin D supplementation, which is now routinely recommended for breastfed infants

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 2-year-old male child presents with fever, hematuria, thrombocytopenia, and diarrhea for the last 3 days. What is isolated from the stool sample?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. E. Coli O157:H7

The given scenario is indicative of hemolytic uremic syndrome, and E. Coli O157:H7 is the likely causative organism.

O157: H7 is a strain of E.coli called enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC), which produces verocytotoxin or Shiga-like toxin. They produce two antigenic forms of the cytotoxic toxin known as Shiga-like toxin 1 and Shiga-like toxin 2. Shiga-like toxin 1 is identical to the Shiga toxin of Shigella dysenteriae type 1. E. coli O157:H7 has a small infective dose (around 100 bacilli) and spreads easily from child to child by the fecal-oral route.

It can cause mild non-bloody diarrhoea to hemorrhagic colitis, or a severe form of diarrhoea, with hemolytic uremic syndrome, a disease resulting in acute renal failure, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia. The most common cause of hemolytic uremic syndrome in the world is E.coli O157:H7. The most common cause of hemolytic uremic syndrome in India is Shigella dysenteriae type I.

EHEC (O157: H7) dysentery is commonly self-limiting, and management is conservative, with the mainstay being the correction of dehydration and electrolyte imbalances and other symptomatic supportive treatment such as blood transfusion in case of severe blood loss anaemia, but antibiotics are not to be used. Therefore, the treatment of HUS is primarily supportive care, which may include:

• Intravenous fluids to prevent dehydration
• Blood transfusions to correct anemia and thrombocytopenia
• Dialysis to treat kidney failure

In some cases, plasma exchange or eculizumab may be used to treat HUS. Plasma exchange is a procedure that removes harmful substances from the blood. Eculizumab is a medication that blocks the complement system, which is part of the body's immune system.

Other options:

Option A: Shigella flexneri produces Shigella enterotoxin (ShET). It enhances local vascular damage of the intestine, kidney, and brain. It is commonly implicated in reactive arthritis, also called Reiter syndrome (post-infectious arthritis).

Option B: Salmonella enteritidis is commonly implicated in osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell anemia.

Option C: Aeromonas is implicated in inflammatory diarrhoea and does not present with fever, hematuria, and thrombocytopenia.
questions.learning: Coli O157:H7 — The given scenario is indicative of hemolytic uremic syndrome, and E. Coli O157:H7 is the likely causative organism.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An infant presents to ophthalmology OPD with lacrimation and photophobia. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Congenital Glaucoma

Congenital glaucoma (buphthalmos) presents in infants with the classic triad of:

• Epiphora (lacrimation)
• Photophobia
• Blepharospasm

Key clinical features:

• Enlarged eye (buphthalmos) due to raised IOP
• Corneal edema → hazy/blue cornea (as seen in image)
• Increased corneal diameter (>12 mm)
• Optic disc cupping (late)

Developmental anomaly of trabecular meshwork → impaired aqueous drainage → ↑ IOP

Why not others:

• Congenital cataract: White pupillary reflex (leukocoria), no photophobia triad
• Ophthalmia neonatorum: Purulent discharge, not corneal haze
• Mucopolysaccharidosis: Corneal clouding but systemic features present

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent surgery for a leg ulcer due to burns. What is the mechanism by which a graft receives its nutritional supply on postoperative day 3?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inosculation

The phase of skin graft uptake in which the graft receives its nutritional supply on postoperative day 3 is known as inosculation. It is the period during which the graft is most at risk for failure.

Split skin graft survives the transplantation surgery by the following process:

• The graft survives the first 48 hours because of the imbibition (option B) of plasma from the wound bed.
• After 48 hours, fine anastomotic connections are made, which leads to the inosculation of blood.
• Neovascularization (option D ) is the process by which new blood vessels form, directly invading the graft and restoring the pink color of the skin. There is no step of diffusion (option C) in the process of graft transplantation.

Skin grafts can be broadly divided into two categories:

Split-thickness skin graft (Thiersch graft ): Partial-thickness skin grafts consisting of the epidermis and a portion of the dermis are called split-thickness skin grafts. Less dermis in the split-thickness skin graft translates into less primary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks in surface area after harvesting and before grafting) and more secondary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks during healing).

Full-thickness skin grafts (Wolfe graft) include the epidermis and entire dermis, with portions of the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles. More dermis in the full-thickness skin graft translates into more primary contraction and less secondary contraction.

Advantages of split skin graft over full-thickness skin graft:

• Large grafts can be harvested.
• In the case of thinner split-thickness grafts, the donor site heals more rapidly and can be reused in severe cases such
• as burns.
• Uptake is good.
• Meshing can be done, i.e., small splits are made in graft and any exudates collected can come out through this, improving graft takeup. It also allows the graft to expand.

Advantages of full-thickness skin graft over split skin graft:

• It has a lesser degree of post-graft contraction
• Best cosmetic appearance as they include the highest number of skin appendage elements.
questions.learning: Inosculation — The phase of skin graft uptake in which the graft receives its nutritional supply on postoperative day 3 is known as inosculation. It is the period during which the graft is most at risk for failure.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 50 -year-old woman presents with a gradual loss of visual acuity in the right eye. A CT head post-contrast reveals thickening of the the structure marked in the picture as a 'tram-track' appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Optic nerve sheath Meningioma

The CT with contrast shows optic nerve thickening and the charachteristic finding of 'tram track appearance' is seen in optic nerve meningioma.

* Axial post contrast T1 weighted image showing the optic nerve involvement and compressed by a contrast enhanced circumferential mass surrounding the optic nerve sheath (tram track sign).

* Optic nerve meningioma is benign tumor arising from the arachnoid cap cells of the optic nerve sheath.

* CT or MRI shows tram track sign.

* The tram-track sign is useful in the differentiation between optic nerve sheath meningioma and optic nerve gliomas.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with fatigue. Laboratory investigations reveal a hemoglobin level of 5.9 g/dL, increased red cell distribution width (RDW) and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), along with low serum ferritin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The laboratory findings are diagnostic for Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA). The patient has severe anemia (Hb 5.9) characterized by increased Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW), which indicates anisocytosis (variation in cell size). The biochemical hallmark of IDA is low Ferritin (depleted iron stores) and increased Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC), as the body tries to increase iron uptake. Sideroblastic anemia (Option A) would show increased ferritin and decreased TIBC. Megaloblastic anemia (Option C) is macrocystic and unrelated to these specific iron parameters. Hemolytic anemia (Option D) usually presents with increased bilirubin and reticulocytes. IDA is the most common cause of anemia worldwide, often due to nutritional deficiency or chronic blood loss (e.g., from hookworms or GI malignancy). Management involves identifying the source of loss and oral iron supplementation. Recognizing the specific pattern of low ferritin and high TIBC is critical for medical licensing examinations
questions.learning: The laboratory findings are diagnostic for Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA). The patient has severe anemia (Hb 5.9) characterized by increased Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW), which indicates anisocytosis (variation in cell size).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A young patient presented with hypoparathyroidism, absent thymus and tetany. Which of the following marked areas in the picture is defective in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3

The given clinical scenario of hypoparathyroidism, absent thymus, and tetany is suggestive of DiGeorge syndrome. It is caused by defective development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouch. In the image of pharyngeal pouches, "3" points to the thymus (derivative of 3rd pharyngeal pouch). Since in the above question, the thymus is absent, option 3 will be the most appropriate answer.

DiGeorge syndrome is a complex embryopathy that is caused by the hemizygous interstitial deletion of chromosome 22. It is characterized by multiple developmental defects, including conotruncal defects, hypoparathyroidism, and dysmorphic syndrome. It is also known as velocardiofacial syndrome (palate, facial, and cardiac defects).

It has variable presentations including Cleft palate, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia leading to T-cell deficiency, Cardiac defects, and Hypocalcemia secondary to parathyroid aplasia (CATCH-22).
questions.learning: 3 The given clinical scenario of hypoparathyroidism, absent thymus, and tetany is suggestive of DiGeorge syndrome. It is caused by defective development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouch.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 27-year-old male patient suffers trauma to his eye with vegetative matter. He now presents with a corneal ulcer, alongside hypopyon and satellite lesions. He reports mild pain with photophobia and redness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fungal keratitis

The given clinical scenario most likely describes fungal keratitis with ulceration.

A fungal corneal ulcer is usually caused by trauma with vegetative or organic matter. Signs are more pronounced than symptoms. The corneal ulcer appears dry.

Causative organisms:

* Aspergillus

* Fusarium

* Candida albicans

Signs of a fungal ulcer:

* Irregular margins of the ulcer.

* Presence of satellite lesions surrounding the ulcer.

* An immune ring (Wesseley) may be seen around the ulcer due to the deposition of the immune complexes.

* Slough is usually dry, with feathery borders surrounded by a yellow line of demarcation.

* Hypopyon may be present or absent. If present, it is thick, and immobile due to the direct invasion of the fungal hyphae into the anterior chamber.

Treatment:

* Topical drugs: These include topical natamycin, voriconazole or amphotericin B drops which are effective against Aspergillus and Fusarium. Nystatin is effective against Candida.

* Systemic drugs: Severe ulcers with hypopyon, perforation or suspected endophthalmitis might warrant the use of oral antifungal agents such as ketoconazole or voriconazole.
questions.learning: Fungal keratitis — The given clinical scenario most likely describes fungal keratitis with ulceration. A fungal corneal ulcer is usually caused by trauma with vegetative or organic matter.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old male working in a stone industry presents with breathlessness and cough. CT Chest shows calcified mediastinal lymph nodes and pulmonary nodules. He is diagnosed with silicosis. Which of the following statements are correct? 1. Silicosis typically involves lower lobes of the lung. 2. The patient is at a higher risk of developing pulmonary tuberculosis. 3. Pulmonary fibrosis after occupational exposure to silica is dose-dependent. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2 and 3 only

• 1. Silicosis typically involves lower lobes: Incorrect

• Silicosis classically produces small rounded opacities predominantly in the upper lobes.
• Hilar and mediastinal lymph-node calcification may produce the characteristic “eggshell” calcification.

• 2. Increased risk of pulmonary tuberculosis: Correct

• Silicosis significantly increases susceptibility to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
• The combination is called silicotuberculosis.

• 3. Pulmonary fibrosis is dose-dependent: Correct

• The risk and severity of silicosis correlate with the cumulative dose and duration of silica exposure.

questions.text: Which vacutainer is commonly used to collect blood samples for serum electrolyte analysis?

Need electrolyte measurement

Avoid clotting + avoid ion interference

Use heparin (green tube)

Accurate electrolyte values

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are correct about endocrine changes in normal pregnancy? 1. Increase in levels of maternal serum iodine. 2. Increase in serum levels of Corticotropin-Releasing Hormone (CRH). 3. Increase in serum levels of aldosterone. 4. Increase in serum levels of ACTH. Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

• 1. Increase in levels of maternal serum iodine. ✗

• Maternal serum iodine levels do not increase. In fact, iodine requirement increases during pregnancy due to increased renal clearance and fetal thyroid hormone production, making pregnant women more prone to iodine deficiency if intake is inadequate.

• 2. Increase in serum levels of Corticotropin-Releasing Hormone (CRH). ✓

• The placenta secretes CRH, and maternal CRH levels rise progressively throughout pregnancy, especially in the third trimester.

• 3. Increase in serum levels of aldosterone. ✓

• Activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) leads to increased aldosterone, promoting sodium and water retention and expansion of plasma volume.

• 4. Increase in serum levels of ACTH. ✓

• Placental CRH stimulates increased maternal ACTH secretion, leading to elevated cortisol levels during pregnancy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented with a fracture of the structure marked below following a road traffic accident. Which of the following symptoms will be seen in this is patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anosmia

The structure marked in the given image is the cribriform plate of the ethmoid and fracture to the cribriform plate will lead to anosmia as the olfactory nerve fibres pierce through it.

Olfactory nerves transmit olfactory information from the sensory receptors in the nasal mucosa to the brain. Damage to these fibres can disrupt this pathway, resulting in a loss of smell. A cribriform plate fracture may also lead to a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak, manifesting as clear, watery nasal discharge.

The olfactory bulbs are located just above the cribriform plate, as the first relay station for olfactory information. Trauma can cause displacement or direct injury to these bulbs, further disrupting the transmission of olfactory signals. Following trauma, inflammation or swelling can occur in the region, potentially leading to additional damage or pressure on the olfactory nerve fibres and bulbs, exacerbating the loss of smell.

Olfactory nerve fibres pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid and can lead to the spread of infection to the intracranial space and trauma can lead to CSF rhinorrhea.
questions.learning: Anosmia — The structure marked in the given image is the cribriform plate of the ethmoid and fracture to the cribriform plate will lead to anosmia as the olfactory nerve fibres pierce through it.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An individual with a history of long-term sexual exposure presents with painful genital ulcers accompanied by tender regional lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of painful genital ulcers with ragged edges and tender, often fluctuant, inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes) is classic for Chancroid, caused by the Gram-negative bacterium Haemophilus ducreyi. This infection is characteristically "painful," which helps distinguish it from other STIs. Gonorrhea (Option A) and Chlamydia (Option B) primarily cause urethritis and discharge rather than genital ulcers. Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) (Option C) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis (L1-L3) and typically presents with an initial painless ulcer followed by painful lymphadenopathy, unlike the painful primary ulcer seen in Chancroid. Syphilis (not listed) also causes a painless chancre. Microscopic examination of Chancroid exudate would show a "school of fish" or "railroad track" arrangement of bacteria. Therefore, the specific presence of painful ulcers and tender nodes points directly to Chancroid
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of painful genital ulcers with ragged edges and tender, often fluctuant, inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes) is classic for Chancroid, caused by the Gram-negative bacterium Haemophilus ducreyi.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy presents with dark-colored urine, reduced urine output, hypertension, and facial edema. His history includes a sore throat approximately two weeks earlier. Urinalysis shows albuminuria, and renal biopsy reveals enlarged, pale glomeruli with epithelial humps. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of "cola-colored" (dark) urine, edema, and hypertension in an 8-year-old following a throat infection (pharyngitis) is pathognomonic for Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN). PSGN typically occurs 1-3 weeks after a Group A Beta-hemolytic Streptococcus infection. The definitive diagnostic hallmark on electron microscopy is the presence of subepithelial humps (immune complex deposits). Nephrotic syndrome (Option C) would present with massive edema but typically lacks hypertension and hematuria. IgA nephropathy (Option D) usually presents within days of an infection ("synpharyngeal") rather than after a two-week latent period. Post-staphylococcal GN (Option A) is more common in adults with other infections. Because the history, age, and pathognomonic "humps" on biopsy all align with the classic post-infectious sequel of Streptococcus, PSGN is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of "cola-colored" (dark) urine, edema, and hypertension in an 8-year-old following a throat infection (pharyngitis) is pathognomonic for Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primi at term presented with labor pain and multiple painful vesicular lesions on her vulva. No rashes were found on other parts of the body. What will be the management of this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acyclovir and elective Cesarean section

The given clinical scenario of a primi in labor pain with multiple, painful vesicular lesions on her vulva is suggestive of an active herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection. Management involves the administration of acyclovir and elective cesarean section.

HSV infection in pregnancy can be caused by either HSV-1 or HSV-2 and transmitted by sexual contact. The infection can be primary, nonprimary, first episode, and recurrent.

HSV infection (both HSV 1 and 2) during pregnancy has a risk of vertical transmission of the infection to the fetus. The risk is higher in the primary than in the recurrent infection. The maximum risk of fetal infection is during labor, although it can occur in utero and post-natally from direct contact.

Suspicious lesions should be sent for PCR testing or culture. Antiviral treatment with acyclovir should be given if found positive. Women with no active genital lesions, asymptomatic, or those with active lesions in non-genital areas can undergo normal labor and delivery.

Management of HSV infection during pregnancy:

• Oral acyclovir or valacyclovir for primary or recurrent infections during pregnancy.
• IV acyclovir followed by oral acyclovir for severe or disseminated infection
• Oral analgesics or topical anesthetics for pain relief
• Catheterization for urinary retention

Cesarean delivery reduces the risk of vertical transmission during labor and is indicated in:

• Cases of active genital lesions - both primary and recurrent
• Prodromal symptoms like vulval itching or burning

Other options:

Option B: The presene of active lesions is a contraindication for induction of labor.

Option C: Spontaneous delivery is contraindicated in the presence of active lesions.

Option D: Even after treatment with acyclovir, normal delivery is not indicated owing to the risk of dormant viral transmission to the fetus.
questions.learning: Acyclovir and elective Cesarean section — The given clinical scenario of a primi in labor pain with multiple, painful vesicular lesions on her vulva is suggestive of an active herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 45-year-old man with a 2-year history of prediabetes presents for routine evaluation. He has gained weight over the past year and has a strong family history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. His BMI is 32 kg/m², and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Laboratory evaluation shows fasting plasma glucose of 157 mg/dL and HbA1c of 7.4%. Serum creatinine is normal, and urine testing shows no detectable albuminuria. Which of the following renal changes is most likely present at this stage of disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased glomerular filtration rate

The earliest functional change in diabetic nephropathy is glomerular hyperfiltration, characterized by an increased GFR despite normal serum creatinine and absence of albuminuria. This occurs due to afferent arteriolar dilation mediated by altered tubuloglomerular feedback: increased proximal glucose and sodium reabsorption reduces sodium delivery to the macula densa, leading to decreased afferent arteriolar resistance and increased intraglomerular capillary pressure.

This phase precedes structural damage and is potentially reversible. Persistent hyperfiltration, however, leads to glomerular injury, basement membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, and eventual microalbuminuria, marking progression of disease.

Why not other options?

A. Decreased intraglomerular capillary pressure → Incorrect; early diabetic nephropathy involves increased, not decreased pressure

B. Decreased peritubular capillary oncotic pressure → Not a defining feature of early diabetic kidney disease

C. Glomerular atrophy → Occurs in late-stage CKD, not early disease

D. Increased oncotic pressure in Bowman space → Seen when significant protein leaks into filtrate (i.e., later stages with proteinuria)
questions.learning: Increased glomerular filtration rate — The earliest functional change in diabetic nephropathy is glomerular hyperfiltration, characterized by an increased GFR despite normal serum creatinine and absence of albuminuria.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Pterygium can lead to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Astigmatism

Pterygium is a fibrovascular growth of conjunctiva extending onto the cornea that can distort corneal curvature, leading to astigmatism.

Mechanism:

• Progressive growth over cornea → mechanical traction and flattening (especially horizontal meridian)
• Causes irregular or with-the-rule astigmatism → decreased visual acuity

Why not others:

• Eye pain: Usually asymptomatic or mild irritation, not significant pain
• Macular edema: Posterior segment pathology, unrelated to pterygium
• Purulent discharge: Seen in bacterial conjunctivitis, not pterygium

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient’s ECG shows tall, peaked T waves, a widened QRS complex, and absent P waves. Which condition is most likely indicated by these findings?
questions.explanation: The ECG findings of tall, tented (peaked) T waves, a wide QRS complex, and an absent P wave are pathognomonic for severe hyperkalemia . As potassium levels rise, the initial sign is T-wave peaking. Further elevation leads to a delay in atrial conduction (loss of P wave) and delayed ventricular conduction (QRS widening), eventually resulting in a "sine wave" pattern and cardiac arrest. Bundle branch block (Option A) shows wide QRS complexes but distinct P waves and different T-wave morphology. Acute MI (Option B) typically presents with ST-segment elevation rather than the global, symmetrical peaking of T waves seen here. Ventricular ectopics (Option D) are isolated beats rather than a global rhythm change. Therefore, the progressive loss of waveforms and the specific T-wave shape identify electrolyte disturbance as the cause. Hyperkalemia is a medical emergency requiring immediate calcium gluconate for cardiac stabilization followed by insulin and glucose
questions.learning: The ECG findings of tall, tented (peaked) T waves, a wide QRS complex, and an absent P wave are pathognomonic for severe hyperkalemia . As potassium levels rise, the initial sign is T-wave peaking.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drugs used in the management of diabetes is associated with unexplained diarrhea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metformin

Correct answer is D because metformin commonly causes gastrointestinal adverse effects including diarrhea due to increased intestinal glucose utilization and altered gut motility.

| Mechanism | Effect

| --------- | ------

| ↑ intestinal motility | faster transit

| ↓ glucose absorption | osmotic effect

| ↑ bile salt malabsorption | irritation

| Altered gut microbiota | fermentation changes

This side effect is dose related and often improves with gradual dose escalation or extended-release formulations.

Metformin is a biguanide that primarily acts on the liver. Key actions:

1️⃣ ↓ Hepatic gluconeogenesis

2️⃣ ↑ Peripheral insulin sensitivity

3️⃣ ↓ Intestinal glucose absorption

Pioglitazone causes edema/weight gain. Sitagliptin is generally well tolerated. Glimepiride mainly causes hypoglycemia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate mesh for use in hernioplasty?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lightweight mesh with large pores

The most appropriate mesh used in hernioplasty is a lightweight mesh with large pores.

Lightweight meshes generally contain less material and induce a less-pronounced foreign body reaction and decreased inflammatory response, which results in better tissue incorporation, increased prosthesis compliance, and decreased patient discomfort and pain.

Meshes with large pores exhibit less inflammatory infiltrate, connective tissue, and scar bridging, which allows increased soft tissue ingrowth. They have greater elasticity and flexibility and also shrink less resulting in lesser adhesions, better tissue incorporation, and decreased patient discomfort and pain. So the best mesh type among the given options is lightweight mesh with large pores.

Meshes used in hernioplasty can be synthetic or biological depending on their composition.

Synthetic meshes are made from polypropylene, polyester, or PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene).

POLYPROPYLENE
POLYESTER
PTFE

monofilament
multifilament
solid

hydrophobic
hydrophilic
hydrophobic

PTFE meshes are hydrophobic with a lower risk of adhesion.

Biological meshes are acellular matrix materials derived from humans or animals and have lesser complications. But due to poor collagen deposition and absorption, they rapidly lose mechanical strength and hence their use is restricted to infected environments.

Note: To promote better tissue integration, a composite mesh was developed which combines the attributes of polypropylene and PTFE by layering the two substances on top of one another.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Best level of evidence as seen in research is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Meta-analysis

In evidence-based medicine (EBM), research studies are ranked according to the strength and reliability of evidence they provide. This ranking is known as the Hierarchy of Evidence. The higher the level, the more reliable the conclusions for clinical decision-making and public health guidelines.

Meta-analysis provides the highest level of evidence as it statistically combines results from multiple high-quality studies, usually randomized controlled trials, increasing power, precision, and reliability of conclusions.

Exam Pearls

⭐ Meta-analysis = highest level of research evidence

⭐ Systematic review often includes meta-analysis

⭐ RCT = gold standard for clinical trials

⭐ Observational studies have lower evidence
questions.learning: Meta-analysis — In evidence-based medicine (EBM), research studies are ranked according to the strength and reliability of evidence they provide. This ranking is known as the Hierarchy of Evidence.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A middle-aged woman presents with flank pain and painful micturition. The pain was relieved by IV analgesics given at a nearby primary healthcare centre. The patient is diagnosed with ureteric colic due to ureteric calculi. What is the best diagnostic modality in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NCCT KUB

NCCT KUB (Non-contrast CT of the kidney, ureters, and bladder) is the best diagnostic modality for the clinical evaluation of ureteric stones.

NCCT is the preferred investigation for evaluation of:

• Renal stones except for indinavir stones
• Ureteric stones
• Head injury
• Salivary gland stones
questions.learning: NCCT KUB NCCT KUB (Non-contrast CT of the kidney, ureters, and bladder) is the best diagnostic modality for the clinical evaluation of ureteric stones.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with episodic palpitations, headache, and excessive sweating, with a blood pressure of 180/100 mmHg. Laboratory evaluation shows elevated 24-hour urinary metanephrine levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of episodic palpitations, headache, and profuse sweating in a hypertensive patient is highly suggestive of a pheochromocytoma. This is a catecholamine-secreting tumor arising from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla. The measurement of 24-hour urinary metanephrines (metabolites of epinephrine and norepinephrine) is the most sensitive diagnostic test to confirm catecholamine excess. Carcinoid tumors (Option A) and carcinoid crisis (Option C) present with flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm, and are diagnosed by urinary 5-HIAA rather than metanephrines. Neuroblastoma (Option D) is a pediatric tumor that can arise in the adrenal medulla but is typically diagnosed in children by elevated dopamine metabolites (HVA/VMA) and presents differently than the adult paroxysmal symptoms seen here. Given the specific clinical symptoms and the elevation of metanephrines, pheochromocytoma is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The classic triad of episodic palpitations, headache, and profuse sweating in a hypertensive patient is highly suggestive of a pheochromocytoma. This is a catecholamine-secreting tumor arising from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a treatment option in Guillain Barre syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Steroids

Steroids are not used in the treatment of Guillain Barre syndrome (GBS).

GBS is an acute, fulminant, ascending polyradiculoneuropathy that is autoimmune in nature. GBS is caused when immune response/antibodies against external antigens like infections, vaccines, etc target similar proteins present in the person's nervous tissue. Hence the preferred treatment is to neutralize these autoantibodies using IVIg (I.V. immunoglobulins) or plasmapheresis (Option B and Option C).

GBS manifests as rapidly evolving ascending areflexic motor paralysis with or without sensory disturbance. GBS paralysis can also affect the muscles of respiration, possibly leading to death due to respiratory failure. In such cases, ventilatory support (Option D) is needed.

Note: Steroid therapy is used in Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy.
questions.learning: Steroids Steroids are not used in the treatment of Guillain Barre syndrome (GBS). GBS is an acute, fulminant, ascending polyradiculoneuropathy that is autoimmune in nature.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following fungal infection is most commonly seen in the maxillary sinus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aspergillosis

Aspergillosis and mucormycosis are the most common fungal infections that involve the maxillary sinuses.

The most common sinus affected by a fungal infection is the maxillary sinus (fungal balls), accounting for approximately 94% of the cases.
questions.learning: Aspergillosis Aspergillosis and mucormycosis are the most common fungal infections that involve the maxillary sinuses. The most common sinus affected by a fungal infection is the maxillary sinus (fungal balls), accounting for approximately 94% of the cases.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 70-year-old man with a known history of DM and HTN on regular medications presents with a history of progressively worsening dyspnoea on exertion. On examination, there is elevated JVP, positive hepatojugular reflux, crackles at the lung bases, hepatomegaly, ascites, and pedal oedema. What is your provisional diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Heart failure

The given symptoms and signs are suggestive of heart failure (Option A).

Portal hypertension (Option D) can be a result of right-sided heart failure, however, the presence of worsening dyspnea along with the other symptoms implies a primary cardiac condition.

Heart failure is a common endpoint for most chronic cardiac conditions such as hypertension, valvular heart disease, and coronary heart disease.
The symptoms of heart failure are commonly due to volume overload with pulmonary and/or systemic venous pressures.

RIGHT HEART FAILURE
LEFT HEART FAILURE

Symptoms occur due to systemic congestion
Symptoms occur due to pulmonary congestion

• Raised pulsatile JVP
• Hepatic congestion
• Tender hepatomegaly
• Pitting pedal edema
• Ascites
• Early satiety

• Shortness of breath
• Orthopnea (dyspnea that occurs within 1-2 mins of lying down)
• Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea(shortness of breath that develops after lying down for 30 mins or longer)
• Pulmonary rales

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Iodine has complex effects on thyroid function. Very high concentrations of iodine inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis and release. This effect is known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Wolff-Chaikoff effect

The Wolff–Chaikoff effect is the transient inhibition of thyroid hormone synthesis and release following exposure to large amounts of iodine. It occurs due to inhibition of iodine organification within the thyroid gland and is the basis for using potassium iodide in thyroid storm and before thyroid surgery.

Why not the other options?

• B. Jod-Basedow effect: Iodine-induced hyperthyroidism, seen in patients with autonomous thyroid tissue (e.g., multinodular goiter).
• C. Reverse Wolff–Chaikoff effect: Refers to the escape phenomenon, where the thyroid resumes normal hormone synthesis after a few days despite continued iodine exposure.
• D. Reverse Jod-Basedow effect: Not a recognized physiological phenomenon.
questions.learning: Wolff-Chaikoff effect — The Wolff–Chaikoff effect is the transient inhibition of thyroid hormone synthesis and release following exposure to large amounts of iodine.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with a growth on the lip as shown. How is the biopsy taken?
options: From the margins of the lesion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. From the margins of the lesion

For ulcerative lesions, particularly squamous cell carcinomas, a biopsy should be taken from the border or edge of the lesion, including some normal tissue, as this area contains the most diagnostically relevant proliferating cells.

| Area of ulcer | What is present

| ------------- | ---------------

| Center | Necrosis / slough

| Edge (margin) | Actively proliferating tumor cells

| Surrounding tissue | Normal epithelium

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old HIV-positive man presents with fever for 3 weeks, dry cough, and significant weight loss. He complains of retrosternal chest pain that is worse on inspiration. His chest X-ray is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia

The most likely diagnosis in a case of pneumonia in a HIV positive patient, along with the presence of fever, and non-productive cough with radiographic findings of diffuse interstitial infiltrates and symmetric perihilar involvement is Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP). A characteristic feature of PCP is retrosternal chest pain, which worsens on inspiration and is described as sharp or burning.

It is important to note that even though the incidence of PCP is the highest at CD4+ counts of <200/μL (80%), it can be seen in patients with higher counts.

Other options:

Option D: Tuberculosis (TB) should be considered as a possibility in cases of pneumonia in people living with HIV. However, the absence of hilar lymph node involvement, non-productive cough, and no extrapulmonary (pleural, pericardial, lymphatic) features are not consistent with tuberculosis.

TB can occur at any stage of HIV infection. In the early stages, pulmonary TB appears typically with upper-lobe infiltrates and cavitation. In advanced HIV infection, with CD4+ T-cell count below 200/μL, TB presents with diffuse interstitial infiltrates, minimal cavitation, pleural effusion, and lymphadenopathy. Extrapulmonary TB is fairly common in HIV, with it being documented in 40-60% of cases.

Option A: Staphylococcal pneumonia most commonly presents with a productive cough, and radiologically presents with pneumatoceles (cavitations)

Option B: Patients with pneumococcal pneumonia also present with fever, dyspnea, and productive cough. Imaging usually shows lobar involvement.

questions.text: A patient from a military background presented with rash, fever, and altered sensorium. There is also a deficiency of the membrane attacking complex. The likely cause can be:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neisseria meningitides

Neisseria meningitidis causes meningococcemia ± meningitis, presenting with fever, rash, and altered sensorium.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with hematuria, and urine microscopy reveals red blood cell casts. Based on these findings, what is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.explanation: The presence of "RBC casts" is a pathognomonic marker of glomerular disease, as it indicates that red cells are passing through the glomerulus and becoming trapped in the renal tubules. In a 10-year-old child presenting with acute hematuria, Post-streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is the most common cause of acute nephritic syndrome. It typically follows a skin or throat infection with Group A Streptococcus. Minimal change disease (Option D) is the most common cause of "nephrotic" syndrome in children but classically presents with massive proteinuria and edema without significant hematuria or RBC casts. FSGS (Option A) and MPGN (Option C) are chronic glomerular diseases that can also cause hematuria, but they are less common than PSGN in the pediatric acute setting. PSGN is usually self-limiting and characterized by low C3 complement levels. Therefore, PSGN is the most likely diagnosis for acute glomerular hematuria in this age group
questions.learning: The presence of "RBC casts" is a pathognomonic marker of glomerular disease, as it indicates that red cells are passing through the glomerulus and becoming trapped in the renal tubules.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with a history of recurrent ear infections. On otoscopic examination, the tympanic membrane is noted to be dull and retracted, with fluid visible in the middle ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Otitis media with effusion (OME)

Otitis media with effusion (OME) is characterized by non-purulent fluid in the middle ear without signs of acute infection, commonly seen in children with Eustachian tube dysfunction.\

•

Findings:

o    Dull, retracted tympanic membrane

o    Fluid level or air bubbles behind TM

o    Reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy

•

Pathophysiology:

o    Poor Eustachian tube function → negative pressure → fluid accumulation

•

Symptoms:

o    Hearing loss, ear fullness

o    Usually no fever or acute pain

Why not other options:

• ASOM: Acute pain, fever, bulging congested TM
• CSOM: Chronic discharge with TM perforation
• Otitis externa: External canal inflammation, normal TM

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient reports autophony and notices that their tympanic membranes move in sync with respiration. Which condition is most likely responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation: The symptoms of autophony (hearing one's own voice or breathing loudly in the ear) and the visualization of the tympanic membrane moving with respiration are pathognomonic for a Patulous Eustachian Tube. This condition occurs when the tube, which is normally closed at rest, remains open. One of the most common causes is significant, rapid Weight loss, which leads to the atrophy of the soft tissues (including the Ostmann fat pad) that surround and normally help keep the tube closed. Meningioma (Option A) and Multiple sclerosis (Option B) are neurological conditions that would typically present with focal deficits rather than this specific otological sign. Wegener's granulomatosis (Option D) can cause middle ear issues due to Eustachian tube blockage (serous otitis media) rather than a patulous state. Management involves staying hydrated, using nasal saline, or in severe cases, surgical interventions to narrow the tube opening. Reassuring patients that weight stabilization often improves symptoms is a key part of clinical management
questions.learning: The symptoms of autophony (hearing one's own voice or breathing loudly in the ear) and the visualization of the tympanic membrane moving with respiration are pathognomonic for a Patulous Eustachian Tube.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The second phase of saliva secretion involves:
options: Active Na+ reabsorption, passive Cl- reabsorption, passive K+ secretion, active secretion of HCO3-
Passive Na+ reabsorption, active Cl- reabsorption, passive K+ secretion, active secretion of HCO3-
Passive Na+ secretion, active Cl- reabsorption, active K+ secretion, passive secretion of HCO3-
Active Na+ reabsorption, passive Cl- reabsorption, active K+ secretion, passive secretion of HCO3-
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Active Na+ reabsorption, passive Cl- reabsorption, active K+ secretion, passive secretion of HCO3-

During the second phase of salivary secretion, Na+ is actively reabsorbed, Cl-  is reabsorbed passively, K+ is secreted actively and HCO3- is secreted passively (part of the secretion may be active as well, but among the given options, option D is the most accurate with respect to all the ions).

Salivary secretion occurs in two stages:

The first stage involves acini, which secrete ptyalin and/or mucin together with some ions. The composition of the ions is similar to that of the extra-cellular fluid.

The second stage involves the ducts. As the primary salivary secretion flows through the ducts, two active transport processes occur:

• Na+ is actively re-absorbed and K+ is actively secreted, in exchange for Na+.
• HCO3- is secreted by the ductal epithelium into the lumen of the salivary ducts. Some of this secretion occurs by passive bicarbonate exchange for Cl- and partly active secretion.

As a result, the Na+ and Cl- concentrations are lower than that of plasma, while K+ and HCO3- concentrations are higher than that of plasma.

Composition of ions:

• Under resting conditions, the Na+ and Cl- concentrations in saliva are about 15 mEq/L each, which is 1/7th to 1/10th of the plasma concentrations.
• K+ concentration is about 30 mEq/L, which is seven times higher than that of plasma.
• HCO3- concentration is 50 to 70 mEq/L, which is two to three times higher than that of the plasma.
questions.learning: Active Na+ reabsorption, passive Cl- reabsorption, active K+ secretion, passive secretion of HCO3- During the second phase of salivary secretion, Na+ is actively reabsorbed, Cl- is reabsorbed passively, K+ is secreted actively and HCO3- is secreted…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient's plasma has high levels of interferon beta. He most likely has an infection due to _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Virus

Interferon-beta is secreted during infection due to viruses.

Interferons are classified as cytokines. Interferons are non-toxic, non-antigenic and species-specific molecules. They are inactivated by proteases. They are stable at pH over 2-10, except INF-γ (labile at pH 2) and are non-dialysable and non-sedimentable.

There are three types of interferons - α, β and γ. IFN-α or leukocyte interferon is produced by leucocytes. It has antiviral activity, is immunoregulaotry and antiproliferative. IFN-β or fibroblast interferon is produced by fibroblasts and epithelial cells. It has antiviral activity and is thus increased in viral infections. It enhances MHC class 1 and NK cell activity. IFN-γ or immune interferon is produced by T-lymphocytes, NK cells . It activates macrophages, increases neutrophil function, enhances both MHC class 1 and class II expression and has anti-proliferative (anti-tumour) functions.
questions.learning: Virus Interferon-beta is secreted during infection due to viruses. Interferons are classified as cytokines.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 34-year-old multiparous woman presents with abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding during labor, and absence of fetal movements. She has a history of occasional smoking. On examination, her pulse rate is 80/min, blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg, and the abdomen feels tense on palpation. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding during labor, and a tense (couvelaire) abdomen on palpation is highly diagnostic of Abruptio Placenta. The lack of fetal movement suggests intrauterine fetal death, a common and severe complication of placental separation. Occasionally smoking and the elevated blood pressure (150/90 mmHg) are significant risk factors for this condition. Placenta previa (Option B) is classically associated with painless vaginal bleeding and a soft, non-tender uterus. Hydramnios (Option C) presents with an overdistended uterus but not acute painful bleeding. Preterm labor (Option D) involves regular contractions without the pathognomonic tenseness and severe hemorrhage seen in abruption. The combination of hypertension, smoking history, and a "wooden" or tense abdomen makes placental abruption the most probable and life-threatening diagnosis for both mother and fetus. Immediate management is required to stabilize the mother and proceed with delivery
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding during labor, and a tense (couvelaire) abdomen on palpation is highly diagnostic of Abruptio Placenta.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding and something coming out of the vagina. Her last childbirth was 10 years back. On bimanual palpation, the uterus is palpable. On examination, the cervix admits 1 finger, and the following is seen. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leiomyomatous polyp

Heavy bleeding with a mass protruding through cervix suggests a Leiomyomatous polyp.

Leiomyomatous Polyp-It is a type of submucosal fibroid that grows inside the uterine cavity and may prolapse through the cervical os.

It is a submucosal fibroid extending into uterine cavity and vagina. Adenomyoma is intramural, inversion presents with absent uterine fundus in the context of shock during labour. Mass through cervix + uterus palpable → prolapsed fibroid polyp.

Management usually includes:

• Vaginal myomectomy (polypectomy)

If multiple fibroids are present:

• Hysterectomy may be considered.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is a risk factor for progression to borderline ovarian tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nulliparity

Borderline Ovarian Tumor are epithelial tumors that show cellular proliferation and atypia but no stromal invasion. They are also called tumors of low malignant potential (LMP).

Several reproductive factors increase the risk of epithelial ovarian tumors and borderline tumors.

| Risk factor | Reason

| ----------- | ------

| Nulliparity | More ovulatory cycles

| Early menarche | Increased ovulation

| Late menopause | Prolonged estrogen exposure

| Infertility | Hormonal imbalance

| Protective factor | Mechanism

| ----------------- | ---------

| OCP use | Suppresses ovulation

| Pregnancy | Anovulation

| Breastfeeding | Reduced ovulatory cycles

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 29-year-old goes on a month-long trek across the Himalayas. Which of the following physiological adaptations would you expect to see in him at high altitudes following acclimatization? 1. Erythropoietin secretion increases 2. Tissue myoglobin decreases 3. Tissue content of cytochrome oxidase increases 4. pH of blood increases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3, 4

At high altitude, decreased atmospheric oxygen causes hypoxia, leading to several acclimatization responses to improve oxygen delivery and utilization.

Key adaptations:

• ↑ Erythropoietin (EPO) secretion → increased RBC production → improved oxygen-carrying capacity.
• ↑ Mitochondrial oxidative enzymes such as cytochrome oxidase, enhancing tissue oxygen utilization.
• Respiratory alkalosis occurs due to hyperventilation, causing an increase in blood pH initially.

Incorrect statement:

• Tissue myoglobin actually increases, not decreases, to improve oxygen storage in muscle.
questions.learning: 1, 3, 4 At high altitude, decreased atmospheric oxygen causes hypoxia, leading to several acclimatization responses to improve oxygen delivery and utilization.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient has sudden loss of vision and there is no fundus glow. There is no history of trauma, what could be the likely cause?
questions.explanation: A sudden, painless loss of vision accompanied by an absent fundus glow (loss of red reflex) is a hallmark of vitreous hemorrhage. In this condition, blood fills the vitreous cavity, obstructing the path of light and preventing the visualization of the retina. Common non-traumatic causes include proliferative diabetic retinopathy and retinal vein occlusion. Acute anterior uveitis (Option B) typically presents with pain, redness, and a constricted pupil, and the fundus glow is usually preserved unless severe inflammatory debris is present. Optic neuritis (Option C) causes sudden vision loss that is often painful with eye movement, but the fundus glow remains intact as the vitreous remains clear. Acute congestive glaucoma (Option D) is characterized by severe pain, a red eye, and a hazy cornea; while the red reflex may be diminished due to corneal edema, "loss of fundus glow" is more specifically associated with vitreous opacity. B-scan ultrasonography is the investigation of choice to evaluate the posterior segment when the fundus is obscured
questions.learning: A sudden, painless loss of vision accompanied by an absent fundus glow (loss of red reflex) is a hallmark of vitreous hemorrhage. In this condition, blood fills the vitreous cavity, obstructing the path of light and preventing the visualization of the retina.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: For a 52-year-old woman receiving radiotherapy for stage IIB carcinoma of the cervix, which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: Point B is 3 cm lateral to point A
Point A is 2 cm above the external os and 5 cm lateral to the internal uterine canal
Point A receives a dose of 7000 cGy
Point B received a dose of 6000 cGy
questions.explanation: In cervical cancer brachytherapy, Point A and Point B are critical reference points for dose calculation. Point A is defined as being 2 cm superior to the vaginal lateral fornix (external os) and 2 cm lateral (NOT 5 cm) to the uterine canal. This point represents the intersection of the ureter and the uterine artery, making its dose critical for both tumor control and safety. Statement B is therefore incorrect. Point B is indeed 3 cm lateral to Point A (total 5 cm from the midline) and represents the dose delivered to the pelvic side wall and lymph nodes (Option A). In standard protocols, Point A typically receives a cumulative curative dose of approximately 7000–8500 cGy (Option C), while Point B receives significantly less, usually around 4500–6000 cGy (Option D). Therefore, the 5 cm lateral definition for Point A is the definitively inaccurate statement
questions.learning: In cervical cancer brachytherapy, Point — A and Point B are critical reference points for dose calculation. Point A is defined as being 2 cm superior to the vaginal lateral fornix (external os) and 2 cm lateral (NOT 5 cm) to the uterine canal.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following are common problems in babies with intrauterine growth restriction delivered at term gestation? 1. Hypothermia 2. Hypoglycemia 3. Hypocalcemia Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) infants have reduced glycogen stores, diminished subcutaneous fat, and impaired metabolic adaptation, making them prone to several neonatal complications. Common metabolic problems include hypothermia, hypoglycemia, and hypocalcemia.

Why are the statements correct?

• 1. Hypothermia ✔️ – Due to decreased brown fat and reduced subcutaneous fat.
• 2. Hypoglycemia ✔️ – Due to low glycogen stores and limited gluconeogenesis.
• 3. Hypocalcemia ✔️ – Common metabolic complication in IUGR infants.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) infants have reduced glycogen stores, diminished subcutaneous fat, and impaired metabolic adaptation, making them prone to several neonatal complications.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the recommended concentration or dose of oxygen to be used during resuscitation of a full-term newborn with respiratory distress?
questions.explanation: According to the current Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP) guidelines, resuscitation of full-term infants should be initiated with room air, which contains 21% oxygen. Research has shown that room air is as effective as 100% oxygen (Option D) for resuscitation and is significantly safer, as it reduces oxidative stress and potential injury to the brain and lungs. Intermediate doses like 50% (Option B) or 70% (Option C) are not used for initial resuscitation in term babies. If the infant’s oxygen saturation (SpO2), measured via pulse oximetry, does not meet specific target levels according to the post-birth timeline, the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) can then be gradually titrated upwards using a blender. For preterm infants ( weeks), resuscitation may start at slightly higher levels (21%–30%), but for the full-term neonate described in the question, room air (21%) is the definitive standard starting point
questions.learning: According to the current Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP) guidelines, resuscitation of full-term infants should be initiated with room air, which contains 21% oxygen.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old G2A1 at 18 weeks of gestation came with complaints of draining PV for the past 4 hours. On examination, membranes are ruptured and uterine contractions present. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a short cervix <25 mm and funneling of internal os >1 cm. What is the diagnosis____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cervical incompetence

Features of Short cervix <25 mm and funneling of internal os >1 cm is seen in cervical incompetence.

Transvaginal ultrasound is the ideal method to follow up and detect cervical incompetence.

The typical history of painless rupture of membranes followed by quick delivery of a live fetus in mid-trimester is very suggestive of cervical incompetence.

Diagnosis of Cervical incompetence in the non-pregnant state:

* The internal os allows the passage of a No.6 to 8 Hegar's cervical dilator or foleys catheter filled with 1 ml water without resistance.

* Premenstrual hysterosalpingography will show the typical funneling of the internal os.

Note:

In cervical incompetence, as the number of pregnancy losses increases, the period of gestation at which the loss occurs decreases.
questions.learning: Cervical incompetence Features of Short cervix 1 cm is seen in cervical incompetence. Transvaginal ultrasound is the ideal method to follow up and detect cervical incompetence.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following does not cause hardness of water?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Calcium carbonate

Calcium carbonate does not cause hardness of water. Hardness of water is caused by bicarbonates and sulphates of calcium and magnesium.

There are two types of hardness of water:

• Temporary (carbonate) hardness is due to bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium.
• Permanent (non-carbonate) hardness is due to sulphates, chlorides and nitrates.
questions.learning: Calcium carbonate Calcium carbonate does not cause hardness of water. Hardness of water is caused by bicarbonates and sulphates of calcium and magnesium.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A neonate with bilateral cataracts, patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and “salt and pepper” retinopathy is most likely suffering from congenital rubella infection.
questions.explanation: The triad of bilateral cataracts, patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and "salt and pepper" retinopathy is diagnostic of Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS). Rubella is most dangerous when contracted during the first trimester, when maternal viremia can lead to severe developmental defects. Cataracts are the most common ocular abnormality in CRS, while PDA and pulmonary artery stenosis are the most frequent cardiac findings. Congenital CMV (Option B) usually presents with jaundice, microcephaly, and chorioretinitis rather than cataracts or heart defects. Congenital toxoplasmosis (Option C) is associated with intracranial calcifications, hydrocephalus, and chorioretinitis. Congenital varicella (Option D) presents with cicatricial skin scarring, limb hypoplasia, and microphthalmia. CRS is prevented through maternal vaccination with the live attenuated MMR vaccine, which is essential for women of childbearing age but contraindicated during pregnancy. Early identification and supportive management are crucial for minimizing long-term disability
questions.learning: The triad of bilateral cataracts, patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and "salt and pepper" retinopathy is diagnostic of Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient was brought to the hospital following a road traffic accident. He was disoriented and a CT head was taken which showed no evidence of bleed but there was raised intracranial tension. Which of the following can be used for the initial management of raised intracranial pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mannitol

Mannitol can be used for the initial management of raised intracranial pressure. It helps decrease the edema associated with the injury.

If there is an associated bleed then craniotomy and evacuation might be needed as well which depends on the clinical picture.

Initial management of raised intracranial pressure (ICP):

* Airway protection

* Positioning the head up 20–30° (reverse Trendelenburg positioning)

* A bolus of mannitol up to 1 g/kg for free water diuresis (the effect is delayed by 20 min)

* Hypertonic saline (3% or 5%)

* Maintaining fluid and electrolyte balance

* Seizure control

* Sedation using a combination of opiates and barbiturates

* Ventriculostomy and/or craniectomy may be needed for definitive decompression.

ICP normally varies between 4 and 14 mmHg. Sustained ICP levels above 20 mmHg can injure the brain. The goal of therapy in raised ICP is to maintain the ICP <20 mmHg.

Note: Cerebellar tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses medullary vasomotor and respiratory centers, classically producing Cushing’s triad. It is comprised of:

* Bradycardia

* Raised blood pressure

* Irregular respirations.
questions.learning: Mannitol Mannitol can be used for the initial management of raised intracranial pressure. It helps decrease the edema associated with the injury.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An elderly diabetic male patient presented with a black, foul-smelling discharge from the nose. On examination, a blackish necrotic mass filling the nasal cavity and eroding the septum and hard palate. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis.

Mucormycosis is an opportunistic infection caused principally by species of Rhizopus, Mucor, and Lichtheimia. The most prevalent species is Rhizopus oryzae. It commonly occurs in patients with diabetes mellitus and immunocompromised individuals.

Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is the most common form of mucormycosis. It commonly occurs in patients with diabetes mellitus. The presenting features are facial pain, numbness, loosening of teeth, conjunctival swelling, congestion, and blurry vision. When the disease spreads to the orbit, proptosis can be present. It can later spread to the brain's frontal lobe and cavernous sinus.

The local tissue destruction with blackish nasal discharge is typically seen in invasive mucormycosis. The blackish discolouration is due to direct fungal invasion causing arterial and venous thrombosis leading to gangrene.

A definitive diagnosis is done with a biopsy and histopathologic examination. It is the most sensitive and specific method. It reveals aseptate fungi with thick-walled, ribbon-like hyphae branching at right angles. Culture isolation is performed on Sabouraud agar without cycloheximide, resulting in grey-white colonies with a thick, cottony, and fluffy surface.

Among the imaging techniques used for diagnosis, MRI is more sensitive to detecting orbital and nervous involvement than CT. Contrast-enhanced MRI is the imaging technique of choice. The 1,3 beta D-glucan assay, which is helpful for the identification of most fungi, cannot be used for the diagnosis of mucormycosis.

Management: The underlying cause and risk factors should be addressed.

* Aggressive surgical debridement of involved tissues should be considered as soon as the diagnosis of any form of mucormycosis is suspected.

* Initial therapy with amphotericin B as the drug of choice.

* Posaconazole and isavuconazole are broad-spectrum azoles that can be used as step-down therapy after response to amphotericin B.

The benefit of hyperbaric oxygen has not been proven yet and is not considered a standard treatment.

Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is characterized by complications such as cavernous sinus thrombosis when advanced cases are encountered. Clinical features suggestive of cavernous sinus thrombosis are bilateral proptosis, chemosis, vision loss, and impairment of extraocular muscle function (ophthalmoplegia).

Other options:

Option A: Bacterial rhinosinusitis typically presents with purulent nasal discharge, pain, and fever, and the CT scan would show mucosal thickening without the characteristic hyperattenuation.

Option C: Allergic fungal sinusitis is an allergic reaction to the causative fungus. It is prevalent in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised hosts. There is no invasion of the sinus mucosa with fungus. It presents with sinonasal polyposis and mucin, which consists of eosinophils, Charcot-Leyden crystals, and fungal hyphae. A CT scan shows mucosal thickening with centrally hyperdense areas. (Double density sign) There is an expansion of the sinus or bone erosion due to pressure, but no fungal invasion.

Option D: Invasive aspergillosis tends to affect immunocompromised individuals and cause more aggressive symptoms like facial swelling, necrosis, and a more destructive pattern on CT.
questions.learning: Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis — The above clinical scenario is suggestive of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is an opportunistic infection caused principally by species of Rhizopus, Mucor, and Lichtheimia.

questions.text: The patency of fallopian tubes can be clinically tested by which of the following methods? 1. Sonosalpingogram 2. Hysterosalpingogram 3. CT scan 4. Laparoscopic chromotubation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 4

Assessment of fallopian tube patency is an important part of infertility evaluation.

Common methods include:

1. Sonosalpingography (SSG)

• Ultrasound-based technique using saline/contrast
•

Demonstrates spill through fallopian tubes

2. Hysterosalpingography (HSG)

•

Contrast dye injected through cervix with fluoroscopic imaging

•

Evaluates uterine cavity and tubal patency

3. Laparoscopic chromotubation

•

Gold standard test

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy presents with fever, headache, cranial nerve palsy, and hydrocephalus. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination shows low glucose, elevated protein, and predominant lymphocytosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tuberculous meningitis

Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is a subacute or chronic meningitis caused by hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to the meninges. It classically involves the basal meninges, leading to cranial nerve palsies, hydrocephalus, and vasculitis with cerebral infarction.

• The combination of fever, headache, cranial nerve palsy, hydrocephalus, and CSF findings of low glucose, high protein, and lymphocytic pleocytosis is characteristic of tuberculous meningitis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Pyogenic meningitis: Acute presentation with neutrophilic predominance, markedly elevated protein, and low glucose.
• C. Fungal meningitis: Usually occurs in immunocompromised patients and has similar CSF findings but is less commonly associated with basal meningeal involvement and cranial nerve palsies in children.
• D. Viral meningitis: Typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis but normal CSF glucose with only mildly elevated protein.
questions.learning: Tuberculous meningitis Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is a subacute or chronic meningitis caused by hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to the meninges.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A primigravida who is a known case of bronchial asthma develops PPH. Which of the following needs to be avoided in this patient?

PPH - Post partum haemorrhage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carboprost

The drug carboprost is contraindicated in patients with bronchial asthma.

Carboprost is a 15-methyl PGF2 alpha derivative used as a 2nd line drug in the treatment of PPH that is unresponsive to oxytocin. The normal dosage is 0.25mg. The maximum dose is 2mg.

Contraindications of carboprost:

Absolute
Relative

• Asthma
• Pulmonary hypertension
• Suspected amniotic fluid embolism

• Pre-eclampsia
• Renal disease
• Liver disease
• Heart disease

Other options :

Option B: Oxytocin is the first-line drug to prevent and treat PPH according to WHO guidelines. Carbetocin, which is a long-acting analogue of oxytocin, can also be used.

Option C: Mifepristone (RU486) is a progesterone antagonist, which blocks the hormonal action on the endometrium, causing the sloughing and shedding of decidua, preventing implantation.

Option D: Methyl ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertensive patients. It is given as an intramuscular injection or slow intravenous to avoid sudden hypertension.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man came with complaints of fever and chills since the last one week. On examination, tachycardia and low BP are present. Peripheral smear findings are given below. What is the likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Plasmodium falciparum

The given clinical history of fever with chills and the peripheral smear showing multiple ring forms in RBCs are suggestive of Plasmodium falciparum.

Falciparum malaria shows a very high percentage of RBCs containing ring forms. This high-level parasitemia is more often seen in Plasmodium falciparum infection than in infection by other plasmodia. After the ring forms in the peripheral blood, the rest of the erythrocytic cycle occurs in the capillaries of the brain and internal organs. So, only ring forms can be seen in the peripheral blood and not the late trophozoites and schizonts. The gametocytes of P. falciparum are crescent-shaped or “banana-shaped” (as shown below), whereas those of the other plasmodia are spherical.

Plasmodium falciparum causes malignant tertian malaria. This means that the fever has a periodicity of 48 hours corresponding to one cycle of erythrocytic schizogony. Malignant because it is a more severe and fatal type of malaria.

Major manifestations of severe falciparum malaria include unarousable coma/ cerebral malaria (failure to localize or respond appropriately to stimuli or coma persisting for >30 min after generalized convulsion), acidosis, severe normocytic normochromic anemia, renal failure, pulmonary edema, hypoglycemia, shock, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Other manifestations include hemoglobinuria, hyperparasitemia, jaundice, and extreme weakness.

The treatment of choice is artesunate given at a dose of 2.4 mg/kg stat IV, followed by 2.4 mg/kg at 12 and 24 hours, and then daily if necessary.

In Plasmodium falciparum, recrudescence can be seen which is defined as the recurrence of asexual parasitemia. It usually occurs within 8 weeks of treatment and is due to incomplete treatment or drug resistance.
