questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text:
The presence of which of the following indicates that CPR is of high quality?

1. Chest compression at a rate of 100-120/minute
2. Breathing rate of 20-25/minute
3. Depth of compression should be 5-6 cm
4. Allow chest recoil
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3, 4 only

Chest compressions at a rate of 100-120/minute, depth of compression 5-6 cm, and allowing complete chest recoil indicate high-quality CPR. The compression-to-ventilation ratio in the absence of an advanced airway should be 30:2 (30 compressions to be followed by 2 breaths). If an advanced airway (endotracheal tube or supraglottic airway device) is present, 10 breaths/minute should be given.
questions.learning: 1, 3, 4 only Chest compressions at a rate of 100-120/minute, depth of compression 5-6 cm, and allowing complete chest recoil indicate high-quality CPR.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not a true statement regarding telomerase?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Involved in DNA repair

The false statement is that telomerase is involved in DNA repair.

Telomeres are the end of chromosomal DNA. Since prokaryotic DNA is circular, it does not have free ends and hence no telomeres. Thus, telomeres are present only in eukaryotes  Telomeres have TG- rich repeats and usually do not code for any proteins. With every DNA replication during cell division, telomere shortening occurs. Once telomeres are almost negligible or non-existent in length, the DNA is unable to replicate and the cell dies. Hence, there is a limit to the number of times a cell can divide.

In stem cells and cancer cells, an enzyme telomerase having reverse transcriptase activity (RNA dependent DNA polymerase) adds telomeres to the chromosome ends, thereby preserving chromosomal length. It allows the stem cells and cancer cells to multiply a lot more number of times than a normal adult cell.
questions.learning: Involved in DNA repair — The false statement is that telomerase is involved in DNA repair. Telomeres are the end of chromosomal DNA.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient with a history of burns in his left lower limb presented to the OPD with the following. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Marjolin’s ulcer

This patient's history of burns and the image is suggestive of a Marjolin's ulcer. It is a rare and aggressive form of squamous cell carcinoma that grows from burns, scars, or poorly healing wounds. It presents as an indurated, non-tender ulcer with raised and everted edges with scarring in the surrounding area with marked fibrosis

The ulcer can spread to the lymph nodes when it reaches the normal skin. A wedge biopsy and MRI of the region involved confirm the diagnosis.

Management is by wide excision, for larger ulcers, amputation is done.
questions.learning: Marjolin’s ulcer — This patient's history of burns and the image is suggestive of a Marjolin's ulcer. It is a rare and aggressive form of squamous cell carcinoma that grows from burns, scars, or poorly healing wounds.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: New Which of the following is considered as a universal methyl group donor in various biochemical reactions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. S-Adenosyl Methionine

Methionine in the form of S-adenosyl methionine is used for various biochemical reactions and is considered the universal methyl group donor.

S-adenosyl methionine is made from methionine and ATP and the reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme methionine adenosyltransferase(MAT) which has 3 isoenzymes. MAT-1 and MAT-3 are seen in the liver whereas MAT-2 is seen in non-hepatic tissues.

Function of S-Adenosyl methionine:

1. Transmethylation reactions:

* Norepinephrine to Epinephrine

* Ethanolamine to Choline

* Acetyl serotonin to Melatonin

* Guanidinoacetate to Creatine

2.  DNA methylation

3.  Polyamine synthesis:

* Cadaverine

* Putrescine

* Spermidine

* Spermine

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a rabies free area ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lakshadweep

In the following options, Lakshadweep is a rabies-free state as water is a natural barrier to rabies.

Rabies occurs in more than 150 countries and territories. A number of carnivorous and bat species serve as natural reservoirs and dogs are the primary sources of infection.

While some countries have achieved "rabies-free" status by vigorous campaigns of elimination, in others the disease has never been introduced. A "Rabies-free"
area has been defined as one in which no case of indigenously acquired rabies has occurred in man or any animal species for 2 years.

Geographic boundaries seem to play an important role here. Water appears to be the most effective natural barrier to rabies.

In India, the Union Territory of Lakshadweep and Andaman and Nicobar islands are free of the disease. Other areas of the world include Australia, China, Taiwan, Cyprus, Iceland, Ireland, Japan, Malta, New Zealand, the U.K., and the islands of the Western Pacific.

Note: A recent initiative by the Worldwide Veterinary Services called the  'Mission Rabies Project' is ongoing in the state of Goa and other parts of India to eradicate the disease. On June 23, 2021 the state of Goa declared that they have not reported a single case of rabies in the past 3 years.
questions.learning: Lakshadweep — In the following options, Lakshadweep is a rabies-free state as water is a natural barrier to rabies. Rabies occurs in more than 150 countries and territories.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the investigation shown in the image?
questions.explanation: The image displays a classic Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP), which is a contrast-enhanced X-ray study of the urinary tract. In this modality, radiopaque contrast is injected intravenously and excreted by the kidneys, opacifying the renal calyces, pelvis, ureters, and the bladder on serial X-rays. It is traditionally used to detect stones, obstructions, or structural anomalies. A Retrograde Pyelogram (Option B) involves injecting contrast directly through a ureteric catheter from below, rather than through the bloodstream. CT Urography (Option C) provides cross-sectional, 3D reconstructed images with much higher detail than plain X-ray based IVP. Magnetic Resonance Urography (Option D) uses T2-weighted sequences without ionizing radiation and does not show real-time excretion in the same manner. Despite the rise of CT, IVP remains a useful tool for evaluating basic urinary tract anatomy and function

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A non alcoholic factory worker in a groundnut factory developed hepatocellular carcinoma. What is the most probable cause in this worker who has been working there for a long time?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aflatoxins

Aflatoxin is the most probable cause in this patient as he is working in a groundnut factory.

Aflatoxins:

* These are a type of mycotoxins produced by Aspergillus species of fungi, such as A. flavus (secretes B1) and A. parasiticus (secretes B1, B2, G1 and G2)

* Frequently present in moldy foods, like groundnuts, corn, and peas.

* These toxins are highly toxic to animals and birds, as well as to human beings.

* Known to cause hepatomas in lower animals, and carcinogenic effects in humans have also been seen.

Risk factors for HCC

* HBV, HCV, aflatoxin, alcohol

* Hereditary hemochromatosis, α1AT deficiency, Wilson disease, metabolic syndrome, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

Other options:

BOAA (Beta oxalyl amino alanine) is the toxic compound causing Lathyrism.

Sanguinarine is the toxic compound causing epidemic dropsy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: One week after having unprotected sexual intercourse, a 25-year-old male develops urethral discharge as shown in the image below. What is the most likely causative organism for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neisseria gonorrheae

The given image shows purulent urethral discharge that developed one week after unprotected sexual intercourse is suggestive of acute urethritis. The most likely causative organism for acute urethritis in males is Neisseria gonorrheae.

Purulent urethral discharge can be seen in gonorrhea caused by Neisseria gonorrhea or lymphogranuloma venerum caused by Chlamydia trachomatis.

Gonorrhea:

Gonorrhea is a disease acquired by sexual contact. The first step in infection is the infection of gonococci to the urethra or other mucosal surfaces. Pilli is involved in this adhesion. The cocci penetrate the intracellular spaces and reach subepithelial tissue by the third day of infection. The incubation period is 2-8 days. The major symptoms include urethral discharge and dysuria, usually without urinary frequency or urgency. The specific symptoms seen in males and females are as follows:

In males :

• The disease starts as acute urethritis. This infection may extend along the urethra to involve the prostate, seminal vesicles, and epididymis.
• Chronic urethritis may lead to stricture formation.
• The infection may spread to the periurethral tissues causing abscesses and multiple discharging sinuses (watercan perineum).

In females :

• The initial infection involves the cervix uteri and urethra which may extend to Bartholin glands, endometrium, and fallopian tubes.
• The vaginal mucosa is not usually affected in adults because the stratified squamous epithelium is resistant to infection by the cocci, and also because of the acidic pH of vaginal secretions.
• Pelvic inflammatory disease and salpingitis may lead to sterility.
• Rarely peritonitis may develop with perihepatic inflammation (Fitz Hugh Curtis syndrome)

Lab diagnosis:

The discharge is collected and subjected to Gram's stain which reveals gram‐negative intracellular diplococci within phagocytes. Stuart's transport medium is used. Cultures can be obtained from chocolate agar or Mueller-Hinton agar. Specifically, Thayer-Martin agar is used to isolate Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

Treatment: Ceftriaxone (250mg, IM) single-dose + azithromycin 1 g PO, single-dose, or doxycycline 100 mg PO BD for 7 days

The image below shows the Gram-stain of a urethral exudate showing typical intracellular gram-negative diplococci and pleomorphic extracellular gram-negative organisms

Non-gonococcal urethritis is caused by:

• Chlamydia trachomatis
• Ureaplasma urealyticum (Option-B)
• Mycoplasma genitalium
• Trichomonas vaginalis (Option-D)
• Herpes simplex virus (rare)
• Adenovirus
• Haemophillus vaginalis
• Mycoplasma genitalium

Other options:

Option B: Ureaplasma urealyticum is the second most common cause of non-gonococcal urethritis next to chlamydia. That is why the initial etiological agent under suspicion always remains gonorrhea.

Option C: Herpes Simplex will be associated with vesicular lesions.

Option D: Trichomonas vaginalis generally presents with a frothy discharge.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old girl is brought to you by her mother with complaints of mouth breathing. She has a flat, expressionless long face with an open mouth. On examination, a high-arched palate and crowded upper teeth are noted. The X-ray is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Adenoid hypertrophy

The clinical scenario along with the x-ray which shows enlarged adenoids suggests the diagnosis of adenoid hypertrophy.

Clinical features:

* Nasal obstruction is the most common symptom. This leads to mouth breathing. Nasal obstruction also interferes with feeding or suckling in a child. As respiration and feeding cannot take place simultaneously, a child with adenoid enlargement fails to thrive.

* Nasal discharge, sinusitis, and epistaxis.

* Bilateral conductive hearing loss and serous otitis media due to eustachian tube obstruction.

* Rhinolalia clausa - hyponasal voice.

* Adenoid facies - elongated face with a dull expression, pinched up nose, absent nasolabial crease, open mouth, prominent and crowded upper teeth.

* Sleep apnoea - chronic cases lead to hypoxemia and pulmonary vasoconstriction. This consequently leads to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

* Aprosexia - lack of concentration.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A person had undergone the serology for suspected hepatitis B infection. His/her serology shows the presence of HBs antigen and also IgG anti-HBc along with the presence of anti-HBe, while HBe antigen is negative. Which one of the following diagnoses is the correct interpretation of the serology results?
options: Chronic hepatitis B infection with active viral replication
Chronic hepatitis B infection with low viral replication
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chronic hepatitis B infection with low viral replication

The serology shows:

• HBsAg positive → Current hepatitis B infection.
• IgG anti-HBc positive → Indicates previous/current natural HBV infection; it is not produced after vaccination.
• HBeAg negative → Active viral replication is not strongly indicated.
• Anti-HBe positive → Suggests seroconversion from HBeAg to anti-HBe, usually associated with reduced viral replication.

Therefore, the pattern is most consistent with chronic HBV infection with low viral replication.

Why not the other options?

• (a) Active hepatitis B infection: Too nonspecific. The presence of HBsAg confirms infection, but the HBeAg-negative/anti-HBe-positive pattern specifically suggests lower replication.
• (b) Chronic HBV with active viral replication: Typically associated with HBeAg positivity and high HBV DNA. However, HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis can occasionally have active replication due to precore/core promoter mutations, so HBV DNA is required for definitive assessment.
• (c) Chronic HBV with low viral replication — Correct: HBsAg +, IgG anti-HBc +, HBeAg −, anti-HBe + is the classic exam pattern.
• (d) Recovery/vaccination: Recovery requires HBsAg negativity and anti-HBs positivity. Vaccination produces anti-HBs only, without anti-HBc.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Based on arterial blood gas results showing a pH of 7.12, pCO2 of 50 mmHg, and HCO3- of 28 mmol/L, what is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.explanation: To interpret the ABG, we first assess the pH (7.12), which is below the normal range (7.35–7.45), indicating acidosis. Next, we evaluate the PaCO₂ (50 mmHg). Since it is elevated (normal 35–45 mmHg) and moves in the same direction as the pH change, the primary disorder is respiratory acidosis. The bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) level is 28 mmol/L, which is slightly above the normal range (22–26 mmol/L). This increase indicates renal (metabolic) compensation, as the kidneys retain bicarbonate to counteract the excess CO₂. However, because the pH remains significantly acidic, the compensation is partial, not complete. Options B and D are incorrect because the primary abnormality is elevated PaCO₂, not bicarbonate, confirming a respiratory rather than metabolic disorder. Option C is incorrect because the pH clearly indicates acidosis, not alkalosis
questions.learning: To interpret the ABG, we first assess the pH (7.12), which is below the normal range (7.35–7.45), indicating acidosis. Next, we evaluate the PaCO₂ (50 mmHg).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with fever, cough, coryza, and a characteristic erythematous rash suggestive of measles. Regarding measles infection, which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: Period of communicability is 14 days after rash
questions.explanation: Measles is a highly contagious viral illness. The inaccurate statement is Option C; the period of communicability is actually from 4 days before to 4 days after the appearance of the rash, not 14 days. Statement A is accurate; the incubation period (from exposure to rash) is approximately 14 days. Statement B is accurate; the Edmonston-Zagreb strain is the standard live-attenuated virus used in the measles vaccine in India. Statement D is accurate; measles is transmitted through large and small respiratory droplets and can remain airborne for up to two hours. Clinically, measles is characterized by the "3 Cs": Cough, Coryza, and Conjunctivitis, followed by pathognomonic Koplik spots and a maculopapular rash that starts behind the ears. Vitamin A supplementation is a critical adjunct in treatment to reduce complications like pneumonia and blindness
questions.learning: Measles is a highly contagious viral illness. The inaccurate statement is Option C; the period of communicability is actually from 4 days before to 4 days after the appearance of the rash, not 14 days.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All are true about intestinal transplantation except ______.
options: Most of the grafts are multi-visceral grafts.
It is not widely used due to vigorous rejection reactions.
The most dangerous complication is sepsis.
The most common indication is the ischemia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Most of the grafts are multi-visceral grafts.

Multivisceral grafts are rarely used in intestinal transplantation. The most common intestinal graft is small bowel graft, with or without the colon or a combined liver and small bowel graft.

All the other statements are correct.

Small bowel transplantation is the final treatment option after the outcome of reconstruction and lengthening procedures are unsatisfactory.

The small bowel transplant is highly immunogenic since it contains a large amount of gut-associated lymphoid tissue, donor dendritic cells, and macrophages. Acute rejection has been reported in 56–75% of patients, with small bowel transplant limiting the overall survival to only one-third of recipients.
questions.learning: Most of the grafts are multi-visceral grafts. Multivisceral grafts are rarely used in intestinal transplantation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A teenage girl presented with irregular cycles and increased facial hair. Her ovaries showed increased volume. Which of the following are used in the first line treatment?

1. Laparoscopic ovarian drilling
2. Anti-androgens
3. Lifestyle modifications
4. Combined oral contraceptive pills
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2,3,4

This patient's irregular menstrual cycles, increased facial hair (signifying clinical hyperandrogenism), and increased ovarian volume are suggestive of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). Anti-androgens, lifestyle modifications, and combined oral contraceptives (2, 3, and 4) constitue first-line treatment modalities for this condition. Laparoscopic drilling is a surgical procedure done when medical therapy fails.

PCOS is an endocrinopathy seen in women of reproductive age, affecting multiple systems. Rotterdam criteria is used to diagnose PCOD. The presence of two of the three components of this criteria establishes the diagnosis:

• Oligo/amenorrhoea, anovulation, infertility
• Hirsutism/acne
• Ultrasound findings:

• Enlarged ovaries with ovarian volume will be more than 10 mm3
• 12 or more small follicles each of 2-9 mm in size placed peripherally

Ultrasound image given below shows an enlarged ovary seen in PCOS with multiple follicles in the periphery.

Treatment of PCOD:

• Weight reduction alone is beneficial in mild hirsutism.
• Lifestyle changes, such as smoking cessation, are recommended.
• Fourth-generation oral contraceptive pills (OCP) containing ethinyl estradiol and drospirenone are used for treating menstrual abnormalities, reducing acne, and hirsutism.
• OCP with cyproterone acetate is prescribed for PCOS patients with hirsutism.
• Patients with PCOD are prone to developing insulin resistance, which can be controlled with metformin. Acarbosecan be used as an alternative if metformin is contraindicated.
• Infertility in PCOD patients is treated with clomiphene as the first-line drug for inducing ovulation. Dexamethasone is used in combination to improve fertility rates. Letrozole is used off-label in clomiphene-resistant cases.

Surgical options include laparoscopic ovarian drilling or puncture of not more than four cysts in each ovary. This is done either by laser or by unipolar electrocautery. It restores endocrine levels and improves fertility. Surgery is indicated only if:

• Medical therapy fails
• Hyperstimulation occurs
• Infertile women
• Previous pregnancy losses
questions.learning: 2,3,4 This patient's irregular menstrual cycles, increased facial hair (signifying clinical hyperandrogenism), and increased ovarian volume are suggestive of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Statement 1: Histopathological examination of a patient with Flaccid bulla and painful erosions showing suprabasal blister and inflammatory infiltrate in the blister cleft. Statement 2: The row of tombstones appearance is diagnostic of Pemphigus vulgaris.
options: Statement 1 is false and Statement 2 is true
Statement 1 is true and Statement 2 is false
Both the statements are true but 2 is not the conclusion of 1
Both the statements are true but 2 is the conclusion of 1
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Both the statements are true but 2 is not the conclusion of 1

Both statements 1 and 2 are correct but statement 2 is not the conclusion of statement 1. Statement 2 is not the conclusion of statement 1 because DIF is used for a definitive diagnosis.

Pemphigus vulgaris is a chronic immunobullous disorder characterized by the presence of antibodies against desmosomal proteins expressed in the skin and mucosa. In the skin, desmoglein 1 is mostly seen in all layers, while desmoglein 3 is more in the lower layers. In the oral mucosa, desmoglein 3 is seen in all layers and desmoglein 1 is present in lower layers.

Clinically, the patients present with ill‐defined, irregular, slow-to-heal oral lesions and erosions. Flaccid blisters filled with clear fluid may arise on normal skin or an erythematous base. The rupture of such blisters produces painful erosions and heals without scarring. Lesions may also involve the mucosa of the conjunctiva, nasopharynx, larynx, esophagus, urethra, vulva, or cervix.

Nikolsky's sign is positive which is elicited by applying firm tangential sliding pressure with a finger on lesional or perilesional skin. This leads to the separation of the normal‐looking epidermis from the dermis, producing erosion.

Direct immunofluorescence is considered the most accurate confirmatory test of this condition. It shows intercellular IgG and C3 deposition on the surface of keratinocytes throughout the epidermis in normal, perilesional skin, in a characteristic fishnet/chickenwire appearance as seen below.

Histology shows a suprabasal split of the epidermis with a characteristic row of tombstone appearance as seen below.

Other investigations include a Tzanck smear showing acantholytic cells. Anti-Dsg ELISA assays can be used to monitor the disease activity.

Systemic corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment for controlling the disease, improving the quality of life and reducing disease activity.
questions.learning: Both the statements are true but 2 is not the conclusion of 1 Both statements 1 and 2 are correct but statement 2 is not the conclusion of statement 1.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which layer is involved in blister formation in a superficial partial thickness burn?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Papillary dermis

The papillary dermis is involved in blister formation in a superficial partial-thickness burn.

First-degree burns involve only the epidermis, with pain, redness, and mild swelling.

Second-degree (partial thickness) burns involve the epidermis and some parts of the dermis (also known as partial-thickness burns). Further divided into:

• Superficial second-degree burns - involves the upper part of the dermis (papillary) and shows pain, blisters, and severe swelling.
• Deep second-degree burns - extends up to the reticular layer of the dermis and appears more pale and mottled, does not blanch to touch, but remains painful to pinprick.

Third-degree or full-thickness burns involve the full thickness of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue.

Fourth-degree burns involve deep structures such as muscle and bone.
questions.learning: Papillary dermis — The papillary dermis is involved in blister formation in a superficial partial-thickness burn. First-degree burns involve only the epidermis, with pain, redness, and mild swelling.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: Consider the following pleural fluid analysis: • pH: 7.6 • Pleural fluid protein: 0.5 g/dL • Serum total protein: 6.5 g/dL • Pleural fluid LDH: 100 U/L • Serum LDH: 300 U/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Myxedema

The pleural fluid analysis is consistent with a transudative pleural effusion according to Light’s criteria:

• Pleural fluid protein/Serum protein = 0.5/6.5 = 0.08 (<0.5)
• Pleural fluid LDH/Serum LDH = 100/300 = 0.33 (<0.6)
• Pleural fluid LDH is not greater than two-thirds the upper limit of normal serum LDH.

These findings indicate a transudative effusion. Myxedema (severe hypothyroidism) is a recognized cause of transudative pleural effusion due to increased capillary permeability and impaired lymphatic drainage.

Why not the other options?

• A. Pancreatitis: Produces an exudative pleural effusion with very high amylase levels.
• C. Sarcoidosis: Rarely causes pleural effusion, but when present it is exudative.
• D. Rheumatoid arthritis: Causes a characteristic exudative effusion with low pH (<7.2), low glucose, and high LDH.

| Transudative Effusion | Exudative Effusion

| --------------------- | ------------------

| Heart failure | Pneumonia (parapneumonic)

| Cirrhosis | Tuberculosis

| Nephrotic syndrome | Malignancy

| Myxedema (hypothyroidism) | Pancreatitis

| Hypoalbuminemia | Rheumatoid arthritis

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 20-year-old patient presented to the clinic with a history of malabsorption, diarrhea, and poor appetite. Duodenal biopsy of the patient showed crypt hyperplasia, villi atrophy, and CD8+ cells in lamina propria. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Celiac disease

The clinical presentation and the histopathological findings are suggestive of celiac disease.

Celiac disease is an autoimmune gluten-induced enteropathy where HLA DQ2 and DQ8 are expressed. In the small intestine, peptides of gluten are presented to helper T cells which mediate mucosal inflammation. Antiendomysial and anti-tTG antibodies are found in serological studies.

Clinically, malabsorption syndrome with diarrhea, abdominal pain, and marked weight loss is seen along with chronic refractory anemia. Dermatitis herpetiformis is seen in 10% of patients with celiac disease. Microscopic findings show villi atrophy, villi flattening, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial T lymphocytes (IEL).

Option A: Environmental enteropathy / tropical sprue is seen in tropical areas with poor sanitation. It is believed to be caused by one or more infectious agents that respond to antibiotics. Mucosa shows variable villous atrophy.

Option C: Whipple's disease is a multisystemic disease caused by T.whipplei. Small intestinal biopsy shows PAS-positive macrophages.
questions.learning: Celiac disease — The clinical presentation and the histopathological findings are suggestive of celiac disease. Celiac disease is an autoimmune gluten-induced enteropathy where HLA DQ2 and DQ8 are expressed.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In comparison to Ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease is associated with
options: Continuous lesions rather than segmented lesions
Less likely to present with daily hematochezia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Less likely to present with daily hematochezia

Patients with Crohn's disease are less likely to present with daily hematochezia compared to patients with ulcerative colitis.

CD is characterized by acute or chronic inflammation of the bowel. The most commonly involved site is the terminal ileum because of which patients present with diarrhea and right lower quadrant pain. Extensive inflammation can result in malabsorption and steatorrhea.

Blood investigations may reveal anemia, elevated ESR and CRP. Fecal calprotectin and lactoferrin levels are used to rule out irritable bowel syndrome and as a marker of ileo-colonic inflammation. A colonoscopy is done as part of the evaluation. It shows characteristic skip lesions and a cobblestone appearance. Biopsy shows transmural inflammation with non-caseating granulomas.

Serological markers that are usually positive in patients with CD include the anti–Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibody (ASCA). Other positive markers (however, with low sensitivity) include antibodies to bacterial proteins (OmpC and I2), flagellin, and bacterial carbohydrates.
questions.learning: Less likely to present with daily hematochezia Patients with Crohn's disease are less likely to present with daily hematochezia compared to patients with ulcerative colitis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 2-year-old was brought to the emergency department with difficulty swallowing for the last few hours. The X-ray is given below. Which is the next best step to manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Esophagoscopy

The clinical picture of the child presenting with difficulty in swallowing and the given x-rays are suggestive of a foreign body lodged in the esophagus, most likely a coin/disc battery.

The given x-rays are anteroposterior and lateral views of the chest and neck. Coins, disk batteries, and small toy items are commonly ingested by children.

The flat surface of a coin in the esophagus is seen on the anteroposterior view (AP view) i.e; they are oriented in the coronal plane. The edge is seen on the lateral view. While coins in the trachea lie in the sagittal plane, those in the oesophagus typically lie in the coronal plane.

Presenting symptoms are choking, gagging, and coughing followed by excessive salivation, dysphagia, food refusal, vomiting, or pain in the neck and throat. Respiratory distress is seen if the esophageal foreign body impinges on the larynx or tracheal wall.

Imaging with PA and lateral views of the chest and abdomen should be done.

Treatment includes the removal of the foreign body by esophagoscopy.

Pearl PF0104: Acute stridor/ Noisy breathing

Stridor indicates an upper airway problem. Look for a history of foreign body aspiration and signs of toxicity.

Important differentials:

Condition
Findings

Croup

Non-toxic, viral prodrome, barking cough

X-ray neck shows steeple sign

Epiglottitis

Toxic child, drooling saliva

Lateral X-ray neck shows thumb sign

Diphtheria
Cervical lymph nodes (bull neck), dirty grey/ white membrane, and un-immunized

Foreign body aspiration
Choking, decreased air entry, unilateral hyperinflation
questions.learning: Esophagoscopy — The clinical picture of the child presenting with difficulty in swallowing and the given x-rays are suggestive of a foreign body lodged in the esophagus, most likely a coin/disc battery.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All are features of postganglionic lesions, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Positive histamine test

A postganglionic lesion refers to nerve damage distal to the dorsal root ganglion (DRG), affecting the peripheral nerve after the sensory neuron cell body.

Features of postganglionic lesions:

• Occur distal to the dorsal root ganglion.
• Better prognosis because peripheral nerves can regenerate.
• Surgical repair may be possible in cases of nerve injury.

Histamine test:

• Used to assess integrity of sensory nerve fibers.
• In postganglionic lesions, the axon reflex is lost, so the flare response is absent → negative histamine test.

Therefore, positive histamine test is not seen in postganglionic lesions, making it the incorrect statement.
questions.learning: Positive histamine test — A postganglionic lesion refers to nerve damage distal to the dorsal root ganglion (DRG), affecting the peripheral nerve after the sensory neuron cell body.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A young male developed 5 episodes of loose stools 2 hours after eating in a restaurant. He is afebrile and has mild dehydration. What should be the treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Only ORS

It is a case of acute diarrhea in an afebrile, stable patient which can be managed with ORS alone.

Management of diarrhea:

• Mild-moderate dehydration - ORS.
• Severe dehydration- IV fluids are given.
• Afebrile patient - No antibiotics are given.
• Febrile patient - empirical antibiotics. If only bacterial etiology is suspected, ciprofloxacin is given. If giardiasis is suspected, metronidazole or tinidazole are recommended.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22 year old female presents within 8 hours of having sexual intercourse and asking for emergency contraception.She says she doesn't want multiple pills and wants just one pill. What will be your advice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg

The patient asks for emergency contraception and the drug used is Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg.

Levonorgestrel (LNG):

Prostinar tablet contains 0.75 mg LNG. One tablet should be taken within 72 h of unprotected intercourse and another 12 h later. Alternately, two tablets can be taken as a single dose. The failure rate is 1.1%. The tablets can be offered up to 120 h but their efficacy decreases with the longer coital-drug interval. LNG prevents ovulation and causes desynchronization of endometrium through its receptors (luteal phase deficiency). The period may come earlier or be delayed.

Side effects are those of progestogens. The hormone is not teratogenic in case pregnancy does occur but the risk of ectopic pregnancy remains.

Advantages:

* It has no estrogen and its associated side effects

* It can be offered to hypertensive, cardiac, and diabetic women

* It can be offered to a lactating woman

* It can be given as late as 120 hours after the unprotected intercourse

* Single-dose therapy is an advantage

Contraindicated in liver disease, contains lactate, and with an allergy to galactose. The drug is also contraindicated in a woman with a history of thrombophlebitis and migraine.

Pearl PF1657: Hormonal contraceptives

Oral pills:

* Combined oral contraceptive pills (COC)

* Mala D - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate

* Mala N - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate (Govt. supply, free of cost)

* Progesterone only pills (POP) - suitable for lactating women

* Norethisterone 350 μg

* Norgestrel 75 μg

* Levonorgestrel (LNG) 30 μg

* Once a month or long-acting pills - highly disappointing results

* Quinestrol (long-acting estrogen) + short-acting progesterone

* Gossypol - male pill : Cottonseed derivative and causes azoospermia and severe oligospermia

* Post-coital pills or interceptive

* Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg, 2 doses, 12 hours apart

* Mifepristone 10-600 mg

* Ulipristal 30 mg, within 5 days of intercourse

* Centchroman 60 mg, 2 tablets, within 24 hrs of intercourse

* GnRH agonists

* CuT IUCD, inserted within 5 days

Injectable contraceptives

* Progesterone only injectables

* DMPA 150 mg IM every 3 months

* NET-EN 200 mg IM every 2 months

* Combined injectables

* Cyclofem - DMPA 25 mg + Estradiol cypionate 5 mg

* Mesigyna - NET-EN 50 mg  + Estradiol valerate 5 mg

Subdermal implants

* Norplant I - Levonorgestrel 35 mg

* Norplant II or Jadelle - 2 rods with levonorgestrel 70 mg in each and released at a rate of 50 μg/day

Others

* Hormonal IUCD - Mirena which contains LNG 52 mg with release rate of 20 μg/day

* Orthoevra patch - Norelgestomin + Ethinyl estradiol weekly for 3 weeks, then patch free for 1 week

* Vaginal ring or Nuvaring - Etonogestrel + ethinyl estradiol daily release, use for 3 weeks with withdrawal for 1 week

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A child under 5 years of age presents with a painless, soft, and fluctuant mass on the lateral side of the neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A painless, soft, fluctuating mass on the lateral side of the neck in a child under 5 years is a classic description of a Cystic hygroma (lymphangioma). These are congenital malformations of the lymphatic system, most commonly found in the posterior triangle of the neck. They characteristically transilluminate brilliantly. A thyroglossal cyst (Option A) is a midline mass that moves with tongue protrusion. Cervical lymphadenopathy (Option C) is usually firmer and often associated with a history of infection or fever. A ranula (Option D) is a mucous extravasation cyst found on the floor of the mouth, though a "plunging" ranula can present in the neck. Cystic hygromas can occasionally grow rapidly if they bleed internally or become infected, potentially causing airway obstruction. While some small lesions may regress, the primary treatment for symptomatic or large cystic hygromas is surgical excision or sclerotherapy using agents like OK-432 or bleomycin to shrink the cysts
questions.learning: A painless, soft, fluctuating mass on the lateral side of the neck in a child under 5 years is a classic description of a Cystic hygroma (lymphangioma).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old male patient came to the outpatient department with complaints of hematuria. A 2x2 cm bladder mass is seen which is a low-grade transitional cell carcinoma. Which among the following is the ideal management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Transurethral resection of the tumour

This patient with low-grade 2x2 cm bladder cancer is likely to have non-muscle invasive bladder carcinoma (NMIBC) should undergo transurethral resection of the bladder tumor (TURBT) for accurate staging purposes.

Bladder cancer is graded (G1/2/3) based on level of differentiation. NMIBC includes stages Tis (in-situ), Ta (non-invasive papillary carcinoma), and T1 (invades lamina propria) while muscle invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) includes stages T2 (invades muscularis propria), T3 (invades perivesicular soft tissue), and T4 (invades adfjacent organs). NMIBC accounts for almost 70% of cases at presentation.

Treatment:

• NMIBC - The initial management of bladder tumors consists of transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) for accurate staging, which aids in determining the subsequent treatment plan. Intravesical therapy, involving chemotherapy (with mitomycin, doxorubicin, or epirubicin) or immunotherapy (BCG), is administered after TURBT to eradicate any remaining cancer cells. This therapy primarily targets the bladder lining and is not effective for cancers that have invaded deeper layers.
• MIBC - The standard treatment for muscle-invasive tumors is radical cystectomy and pelvic lymphadenectomy with urinary diversion (ileal conduit) (option B). Systemic adjuvant and neoadjuvant chemotherapy with M-VAC (Methotrexate, vinblastine, doxorubicin, and cisplatin) has shown to be beneficial (option D).

Option C: Partial cystectomy can be attempted in patients with focal bladder cancer, but the risk of recurrence remains high.
questions.learning: Transurethral resection of the tumour — This patient with low-grade 2x2 cm bladder cancer is likely to have non-muscle invasive bladder carcinoma (NMIBC) should undergo transurethral resection of the bladder tumor (TURBT) for accurate staging purposes.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 45-year-old truck driver with a history of multiple sexual partners presents to the dermatology department with the findings shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The provided image shows a characteristic maculopapular rash on the palms, which is a classic clinical finding for secondary syphilis. The patient's social history (truck driver with multiple sex partners) places him at a significantly higher risk for sexually transmitted infections. Secondary syphilis is the "great imitator" but its presence on palms and soles is a highly specific clue. Lichen planus (Option B) typically presents as itchy, purple papules on the wrists rather than generalized palmar macules. Scabies (Option C) would present with intense itching and burrows, usually visible in the finger webs rather than discrete reddish macules. Psoriasis (Option D) on the palms would show thick, scaly plaques and fissures. Given the risk factors and the pathognomonic palm-involved rash, the diagnosis of secondary syphilis must be suspected and confirmed using non-treponemal (RPR) and treponemal (TPHA) tests

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presented with painless decrease in vision and metamorphopsia. Fundus examination revealed the lesion shown in the image. What is the expected finding on angiography?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Double circulation

The clinical vigenette is of a patient presenting with painless dimunition of vision and metamorphopsia with the right fundus showing choroidal melanoma superotemporal to the optic disc and involving the macula.

In this patient a “Double circulation” pattern consisting of an internal circulation within the lesion and the normal vascularity of the overlying retina will be seen on angiography.

Although collar stud(Option C) appearance is pathagnomic for choroidal melanoma, it can be seen on B-scan and not on angiography.

Choroidal melanoma is a primary intraocular malignancy in adults that peaks around 60 years of age.

Symptoms include a range of visual disturbances such as painless decrease in vision and metamorphosia when macula is involved.

Other features of Choroidal melanoma includes:

• A solitary elevated subretinal grey-brown dome shaped mass
• Clumps of orange pigment are common over the mass
• Collar stud appearance on B-scan (option C): It is pathagnomic of choridal melanoma. It is seen if the tumour breaks through the Bruch's membrane into the subretinal space .
• Associated haemorrhage

Smoke stack pattern (option A) and ink blot (option B) pattern is seen on FFA in central serous retinopathy (CSR).

CSR is the spontaneous serous detachment of the sensory neuroretina in the foveal region with or without retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) detachment.

This occurs due Choroidal vascular hyperpermeability.

On FFA it is initially seen as an ink-blot pattern or smoke stack pattern of hyperfluorescence which then spreads to take the configuration of mushroom or umbrella pattern.

The below given images depict the smoke stack pattern and mushroom pattern respectively
questions.learning: Double circulation — The clinical vigenette is of a patient presenting with painless dimunition of vision and metamorphopsia with the right fundus showing choroidal melanoma superotemporal to the optic disc and involving the macula.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: General Pharmacology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following cause pleural fibrosis except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Metformin

Pleural fibrosis is a known adverse effect of several drugs due to chronic inflammatory or fibrotic reactions in lung and pleural tissue. Methysergide can cause pleuropulmonary fibrosis with long-term use due to serotonergic stimulation of fibroblasts. Bleomycin induces pulmonary and pleural fibrosis via free radical–mediated lung injury. Nitrofurantoin, especially with prolonged use, is associated with chronic interstitial lung disease and pleural fibrosis.

Metformin, however, is an oral antidiabetic drug that does not cause pulmonary or pleural fibrosis and has no fibrogenic pulmonary toxicity.

Why other options are incorrect:

B. Methysergide: Causes pleuropulmonary fibrosis.

C. Bleomycin: Classic cause of lung and pleural fibrosis.

D. Nitrofurantoin: Long-term use causes chronic pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Reverse splitting of second heart sound is most commonly seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. LBBB

Paradoxical (reverse) splitting of the second heart sound (S2) occurs when aortic valve closure (A2) is delayed, causing P2 to occur before A2. The split is heard during expiration and narrows or disappears during inspiration, which is the opposite of normal physiological splitting.

• Most common cause: Left bundle branch block (LBBB) due to delayed left ventricular depolarization and prolonged left ventricular ejection.
• Other causes:

• Severe aortic stenosis
• Left ventricular pacing
• Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM)

Differentiate from other options:

• A. ASD: Fixed wide splitting of S2.
• B. Severe MR: Produces a pansystolic murmur; paradoxical splitting is not a typical finding.
• D. Pulmonary hypertension: Loud P2; splitting may become narrow but is not paradoxical.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. He is pale, diaphoretic, and hypotensive (BP 75/50 mmHg) with tachycardia. Investigations reveal a ruptured spleen with massive hemoperitoneum. He is taken for emergency exploratory laparotomy. Which of the following induction agents is the most appropriate in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ketamine

Ketamine is the induction agent of choice in patients with hypovolemic shock or trauma because it preserves airway reflexes and stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, leading to increased heart rate, blood pressure, and cardiac output. Unlike most intravenous induction agents, ketamine does not cause significant cardiovascular depression, making it ideal for hemodynamically unstable patients.

Ketamine:

• Produces dissociative anesthesia
• Increases BP and HR via catecholamine release
• Maintains cardiac output
• Preserves spontaneous respiration and airway reflexes

Therefore, it is the preferred induction agent in this hemodynamically unstable patient.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sevoflurane: An inhalational anesthetic used mainly for induction in children; it causes vasodilation and hypotension, making it unsuitable in hemorrhagic shock.
• B. Propofol: Causes marked vasodilation and myocardial depression, leading to significant hypotension; contraindicated in hypovolemic shock.
• C. Thiopentone sodium: Produces myocardial depression and peripheral vasodilation, which can worsen hypotension in trauma patients.
questions.learning: Ketamine Ketamine is the induction agent of choice in patients with hypovolemic shock or trauma because it preserves airway reflexes and stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, leading to increased heart rate, blood pressure, and cardiac output.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of single-unit (visceral) smooth muscle?
options: Innervated by a single nerve ending per fiber
Fibers are connected via many gap junctions and contract as a syncytium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fibers are connected via many gap junctions and contract as a syncytium

Single-unit (visceral) smooth muscle functions as a functional syncytium because the individual muscle fibers are electrically coupled by numerous gap junctions.

• Many gap junctions connect adjacent cells.
• Electrical activity spreads from cell to cell, so the muscle contracts as a coordinated unit (syncytium).
• Usually innervated by a few nerve fibers, not one nerve per cell.
• Often shows spontaneous rhythmic activity.

Examples:
• Gastrointestinal tract
• Uterus
• Urinary bladder
• Small blood vessels

Contrast with multiunit smooth muscle:
• Fibers act independently
• Few or no gap junctions
• Each fiber has individual innervation (e.g., iris, ciliary muscle).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman with chronic ear discharge presents with a hectic (picket-fence) fever pattern, tenderness and edema over the mastoid tip, and pain along the course of the internal jugular vein. During lumbar puncture with manometry, compression of the contralateral (normal-side) jugular vein produces a prompt rise in CSF pressure, but compression of the ipsilateral (diseased-side) jugular vein produces no change. Which of the following best describes this finding and the underlying diagnosis?
options: This is a positive Queckenstedt's test performed to confirm otogenic tetanus
This is a positive Tobey-Ayer test, confirming sigmoid (lateral) sinus thrombophlebitis with obstruction of the ipsilateral sinus
This is a positive Crowe-Beck sign, confirming papilledema secondary to raised intracranial pressure alone
This is a negative Queckenstedt's test, ruling out any intracranial complication
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. This is a positive Tobey-Ayer test, confirming sigmoid (lateral) sinus thrombophlebitis with obstruction of the ipsilateral sinus

| Feature | Detail

| ------- | ------

| Pathogenesis | Mastoiditis → peri-sinus abscess → intra-sinus abscess → thrombosis of sigmoid/lateral sinus

| Picket-fence/hectic fever | Due to septic embolization

| Griesinger's sign | Tenderness/edema over mastoid (from mastoid emissary vein thrombosis)

| Tenderness over jugular vein | IJV blockade

| Tobey-Ayer / Queckenstedt's test | Compression of the normal (contralateral) jugular vein → rise in CSF pressure (positive); compression of the thrombosed (ipsilateral) side → no rise, since that sinus is already occluded

| Crowe-Beck sign | Compression of the normal jugular vein → papilledema (engorgement of retinal veins)

| Confirmatory imaging | CT/MRI venography — delta sign / empty triangle sign

| Management | IV antibiotics + modified radical mastoidectomy

The Tobey-Ayer test relies on a differential response: since the ipsilateral sigmoid sinus is already thrombosed, compressing that jugular vein cannot further obstruct CSF venous drainage, so no additional pressure rise is seen — whereas compressing the still-patent contralateral vein produces the expected physiological rise. This asymmetry is diagnostic of sigmoid sinus thrombophlebitis, later confirmed radiologically by the delta/empty triangle sign on contrast imaging.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presents with unilateral hearing loss. On examination, a small perforation is noted on his left tympanic membrane. What will be the left-sided Rinne's test finding in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Negative

This patient with unilateral hearing loss and a small perforation of his tympanic membrane is likely to have conductive hearing loss in the left ear, which will show a negative Rinne's test in the affected ear.

Tuning fork tests are performed commonly with tuning forks of frequencies such as 128, 256, 512, 1024, etc. The tuning fork of 512 Hz is considered ideal as forks of lower frequencies produce a sense of bone vibration while those of higher frequencies have a shorter decay time. Some examples of commonly done tuning fork tests are as follows:

Rinne’s test is done by placing a vibrating tuning fork on the patient’s mastoid and when he stops hearing, it is brought beside the external auditory meatus (EAC). If he still hears the sound, air conduction (AC) is better than bone conduction (BC). The inferences are as follows:

• Rinne's test is considered positive (normal) when the air conduction AC>BC is seen in normal people and people with sensorineural deafness.
• It is considered negative when the BC>AC, and is seen in patients with conductive deafness. It suggests a minimum hearing loss of 15-20 dB.

Weber test is done by placing a vibrating tuning in the middle of the forehead or the vertex and the patient is asked in which ear the sound is heard. The inferences are as follows:

• A normal result is achieved when the sound heard equally in both ears
• In conductive deafness, it is lateralized to the worse ear
• In sensorineural deafness, it is lateralized to the better ear

Other options:

Option A: Rinne's test is positive in normal subjects.

Option B: Rinne's test is falsely negative in patients with sudden severe unilateral sensorineural hearing loss.

Option B: There is no such interpretation as intermediate in Rinne's test.
questions.learning: Negative — This patient with unilateral hearing loss and a small perforation of his tympanic membrane is likely to have conductive hearing loss in the left ear, which will show a negative Rinne's test in the affected ear.

questions.text: Which of the following vessels is involved in the condition affecting the region marked in red in the image shown below?

Correct answer: B. Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery

The given image is suggestive of lateral medullary syndrome/Wallenberg syndrome. This may result from a stroke affecting the Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery.

The clinical findings correspond to the neuroanatomical structures affected in the lateral portion of the medulla:

• Descending tract and nucleus of CN V (trigeminal)- loss of pain and sensation over the ipsilateral half of the face.
• Inferior cerebellar peduncle – ipsilateral ataxia (gait and limb)
• Lateral spinothalamic tract – loss of pain and temperature sensation over the contralateral half of the body.
• IX and X CN - ipsilateral paralysis of palate, vocal cord, diminished gag reflex giving rise to dysphagia, dysarthria.
• Vestibular nucleus - Nystagmus, diplopia, vertigo, nausea
• Descending sympathetic tract – ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome (miosis, ptosis, and anhidrosis).

questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 48-year-old man with diabetes undergoes stress testing. He walks for 7 minutes without chest pain. Peak heart rate is 132/min, BP increases from 95 to 112 mmHg. Which of the following parameters was most likely decreased during peak stress?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Total systemic vascular resistance

During exercise or stress testing, increased metabolic activity in skeletal muscles causes local vasodilation due to accumulation of metabolites (adenosine, CO₂, H⁺, K⁺).

Physiological changes during exercise:

• ↑ Heart rate
• ↑ Cardiac output
• ↑ Systolic blood pressure
• ↑ Venous return
• ↓ Total systemic vascular resistance (SVR) due to vasodilation in active muscles

Even though sympathetic tone increases, the metabolic vasodilation in skeletal muscles predominates, causing an overall decrease in SVR.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Which is the correct sequence of steps in the isolation of desirable protein using recombinant DNA technology?

1. Expression of protein and lysis of bacterial cell
2. Incorporation of genes into bacteria
3. SDS PAGE
4. Protein elution

5. Hybridization
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2, 1, 3, 5, 4

The correct sequence of isolation of desirable protein in recombinant DNA technology is 2, 1, 3, 5, 4.

I) Incorporation of genes into bacteria: The gene needed to produce the desired proteins is to be incorporated into the bacteria. This is done using cloning vectors like bacterial plasmids, phages, or cosmids. The DNA of interest is ligated into the vector DNA and is called recombinant DNA. This vector is then inserted into a competent host cell (eg: E.coli bacteria) where it is replicated.

II) Expression of protein and lysis of bacterial cell:  After incorporation of recombinant DNA, bacteria express the inserted gene and produce the desired protein on a large scale along with other indigenous bacterial proteins. To release these proteins bacterial cell is lysed.

III) SDS-PAGE (sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis): It is the most widely used method for determining the purity of a protein. After the proteins are released, to separate the desirable protein, we subject it to SDS-PAGE. It separates proteins based on molecular weight.

IV) Hybridization and blotting: It is done to confirm that the isolated protein is the desired protein. It is done using western blotting techniques on nitrocellulose paper.

V) Protein elution - extraction of the produced protein.

The practical applications of recombinant DNA technology include:

• Gene mapping using techniques such as fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH).
• Producing proteins such as:

• Interferons, tPA (tissue plasminogen activator)
• Insulin, growth hormone
• Hepatitis B vaccine

• Molecular analysis of disease, to detect gene variations and mutations.
• Restriction Fragment Length polymorphism (RFLP) and single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)
• Microsatellite DNA polymorphisms
• Gene therapy and bone marrow transplantation
questions.learning: 2, 1, 3, 5, 4 The correct sequence of isolation of desirable protein in recombinant DNA technology is 2, 1, 3, 5, 4. I) Incorporation of genes into bacteria: The gene needed to produce the desired proteins is to be incorporated into the bacteria.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In clinical trials, to ensure reliable and valid results, selection bias—where the sample may not accurately represent the broader population— must be minimized. Which method is primarily used in clinical trial protocols to reduce the risk of selection bias?
questions.explanation: Randomization is the hallmark of a high-quality clinical trial and is the primary method used to eliminate or minimize selection bias. It involves assigning participants to different study groups (e.g., treatment vs. control) purely by chance, ensuring that both known and unknown confounding variables are distributed equally between the groups. This process makes the groups comparable and ensures that any observed differences in outcomes can be attributed to the intervention itself rather than baseline participant characteristics. Selecting the population (Option A) relates to the external validity or generalizability of the study but doesn't fix internal bias between groups. Intervention (Option B) is the treatment being tested. Written informed consent (Option D) is a fundamental ethical requirement to protect patient autonomy but does not impact the statistical validity or the reduction of bias. Therefore, randomization remains the most powerful statistical tool for maintaining the integrity and scientific rigor of a randomized controlled trial (RCT)

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Haglund deformity is seen around which of the following joints?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ankle

Haglund deformity, pump bump, or Mulholland deformity is seen around the ankle joint. It refers to retrocalcaneal exostosis formed at the posterosuperior aspect of the calcaneum.

retrocalcaneal bursa usually protects the Achilles tendon from the calcaneal tuberosity. But in Haglund deformity, there is chronic inflammation of this retrocalcaneal bursa due to increased or repetitive chafing between the tuberosity and Achilles tendon. Due to prolonged inflammation, degenerative changes occur and osteophytes form within the tendon leading to calcification at the site of the tendon insertion.  This leads to deformity and pain symptoms.

Management is usually conservative, using a heel lift, silicone pads in closed shoes, ice application, anti-inflammatory drugs, and stretching exercises of the calf.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text:
A male patient comes to you with a history of UTI, the cause of which is suspected to be bacteria. Which of the following is used by the bacteria for adherence?

UTI - Urinary Tract Infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fimbriae

Bacteria utilise fimbriae for adherence.

Fimbriae, also called pili are hair-like surface appendage that projects from the cell surface as straight filaments. Fimbriae are classified based on the function of ordinary pili and sex pili.

Functions of pili:

• Bacterial adhesion of symbiotic and pathogenic bacteria to host cells using adhesins.
• Resistance to phagocytosis.
• Antigenic pilin proteins are responsible for the immune response.
• Twitching motility to bacteria.
• Bacterial conjugation through sex pili, in which transfer of genetic material occurs.

Other options:

Option A: The cytoplasmic membrane, or plasma membrane, is a fundamental structure of all cells, including bacteria. It acts as a selective barrier, regulating the entry and exit of substances.

Option B: In organisms like protozoa, cilia are used for locomotion and feeding. These organisms use their cilia to move through water and to sweep food particles towards their oral groove.

Option D: Flagella are thread-like appendages composed of protein. They are the organs of locomotion but motility via pili is completely different from flagellar motion because of the helical arrangement of pilin molecules.
questions.learning: Fimbriae Bacteria utilise fimbriae for adherence. Fimbriae, also called pili are hair-like surface appendage that projects from the cell surface as straight filaments.

questions.text: The recommended amount of space per student in a classroom should be
questions.explanation: In school health and environmental sanitation standards, providing adequate space is essential to prevent overcrowding and the spread of respiratory infections. The government-recommended minimum floor space for a student in a classroom is more than 10 square feet. This standard ensures sufficient room for a desk and chair while allowing for adequate air circulation and easy movement within the room. Options A, C, and D do not reflect the standard Indian public health guidelines for school infrastructure. Overcrowding in classrooms is a major risk factor for the transmission of airborne diseases such as tuberculosis, influenza, and meningococcal meningitis. In addition to floor space, classrooms should have a minimum ceiling height and adequate ventilation (at least 10% of the floor area should be windows). Maintaining these environmental standards is a critical component of the school health service to ensure a safe and healthy learning environment for children's physical and cognitive development

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Which of the following are done in Breast Conservation Surgery?

1. Wide local excision
2. Axillary node dissection
3. Frozen section (biopsy) to be done during surgery
4. Post-operative radiotherapy optional
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3

Wide local excision, axillary node dissection, and frozen section (biopsy) during surgery are done as a part of Breast Conservation Surgery (BCS). All patients with BCS must receive radiotherapy (Statement 4) and are together known as Breast Conservation Therapy (BCT).

Breast conservation surgery involves removing the tumor with a 1mm margin of normal breast tissue. Removal of primary breast cancer is also called lumpectomy/ tylectomy/ partial mastectomy/ wide local excision (Statement 1). Histological examination via intraoperative frozen section (Statement 3) is done to examine for positive margins. Patients with positive margins should have a revision of margins known as ‘cavity shave’. Assessment of regional lymph nodes is done via a separate incision in the axilla (Statement 2).

Absolute contraindications of BCT:

• 1st trimester of pregnancy (may be done for some 2nd and many 3rd trimester patients who can receive radiation after delivery)
• Persistently positive margin (2 microscopy shows positive margins)
• Multicentric lumps
• Diffuse microcalcification
•

Extensive ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS)

•

Inflammatory breast cancer

Relative contraindications of BCT:

• Active SLE (systemic lupus erythematosus), scleroderma
• Large lump-to-breast ratio (>5 cm size lump)
• Known or suspected genetic predisposition to breast cancer (i.e., BRCA1, BRCA2), Li-Fraumeni syndrome (p53 mutation)
• Multifocal disease
• Prior radiation therapy to the chest wall or breast
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 Wide local excision, axillary node dissection, and frozen section (biopsy) during surgery are done as a part of Breast Conservation Surgery (BCS).

o    Bone marrow

o    Liver

• Causes pancytopenia due to marrow infiltration

Clinical features:

• Pancytopenia (anemia, thrombocytopenia)
• Bone pain and fractures

Why other options are incorrect:

• Alpha-galactosidase: Fabry disease
• Alpha-glucosidase: Pompe disease
• Beta-galactosidase: GM1 gangliosidosis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A known patient of tuberculosis, on INH for the past 3 months complains of numbness, tingling and burning sensation in all the extremities. What could be vitamin deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B6

Isoniazid (INH) therapy in tuberculosis can cause vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency, leading to peripheral neuropathy (numbness, tingling, burning sensation).

• INH forms complexes with pyridoxine and increases its excretion
• This leads to ↓ availability of pyridoxal phosphate (active B6)
• Pyridoxal phosphate is required for neurotransmitter synthesis (e.g., GABA)

Deficiency results in:

• Peripheral neuropathy
• Paresthesia (glove and stocking pattern)

Prevention: Always give prophylactic vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) with INH therapy

Why other options are incorrect:

• Vitamin B12: Causes neuropathy but not specifically linked to INH
• Vitamin B1 (Thiamine): Causes beriberi/Wernicke’s
• Vitamin B3 (Niacin): Causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia)

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient with CSOM presented to the OPD with seizures, headache, vomiting and photophobia. On eye examination, homonymous hemianopia was noted. CT brain showed the following findings. Identify the condition. Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Temporal lobe abscess

The clinical vignette depicting features of seizures, headache, vomiting, and photophobia in a patient with a chronic ear infection and the CT image showing a ring-enhancing lesion point to a diagnosis of a temporal lobe abscess.

Temporal lobe abscess is an intracranial complication that can arise from chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM).

Brain abscess typically progresses through 4 stages.

* The first stage is the stage of invasion (initial encephalitis), which often goes unnoticed. Symptoms such as headache, malaise, low-grade fever, and drowsiness may be present.

* The second stage is the stage of localization (latent abscess), during which a capsule forms around the abscess, effectively localizing the pus.

* The third stage is the stage of enlargement (manifest abscess). The abscess enlarges, leading to increased intracranial pressure (ICP) and the development of edema surrounding the abscess. As a result, symptoms worsen.

* The final stage is the stage of termination (rupture of abscess). At this point, the abscess expands and eventually ruptures into the ventricle or subarachnoid space, which can result in potentially fatal meningitis.

Characteristic findings associated with temporal lobe abscess include nominal aphasia, homonymous hemianopia, seizures, contralateral motor paralysis, pupillary changes, and oculomotor palsy. Signs of raised ICP like headache, nausea, vomiting, lethargy, drowsiness, confusion, papilledema, and coma may also be seen.

The preferred diagnostic imaging modality for temporal lobe abscess is a CT scan of the brain. This imaging study reveals a ring-enhancing lesion indicative of a brain abscess.

Medical treatment involves initiating intravenous antibiotics, typically metronidazole. Raised ICP can be addressed using dexamethasone or mannitol. Surgical intervention is the definitive management and involves drainage of the abscess followed by radical mastoidectomy to address the underlying CSOM.

Other options:

Option B: Cerebellar abscess is a form of brain abscess and is usually associated with an otogenic source of infection. It can occur as a direct extension through Trautmann's triangle or via retrograde thrombophlebitis.

An MRI image showing cerebellar abscess is given below:

Option C: Subdural abscess refers to the focal collection of purulent material between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater.

An MRI image showing subdural abscess is given below:

Option D: Meningitis is the inflammation of the leptomeninges which includes the arachnoid mater and pia mater. It can be due to an infectious or noninfectious etiology. It presents with fever, vomiting, neck stiffness, and signs of meningeal irritation. Ring-enhancing lesion on neuroimaging is not a feature of meningitis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following is correct about the recruitment of fast fatiguable motor unit?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Recruited last

Motor units are recruited according to the Henneman size principle, which states that motor neurons are activated from smallest to largest depending on the force required.

Recruitment order:

1.      Slow (Type I) motor units – small neurons, fatigue-resistant, used for low-force, sustained activities.

2.      Fast fatigue-resistant (Type IIa) – moderate force and endurance.

3.      Fast fatigable (Type IIb/IIx) – large neurons producing high force but fatigue quickly.

Therefore, fast fatigable motor units are recruited last, only during high-intensity or powerful muscle contractions.
questions.learning: Recruited last Motor units are recruited according to the Henneman size principle, which states that motor neurons are activated from smallest to largest depending on the force required.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: 2,3-BPG causes the unloading of oxygen to tissues by _________.
options: Binding to beta subunit of Hb
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Binding to beta subunit of Hb

2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (BPG) causes the unloading of oxygen to tissues by binding to the beta subunit of Hb.

2,3 BPG is formed from glycolysis. It is found in high amounts in red blood cells and in trace amounts in most other cells. 2,3 BPG facilitates increased oxygen delivery by reducing the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen.

Hemoglobin exists in 2 forms in the blood. The deoxyhemoglobin form is called the taut or T form. This hemoglobin has a low affinity for oxygen. The oxyhemoglobin form is called the relaxed or R form. This hemoglobin has a high affinity for oxygen.

2,3 BPG binds more selectively to deoxyhemoglobin and stabilizes the taut conformation of hemoglobin (Option C).

Other options:

Options A and D: The process of unloading oxygen by 2,3 BPG is independent of ATP production.
questions.learning: Binding to beta subunit of Hb 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (BPG) causes the unloading of oxygen to tissues by binding to the beta subunit of Hb. It is found in high amounts in red blood cells and in trace amounts in most other cells.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
What contributes to the latent period of muscle twitch?

1. Neuromuscular transmission
2. Excitation contraction coupling
3. Reuptake of calcium back into sarcoplasmic reticulum
4. Transmission of impulse from nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1,2,4

Neuromuscular transmission, Excitation contraction coupling and transmission impulse from nerve coupling contribute to latent period of muscle twitch.

The latent period of a muscle twitch is the brief delay between the application of a stimulus (such as a nerve impulse) and the onset of muscle contraction. During this period, several physiological processes occur, but neuromuscular transmission and excitation-contraction coupling primarily contribute to this delay.

Neuromuscular transmission: The action potential travels down the motor neuron to the neuromuscular junction. Acetylcholine (ACh) is released into the synaptic cleft and binds to receptors on the muscle fiber's sarcolemma, triggering an action potential in the muscle fiber. (Statement 1)

Excitation-contraction coupling: The action potential propagates along the sarcolemma and into the transverse (T) tubules. This triggers the release of calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytosol. Calcium binds to troponin, initiating the interaction of actin and myosin filaments. (Statement 2)

Reuptake of calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum: This occurs during the relaxation phase, not the latent period. (Statement 3)

Transmission of impulse from nerve: This is a part of neuromuscular transmission and is involved in the latent period. (Statement 4)
questions.learning: 1,2,4 Neuromuscular transmission, Excitation contraction coupling and transmission impulse from nerve coupling contribute to latent period of muscle twitch.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol use and recent binge drinking presents with an episode of hematemesis involving bright red blood. His vital signs are stable. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is performed, and the image is shown. Based on these findings, what is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of an alcoholic patient with binge drinking followed by hematemesis (vomiting bright red blood) is the classic presentation of a Mallory-Weiss Tear. The provided endoscopic image confirms the diagnosis, showing a longitudinal, linear mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction. These tears result from forceful vomiting or retching. Boerhaave syndrome (Option B) is a more severe, "full-thickness" rupture of the esophagus that presents with severe pain and sepsis, not typically stable vitals and isolated bleeding. Tension pneumothorax (Option A) and gastric ulcer perforation (Option D) are surgical emergencies that present with respiratory distress or "air under the diaphragm" on imaging, rather than primary hematemesis. Because the image shows a superficial mucosal tear specifically at the cardia/GE junction in a stable patient, Mallory-Weiss Tear is the definitive diagnosis. Most cases heal spontaneously with supportive care
questions.learning: The clinical history of an alcoholic patient with binge drinking followed by hematemesis (vomiting bright red blood) is the classic presentation of a Mallory-Weiss Tear.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the primary identification made by a CBNAAT/gene expert?
questions.explanation: CBNAAT (Cartridge Based Nucleic Acid Amplification Test), commonly known as GeneXpert, is a revolutionary molecular test for tuberculosis. Its primary function is the simultaneous identification of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) genome and the presence of mutations in the rpoB gene, which indicates Rifampicin resistance. Because Rifampicin is a surrogate marker for multi-drug resistance (MDR-TB), this test provides rapid, critical information for treatment planning. While it identifies the bacteria itself (Option A), its most significant clinical advantage is the rapid resistance testing. Standard GeneXpert does not identify resistance to Isoniazid (Option C) or Ethambutol (Option D); those require more advanced molecular tests or traditional cultures. GeneXpert is highly sensitive, providing results in less than two hours, making it the first-line diagnostic tool in the National TB Elimination Programme of India for both pulmonary and extrapulmonary tuberculosis

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A gentleman presents to the OPD with a saddle nose deformity. He gives a past history of cough, on/off fever, and hemoptysis. On examination, septal perforation is present with pale granuloma. His chest x-ray showed multiple cavitary lesions, and the biopsy showed granuloma, multinucleate giant cells, and caseous necrosis. What would be the probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tuberculosis

In a patient with saddle nose deformity, septal perforation with pale granuloma and caseous necrosis on biopsy is consistent with tuberculosis (TB). The history of fever, cough, and hemoptysis along with cavitary lesions on chest x-ray support the diagnosis of TB.

While other conditions like Wegener's granulomatosis (Option A), syphilis (Option C), and sarcoidosis (Option D) can also cause saddle nose deformity, caseous necrosis on biopsy makes TB a more likely diagnosis.

Saddle-nose deformity refers to a depressed nasal dorsum that can involve either the bony, cartilaginous, or both components.

The most common cause is nasal trauma resulting in depressed fractures. Other causes include excessive submucosal resection, destruction of septal cartilage due to hematoma or abscess, and infections such as leprosy, tuberculosis, or syphilis, as well as inflammatory conditions like granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener granulomatosis) and sarcoidosis.

Chronic granulomatous conditions such as lupus, tuberculosis, and leprosy can affect the cartilaginous part, syphilis primarily affects the bony part, and Wegener's granulomatosis and T-cell lymphoma can lead to total (bony and cartilaginous) septal destruction involving both the bony and cartilaginous portions.

TB is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and primarily affects the lungs but can also involve the nose and sinuses.

Common symptoms of TB include fever, productive cough, weight loss, night sweats, and hemoptysis. Chest x-ray often shows multiple cavitation lesions affecting the upper lobe and hilar lymphadenopathy. Biopsy findings in tuberculosis typically reveal granulomas, caseous necrosis, and multinucleate giant cells (Langhan's giant cells).

The following images show the histopathological image of tuberculosis:

Other options:

Option A: Wegener's granulomatosis is characterized by vasculitis affecting small to medium-sized vessels. It affects the upper respiratory tract (ear, nose, sinuses, and throat), lower respiratory tract (lung), and kidney and is characterized by necrotizing granuloma which is non-caseating.

Option C: Although nose deformity is seen in syphilis, gummatous lesions (caseating granulomas) are present in tertiary syphilis which is not seen in this patient. Fever, cough, and hemoptysis are not features of syphilis.

Option D: Sarcoidosis most commonly affects the lungs forming non-caseating granuloma with no central necrosis. Laminated calcium and protein-containing bodies called Schaumann bodies and star-shaped inclusions called asteroid bodies are also found in the giant cells of most of these granulomas. Chest x-ray would show interstitial fibrosis and hilar lymphadenopathy.

The image below shows the characteristic non-caseating sarcoid granuloma:
