questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old chronic alcoholic with a history of chronic liver disease presents to the emergency department with massive, sudden onset hematemesis. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bleeding esophageal varices

The given clinical scenario of a chronic alcoholic with sudden onset haematemesis is suggestive of esophageal variceal bleeding.

The management of esophageal variceal bleeding involves:

* Resuscitation with IV fluids, airway protection, and oxygen

* Blood transfusion to maintain Hb between 7-9g/dL

* Antibiotic prophylaxis with ceftriaxone before endoscopy

* An attempt at hemostasis with octreotide or terlipressin or vasopressin

* Fluid resuscitation followed by an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy within 12 hours to determine the cause of the bleeding

* Endoscopic variceal band ligation or sclerotherapy

* In case, of failure or rebleeding - TIPS

Nonselective beta-blockers like propranolol and nadolol are used in the prophylaxis of variceal bleeding.
questions.learning: Bleeding esophageal varices — The given clinical scenario of a chronic alcoholic with sudden onset haematemesis is suggestive of esophageal variceal bleeding.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The fracture seen in the Xray given below is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Galeazzi's fracture

The X-ray reveals an oblique fracture in the lower third of radius with dislocation of the distal radio-ulnar joint, which is suggestive of Galeazzi's fracture.

In Galeazzi's fracture, there is a radial bone fracture at the middle and distal third junction and associated distal radio-ulnar joint subluxation or dislocation. It may be possible to demonstrate the instability of the radioulnar joint by ‘ballotting’ the distal end of the ulna (‘piano-key sign’).

Galeazzi's fracture is the fracture of the lower third of the radius and the subluxation or dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint. This injury usually happens when one falls on an outstretched hand. The most common clinical feature is tenderness over the distal end of the forearm.

The aim of treatment for this fracture is to preserve supination and pronation of the forearm. In children, closed reduction is usually enough to achieve perfect reduction. However, in adults, open reduction using a k-wire fixation or compression plating is usually required. It is also important to look for ulnar nerve damage.

Galeazzi's fracture can cause complications such as malunion due to displacement of the fragment. This often results in deformity and limitation in supination and pronation.

Other Options:

Option B: Monteggia fracture: It is the fracture of shaft of ulna with dislocation of proximal radio-ulnar joint

Option C: Smith's fracture: It is also known as "Reverse Colle's fracture". It is the fracture of the distal radius with palmar angulation of the distal bone fragment.

Option D: Colle's fracture: It is the fracture of the distal radius with dorsal angulation of the distal bone fragment.

Pearl PF0377: Named fractures of the upper limb

Colle's fracture: Fracture of the distal radius with dorsal angulation of the distal bone fragment.

Smith's fracture: Reverse Colles' fracture. Fracture of the distal one-third of the radius with palmar displacement.

Galeazzi fracture-dislocation: Fracture of the lower third of the radius and subluxation of the distal radio-ulnar joint.

Monteggia fracture-dislocation: Fracture of the shaft of the ulna with dislocation of a proximal radio-ulnar joint.

Barton’s fracture: Intra-articular fracture of the distal radius.

Rolando's fracture: Intra-articular comminuted fracture of the base of the first metacarpal with a T or Y configuration.

Chauffeur's fracture or the Hutchinson fracture: Fracture of the radial styloid.

Essex–Lopresti lesion: Fracture of the radial head with disruption of the interosseous membrane and distal radial ulnar joint ligaments.

Nightstick fracture: Isolated fracture of the ulnar bone.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with raised, erythematous nodular skin lesions, respiratory symptoms, and lymphadenopathy. Chest X-ray reveals bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and biopsy demonstrates granulomas without central necrosis. Based on this presentation, which histopathological finding is most likely to be seen?
questions.explanation: The clinical constellation of skin nodules (erythema nodosum), respiratory symptoms, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is highly characteristic of Sarcoidosis. The definitive histological marker for sarcoidosis is the presence of Non-caseating granulomas. These are well-formed aggregates of epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells that lack central (caseous) necrosis. Caseating granulomas (Option A) are the hallmark of tuberculosis, which presents similarly but shows central necrotic "cheesy" debris. Stellate granulomas (Option B) are seen in cat-scratch disease or lymphogranuloma venereum. Eosinophilic granulomas (Option D) are a manifestation of Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Sarcoidosis granulomas may also contain inclusions like Asteroid bodies or Schaumann bodies. Diagnosis is established when these histological findings are correlated with the classic radiographic signs. While many cases resolve spontaneously, symptomatic pulmonary involvement often requires treatment with corticosteroids to suppress the granulomatous inflammation and prevent long-term fibrosis. Accurate histological identification is critical for differentiating sarcoidosis from systemic infections like TB
questions.learning: The clinical constellation of skin nodules (erythema nodosum), respiratory symptoms, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is highly characteristic of Sarcoidosis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of prospective screening?
options: Cervical Pap smear in a 40 year old patient
Neonatal screening of a new-born baby for hypothyroidism
Screening of immigrants to a country
Urine for sugar screening in a 40 year old man
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Screening of immigrants to a country

Screening of immigrants to a country is an example of prospective screening.

Screening of disease is done to detect unrecognized disease or defect, in apparently healthy individuals, by means of rapidly applied tests, examinations, or other procedures.

The difference between prospective and prescriptive screening is given below:

Prospective screening
Prescriptive screening

Definition
People screened for others benefit
People screened solely for their own benefit

Essential purpose
Disease control
Case detection

Request for screening
Specific request from the authority
Request from physician

Example

• Immigrants for infectious diseases like tuberculosis syphilis, yellow fever, etc;
• HIV screening during antenatal visits, sex workers.
• Screening of blood donors.

• Neonatal screening for hypothyroidism.
• Pap smear for detection of cervical cancer.
• Testing of urine sugar for diabetes mellitus.

Note: Most common neonatal disease to be screened for is neonatal hypothyroidism.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncle occurs at which level?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Midbrain

The decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncle occurs in the midbrain, at the level of the inferior colliculus.

The midbrain has four decussations:

• At the level of the superior colliculus:

• Ventral tegmental decussation of the rubrospinal tract
• Dorsal tegmental decussation of the tectospinal tract

• At the level of the inferior colliculus:

• Decussation of superior cerebellar peduncles
• Decussation of trochlear nerve

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text:
Which of the following is the most effective drug in smoking cessation?

SR: Sustained release
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Varenicline

Varenicline is the most effective drug in smoking cessation.

Nicotine is the principal constituent of tobacco responsible for its addictive behaviour. One of the newest agents introduced to aid in smoking cessation is varenicline.

Varenicline works by blocking the effects of nicotine on the brain. It blocks α-4, β-2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subtypes and varenicline inhibits dopaminergic activation produced by smoking through their partial agonism, and decreases the craving and withdrawal syndrome that occurs with cessation attempts. It prevents nicotine stimulation of the mesolimbic dopamine system associated with nicotine addiction, thus helping to occlude the "rewarding" effect of smoking.

Varenicline is prescribed only to patients 18 years or older. Varenicline is taken orally and the dose taken is 0.5 mg once daily on days 1 to 3, increased to 0.5 mg twice daily on days 4 through 7 and 1 mg twice daily after day 8 for 11 weeks. Therapy should start one week before the target quit date. It can be continued for another 12 weeks (1 mg BD) to maintain abstinence.

The adverse effects include nausea, which can be mitigated by starting at lower doses and gradually increasing the dose. Other symptoms include disturbed sleep, sleepwalking, agitation, drowsiness, and constipation and may also increase the risk of pancreatitis. Varenicline has also been implicated in specific skin syndromes such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, erythema multiforme, and photosensitivity. Varenicline can cause renal failure and kidney stones, thus renal function must be monitored.

The FDA has issued a warning about mood and behavioral changes associated with its use, and there is some evidence of increased cardiovascular risk.

Other options:

Option B: Buspirone sustained release is a partial agonist at 5HT receptors but affinity for D2 receptors may also be present. Its effects are slow onset, over a couple of weeks and is used in the management of generalised anxiety states.

Option C: Nicotine gum has nicotine which is an agonist at Nn type nicotinic cholinergic receptors and is also advised for smoking cessation along with psychotherapy. However, varenicline was more effective when compared with single‐product nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) and was similarly effective compared with combination NRT.

Option D: Rimonabant is an inverse agonist at cannabinoid receptor CB1 which decreases neurotransmitter release at GABAergic and glutamatergic synapses; its usage for smoking cessation and treat obesity was stopped after serious side effects notably severe depression and increased risk of suicide. However, it continues to be used off-label for smoking cessation.
questions.learning: Varenicline Varenicline is the most effective drug in smoking cessation. Nicotine is the principal constituent of tobacco responsible for its addictive behaviour.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding progesterone-only pills are correct? 1. They contain high-dose progesterone as there is no estrogen component. 2. They do not have “on and off” regimen. 3. They can be used with hepatic enzyme-inducing drugs. 4. The failure rate is 0.3 to 2 per hundred women-years of use. Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2 and 4

1. High-dose progesterone: Incorrect.

• Progestin-only pills (POPs) contain a low dose of progestin, not high-dose progesterone.
• They do not contain estrogen.

2. No “on and off” regimen: Correct.

• POPs are taken continuously every day, without the hormone-free interval used with combined oral contraceptives.

3. Can be used with hepatic enzyme-inducing drugs: Incorrect.

• Enzyme-inducing drugs can increase progestin metabolism and reduce contraceptive effectiveness.

4. Failure rate 0.3–2 per 100 woman-years: Correct.

• POPs are highly effective when taken correctly, with a low failure rate in typical exam-based figures.
questions.learning: High-dose progesterone: Incorrect. • Progestin-only pills (POPs) contain a low dose of progestin, not high-dose progesterone. • They do not contain estrogen.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 34-year-old patient presents with lethargy and tiredness. On examination, he has hyperpigmentation around the lips. His BP is 90/60 mm Hg and heart rate is 110/min. Labs revealed a Na⁺ of 125 mEq/L and a K⁺ of 5.5 mEq/L. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone

| Finding | Meaning

| ------- | -------

| Hyperpigmentation | ↑ ACTH → primary cause

| Hypotension | cortisol deficiency

| Hyponatremia | aldosterone deficiency

| Hyperkalemia | aldosterone deficiency

Findings suggest primary adrenal insufficiency with cortisol and aldosterone deficiency causing hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hyperpigmentation. Treatment requires glucocorticoid plus mineralocorticoid replacement.

GLUCOCORTICOID:

Hydrocortisone → 15–25 mg/day (divided doses)

• 10 mg morning + 5 mg afternoon (± 5 mg evening)

MINERALOCORTICOID:

Fludrocortisone → 0.05–0.2 mg/day (usually 0.1 mg once daily)

GOALS:

• Maintain BP, electrolytes (Na↑, K↓)

• Avoid hypotension & hyperkalemia

STRESS DOSE (VERY IMPORTANT):

• Increase hydrocortisone 2–3× during illness/surgery

ACUTE CRISIS:

• IV Hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus → then 200 mg/day

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old man sustains deep partial-thickness burns to the upper torso after a kitchen fire. Over the next several hours, the area surrounding the central necrotic burn shows progressive tissue hypoperfusion. This region demonstrates vascular constriction and platelet microthrombus formation. Which zone of burn injury does this describe?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Zone of stasis

Burn wounds are divided into three concentric zones described by Jackson: coagulation, stasis, and hyperemia.

Zone of stasis (Correct answer)

• Surrounds central zone of coagulation

• Characterized by reduced perfusion, vasoconstriction, and microvascular thrombosis

• Tissue is initially viable but at risk of progressing to necrosis if perfusion is not restored

• Major target of burn resuscitation and wound care

Zone of coagulation:

• Central area of burn

• Irreversible tissue necrosis

• Protein denaturation and cell death

Zone of hyperemia:

• Outer zone

• Increased perfusion and inflammation

• Usually recovers completely

Proper burn management aims to:

• Maintain perfusion (adequate fluids)

• Prevent infection

• Avoid pressure or hypoxia

→ to salvage the zone of stasis

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: When a victim of an unlawful act was dying, the police recorded the dying declaration. The doctor certifies that the victim was conscious and mentally oriented. The dying declaration will be considered invalid if?
options: It is not done by the doctor
The victim didn't sign the declaration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The victim is not dead

If the victim is not dead, then the dying declaration is invalid and the victim has to testify in court.

Dying declaration: It is a written or oral statement of a person, who is dying as a result of some unlawful act, relating to the material facts of the cause of his death or bearing on the circumstances.

In India, the dying declaration is accepted under IEA section 32 and BSA 26 (a).

Procedure:

* As soon as the severely injured person is brought to the hospital, the medical officer should inform the magistrate to have a dying declaration recorded.

* The doctor can record it himself or herself if he thinks that the person will not survive till the arrival of the magistrate.

* Treatment should not be delayed while recording dying declaration.

* The doctor has to ascertain that the person is of sound mind (compos mentis).

* If the person dies or becomes unconscious while recording the dying declaration, the doctor must record the information obtained up to that point.

* Usually recorded in the forms of questions and answers in the patient's own language

* No suggestions or leading questions

* No outsider is allowed to be present

* After completing the writing, it has to be read back to the patient who has to approve it by signing/thumb impression. The signature of two witnesses is also mandatory.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with fever and altered sensorium. Peripheral blood smear examination reveals multiple ring forms of the parasite. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: The combination of fever and altered sensorium indicates cerebral malaria, which is a severe form of malaria typically caused by Plasmodium falciparum. The presence of multiple ring stages on a peripheral smear strongly supports this diagnosis. Current WHO and national guidelines recommend intravenous Artesunate as the first-line treatment for severe malaria. It is preferred over quinine due to its superior safety profile, faster parasite clearance, and significant reduction in mortality rates. Primaquine (Option A) is used specifically for the radical cure of P. vivax and P. ovale to target liver hypnozoites. Quinine (Option B) was historically the drug of choice but has been replaced by artesunate. Chloroquine (Option C) is ineffective in this case due to widespread resistance in P. falciparum. Therefore, prompt administration of IV artesunate is the most critical intervention for this patient
questions.learning: The combination of fever and altered sensorium indicates cerebral malaria, which is a severe form of malaria typically caused by Plasmodium falciparum.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Mw vaccine is extracted from which bacteria, mentioned below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. M. indicus pranii

Mw vaccine is extracted from M. indicus pranii

MIP immunotherapy is used as an adjunct to chemotherapy for category II tuberculosis.

Here, indicus stands for India, where the M. indius pranii was isolated; and pranii stands for the person who discovered the species (Prof. Pran Talwar) and National Institute of Immunology (nii), where trials were conducted (pran + nii).

Administration: 0.1 ml intradermal.  It is divided into two equal doses and given on both arms. Booster doses are injected only on one arm.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The fate of the Mullerian duct is determined by the:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Y chromosome

The fate of the Mullerian duct is determined by the presence or absence of the Y chromosome as follows:

• In presence of the Y chromosome, the SRY gene (Sex-determining Region of the Y chromosome) produces the protein called the testis determining factor which leads to the gonads developing as the testes. The Sertoli cells of the testis will then produce a peptide hormone, the Müllerian inhibiting substance (MIS), also known as Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), and cause the Müllerian ducts to regress.
• In absence of the Y chromosome and the SRY gene consequently, the gonads will develop as ovaries and the Mullerian duct will differentiate into the fallopian tubes and the upper part of the vagina. The WNT4 gene on the 1st chromosome promotes female sex development.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the investigation and the lesion depicted in the image given below.
options: Retrograde cystourethrogram with membranous urethra stricture
Retrograde cystourethrogram with penile urethral stricture
Micturating cystourethrography with prostratic urethra stricture
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retrograde cystourethrogram with penile urethral stricture

The given image shows retrograde cystourethrogram with findings consistent with penile urethral stricture.

The male urethra can be visualized by retrograde urethrography (RGU) or voiding cystourethrogram (VCU), also known as micturating cystourethrogram (MCU).

In RGU, the urethra is visualized with the instillation of contrast into the anterior urethra (penile urethra and bulbar urethra). It is helpful for diagnosing anterior urethral abnormalities.

The following image shows an RGU with bulbar urethral stricture:

In VCU, after injecting contrast into the bladder using a Foleys catheter, the posterior urethra (membranous urethra and prostatic urethra) is visualized during micturition. It is helpful for diagnosing posterior urethral abnormalities and bladder abnormalities. It is the investigation of choice for vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) and posterior urethral valve.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In countries with low levels of measles transmission, what should be the appropriate age for starting immunization with measles-containing vaccine (MCV)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 12 months

The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that the age of the first dose of measles-containing vaccine (MCV1) depends on the level of measles transmission in the country. In countries with low measles transmission, vaccination is started at 12 months of age, as maternal antibodies have largely disappeared, resulting in a better immune response.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. 6 months: Reserved for outbreak situations or infants at high risk; this dose does not replace the routine first dose.
• B. 9 months: Recommended in countries with high measles transmission (including India under UIP) to provide early protection.
• D. 15–18 months: This is the age for the second dose (MCV2/MR2), not the first dose.
questions.learning: 12 months The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that the age of the first dose of measles-containing vaccine (MCV1) depends on the level of measles transmission in the country.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding all types of shock?
options: Low pH mainly activates lysosomal enzymes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Low pH mainly activates lysosomal enzymes

The true statement among the given options is that low pH mainly activates lysosomal enzymes.

Lysosomes are membraned organelles that enclose all the hydrolyzing enzymes capable of breaking down biological polymers. The lysosomal enzymes are only active in acidic pH (low pH value) and this pH is maintained within the organelle. Hypoxic tissue injury during shock causes membrane damage, and extravasation of the enzymes from lysosomes. Thus, leading to tissue death.

Other options:

Option A: Anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid. Accumulation of lactic acid causes metabolic acidosis.

Option C: Peripheral vasoconstriction is seen in all types of shock, except septic shock.

Option D: Renal perfusion is maintained during the compensated shock stages. There is renal decompensation as shock progresses causing oliguria, and eventually anuria.

Shock is a state of circulatory failure resulting in tissue hypoperfusion and hypoxia. Prolonged shock eventually leads to irreversible tissue damage.

In cases of shock, there is inadequate oxygenation. Thus cells switch from aerobic to anaerobic respiration where lactic acid, not carbon dioxide, is produced. The accumulation of lactic acid in the blood leads to systemic acidosis.

Shock progresses through a series of well-defined stages:

1. Initial nonprogressive stage: Compensatory neurohumoral mechanisms come into play to preserve tissue perfusion.
2. Progressive stage: Tissue hypoperfusion leads to circulatory and metabolic disturbances. Acidosis occurs due to intracellular anaerobic glycolysis. This causes peripheral pooling, thereby leading to reduced cardiac output and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
3. Irreversible stage: Tissue injury cannot be reversed even with hemodynamic correction. There is worsening myocardial contractility, renal function impairment, and bacteremia (due to the release of intestinal flora into the circulation).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The cover–uncover test is commonly used to assess ocular alignment disorders. Which of the following conditions cannot be detected using this test?
questions.explanation: Amblyopia, or "lazy eye," is a reduction in vision that occurs because the brain favors one eye over the other during early development. While it can be caused by strabismus, the cover-uncover test itself is used only to detect ocular deviations, not to diagnose amblyopia. Latent squint or heterophoria (Option A) is detected by the uncover test, as the eye moves to refixate only when the cover is removed. Manifest squint or heterotopia (Option B) is identified by the cover test, where the eye under the paddle remains still while the uncovered eye moves to take up fixation. Lateral nystagmus (Option C) refers to involuntary rhythmic eye movements; although the cover-uncover test is not the primary diagnostic tool, it can sometimes exacerbate or reveal these movements. The cover-uncover test is a fundamental part of the pediatric ophthalmic exam for identifying horizontal and vertical strabismus

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of which arch artery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 6th arch

The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of the left 6th arch artery.

During the development, the laryngeal nerves initially arise below the 6th arch artery and cross here to innervate the intrinsic muscles of the larynx. As the larynx moves cranially relative to the aortic arch arteries, the recurrent laryngeal nerves on the right and left sides are caught under the 6th arch arteries.

On the right side, the distal 6th arch artery disappears. Since there is no 5th arch artery, the right recurrent laryngeal nerve is caught under the 4th arch artery which becomes the future right subclavian artery.

On the left side, the 6th arch artery persists, which develops into ductus arteriosus, which later forms ligamentum arteriosum. Due to the persistence of the 6th arch artery, the left recurrent laryngeal nerve is caught under it and therefore, has a relatively long course.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 48-year-old man presents with complaints of facial puffiness, frothy urine, and hypertension. He gives a history of infection with hepatitis B. Urine examination reveals microscopic hematuria. The histopathological image of the kidney biopsy shows a spike and dome pattern. What is the diagnosis of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Membranous nephropathy

The diagnosis of the patient based on the given clinical scenario and the histopathology showing spike and dome pattern is membranous nephropathy.

Membranous nephropathy is one of the most common causes of nephrotic syndrome in adults. It occurs commonly in men aged between 30-50 years. The majority of cases are idiopathic/primary that occur due to the autoantibodies against the renal antigen phospholipase A2 receptor. These autoantibodies are absent in secondary membranous nephropathy.

The various conditions leading to secondary membranous nephropathy are

• Drugs: Captopril, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs NSAIDs, penicillamine, etc.
• Infections: Hepatitis B and C, syphilis, malaria
• Malignancy of lung, colon, and melanoma
• Autoimmune diseases like SLE, Sjorgen syndrome, sarcoidosis, primary biliary cirrhosis, etc.

As in this case, there is a history of hepatitis B infection, the likely etiology is secondary membranous nephropathy. Hence, PLA2R autoantibodies are absent.

Patients present with symptoms of nephrotic syndrome, nonselective proteinuria, and microscopic hematuria.

Diagnosis:

• Light microscopy shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall without cellular proliferation. Irregular spikes and dome pattern on silver staining.
• Immunofluorescence microscopy shows granular deposits containing IgG and complement proteins along the glomerular basement membrane. IgG4 is the principal immunoglobulin deposited in most cases of primary membranous nephropathy.
• Electron micrograph: electron-dense subepithelial deposits (epimembranous spikes) and effacement of foot processes of podocytes

Management is primarily by the administration of immunosuppressive drugs such as steroids, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, and mycophenolate mofetil.

Image: The silver stain of the glomerulus highlights the proteinaceous basement membranes in black. There are characteristic "spikes" of the basement membrane between the immune deposits of membranous nephropathy. As the disease progresses, these spikes thicken to form dome-like protrusions. The black basement membrane material shown here appears as projections in the capillary loops.

Other options:

Option A: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (peaks between 2–6 years).

Biopsy findings in this condition are as follows:

• Light microscopy - glomeruli appear normal (hence called 'minimal change')
• Immunofluorescence studies - no Ig or complement deposits
• Electron microscopy - diffuse effacement of foot processes of visceral epithelial cells (podocytopathy)

Option C: FSGS is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults. It is a podocytopathy, with characteristic degeneration and focal disruption of visceral epithelial cells as well as effacement of foot processes. The electrophoretic pattern is more likely to yield a less prominent band in A, a more prominent band in C as there is a fall in the level of albumin with rising in the level of α2.

The histology of FSGS reveals focal and segmental hyalinosis and sclerosis of the capillary wall. Lipid droplets and foam cells are present in the sclerosed area.

Option D: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is characterized by the sudden onset of gross hematuria, edema, hypertension, and renal insufficiency. It usually occurs following a throat infection by nephritogenic strains of group A β-hemolytic streptococci.

Microscopic findings in PSGN:

• Light microscopy: Enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with diffuse mesangial and endothelial proliferation and leukocyte infiltration.
• Immunofluorescence: Granular deposits of IgG and complement C3 along the glomerular basement membrane(GBM)and in the mesangium.
• Electron microscopy: Electron-dense deposits, or humps, are observed on the epithelial side of the GBM.

questions.text: All of the following are true regarding Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase structure, except:
options: ATP binding site is located intracellularly
K⁺ binding site is on the extracellular side
Ouabain binds to the cytoplasmic domain
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ouabain binds to the cytoplasmic domain

The Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump is a membrane-bound enzyme that maintains the electrochemical gradients of sodium and potassium across the cell membrane.

• ATP binding site: located on the intracellular side.
• Phosphorylation site: also on the intracellular domain of the pump.
• K⁺ binding site: located on the extracellular side.
• Ouabain (cardiac glycoside) binding site: located on the extracellular surface of the pump.

Function:

• Pumps 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ into the cell using ATP hydrolysis.

Therefore, the incorrect statement is that ouabain binds to the cytoplasmic domain, because it actually binds to the extracellular side of the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient is found to have accumulation of glucocerebroside within cells. Dysfunction of which intracellular organelle is most likely responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lysosome

Glucocerebroside accumulation is the hallmark of Gaucher disease, a lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of β-glucocerebrosidase (β-glucosidase). Defective lysosomal degradation of glucocerebroside leads to its accumulation within macrophage lysosomes, forming characteristic Gaucher cells with wrinkled (“crumpled tissue paper”) cytoplasm.

Why not the other options?

• B. Peroxisome: Involved in β-oxidation of very long-chain fatty acids and α-oxidation of branched-chain fatty acids; disorders include Refsum disease, Zellweger syndrome, and X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.
• C. Golgi apparatus: Responsible for protein modification, glycosylation, and sorting; not involved in degradation of sphingolipids.
• D. Mitochondria: Site of ATP production, oxidative phosphorylation, and apoptosis; not involved in lysosomal substrate degradation.
questions.learning: Lysosome Glucocerebroside accumulation is the hallmark of Gaucher disease, a lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of β-glucocerebrosidase (β-glucosidase).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During first-trimester ultrasonography, which measurement is the most accurate parameter for determining gestational age?
questions.explanation: Accurate dating of pregnancy is fundamental to obstetric care. During the first trimester (specifically between 7 and 13 weeks), the Crown Rump Length (CRL) is universally recognized as the most reliable and accurate parameter for determining gestational age. The margin of error for CRL is remarkably low, typically within 3–5 days. Biparietal diameter (BPD, Option A) and head circumference (HC, Option B) become primary dating parameters during the second trimester (after 14 weeks), but they are less accurate than first-trimester CRL due to increased biological variability in fetal growth. Abdominal circumference (AC, Option D) is primarily used in the third trimester to estimate fetal weight and screen for growth restriction, rather than for initial dating. Once the CRL exceeds 84mm, dating is shifted to BPD. Therefore, CRL remains the gold standard for early pregnancy dating and establishing the "due date" for all subsequent monitoring

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The serum level of tetanus antitoxin that gives clinical protection is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. >0.01 IU/ml

The serum level of tetanus antitoxin that gives clinical protection is 0.01 IU/ml.

Tetanus is best prevented by tetanus toxoid. It provides active immunization by stimulating the production of protective antitoxin. Vaccination should be aimed at maintaining the serum protective level of antitoxin (approximately 0.01 IU/ml) throughout life and covering the entire community.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding embryological derivatives?
options: Stapes – 2nd Pharyngeal Pouch; External auditory meatus (EAM) – 1st Pharyngeal Pouch
Stapes – 3rd Pharyngeal Pouch; EAM – 2nd Pharyngeal Pouch
Stapes – 2nd Pharyngeal Arch; EAM – 1st Pharyngeal Cleft
Stapes – 2nd Pharyngeal Cleft; EAM – 2nd Pharyngeal Cleft
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stapes – 2nd Pharyngeal Arch; EAM – 1st Pharyngeal Cleft

• The stapes develops from the cartilage of the 2nd pharyngeal (hyoid) arch (Reichert cartilage).
• The external auditory meatus (external acoustic canal) develops from the 1st pharyngeal cleft (groove).
• The 1st pharyngeal pouch forms the middle ear cavity (tympanic cavity) and auditory (Eustachian) tube, not the EAM.
• The tympanic membrane is formed by the 1st cleft + 1st pouch + intervening mesoderm.
• The malleus and incus arise from the 1st pharyngeal arch (Meckel cartilage).
• The stapes is the only auditory ossicle derived predominantly from the 2nd arch.
• 2nd, 3rd, and 4th pharyngeal clefts are normally obliterated by the overgrowth of the 2nd arch.
• Persistence of these clefts can result in branchial cysts, sinuses, or fistulas.
• Pouches form internal structures, whereas clefts form external structures.

High-yield pearl:

• EAM = 1st cleft
• Middle ear & Eustachian tube = 1st pouch
• Stapes = 2nd arch

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A hypertensive patient comes to the OPD with complaints of visual disturbances. On fundoscopy, multiple flame-shaped hemorrhages , cotton wool spots, and disc edema were found. What is the grade of hypertensive retinopathy in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Grade IV

Cotton wool spots and flame shaped hemorrage with disc edema is seen in grade IV of hypertensive retinopathy.

Grading of hypertensive retinopathy:

* Grade 1: Mild generalized retinal arteriolar narrowing

* Grade 2: Focal arteriolar narrowing and arteriovenous nipping.

* Grade 3: Grade 2 plus retinal hemorrhages (dot, blot, flame) or exudates (chronic retinal edema may result in the deposition of hard exudates around the fovea as a ‘macular star’ and cotton wool spots; may also be associated with banking of veins distal to arteriovenous crossings (Bonnet sign), tapering of veins on either side of the crossings (Gunn sign); copper-wire appearance; more prominent arteriovenous compression.

* Grade 4: Severe grade 3 plus optic disc swelling (a marker of malignant hypertension) and silver-wiring of arterioles.

Copper T-380A (Paraguard): It is named so for the 380 mm2 of copper surface area. A higher surface area of copper results in higher contraceptive efficacy. Hence the Copper T-380A has been able to achieve superior contraception while maintaining a similar side-effect profile

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman who works as a laborer presents with a visible, soft, and fluctuant swelling located anterior to the knee over the patella, accompanied by discomfort and difficulty in knee movements. MRI findings are provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: "Housemaid's knee" is the clinical term for prepatellar bursitis, which is the inflammation of the fluid-filled bursa located directly in front of the patella. It is caused by repetitive trauma or prolonged pressure from kneeling, making it common in laborers. The characteristic presentation is a soft, fluctuating swelling over the kneecap that causes discomfort during movement. A subdermal abscess (Option B) would be tender, red, and warm with pus accumulation rather than just fluid. Gout (Option C) typically causes intense inflammation within the joint itself, presenting with severe pain and redness. Rheumatoid arthritis (Option D) is a systemic autoimmune disease affecting joints symmetrically with stiffness and deformity. MRI findings in bursitis show a clear fluid-filled space anterior to the bone. This condition is distinct from "clergyman's knee," which involves the infrapatellar bursa
questions.learning: "Housemaid's knee" is the clinical term for prepatellar bursitis, which is the inflammation of the fluid-filled bursa located directly in front of the patella.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Sequentially arrange the steps involved in excitation-contraction coupling of smooth muscle cells. 1. Myosin phosphorylation 2. Increased influx of Ca2+ into the cell 3. Activation of calmodulin-dependent myosin light chain kinase 4. Binding of myosin to actin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2-3-1-4

In smooth muscle excitation–contraction coupling, contraction is regulated by Ca²⁺-dependent phosphorylation of myosin rather than troponin (as in skeletal muscle).

Correct sequence:

1.      Increased influx of Ca²⁺ into the cell (via voltage-gated or receptor-operated channels).

2.      Ca²⁺ binds to calmodulin, activating calmodulin-dependent myosin light chain kinase (MLCK).

3.      MLCK phosphorylates myosin light chains.

4.      Phosphorylated myosin binds to actin, initiating cross-bridge cycling and contraction.
questions.learning: 2-3-1-4 In smooth muscle excitation–contraction coupling, contraction is regulated by Ca²⁺-dependent phosphorylation of myosin rather than troponin (as in skeletal muscle).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with abdominal pain and vomiting, along with a 2-day history of constipation and abdominal distension. On examination, the abdomen is distended with exaggerated, high-pitched bowel sounds, and an abdominal X-ray shows dilated loops of the small intestine. Based on these findings, what is the most likely cause of his condition?
questions.explanation: The patient's presentation of abdominal pain, vomiting, distension, and absolute constipation (obstipation) forms the classic quartet of symptoms for intestinal obstruction. The examination finding of high-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds further supports a mechanical blockage. The definitive diagnostic clue is the X-ray showing dilated loops of small bowel, which typically appear centrally located with valvulae conniventes that cross the entire width of the lumen. Colonic malignancy (Option A) would more likely cause large bowel obstruction, where the X-ray would show peripheral dilation and haustral markings. Acute pancreatitis (Option C) usually presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and elevated lipase, without specific dilated bowel loops unless a localized ileus (sentinel loop) is present. Gastric ulcers (Option D) typically cause dyspepsia or localized pain, not generalized distension and mechanical obstruction symptoms. Small bowel obstruction is a surgical emergency often caused by adhesions, hernias, or neoplasms, requiring prompt decompression and evaluation for strangulation
questions.learning: The patient's presentation of abdominal pain, vomiting, distension, and absolute constipation (obstipation) forms the classic quartet of symptoms for intestinal obstruction.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: After the age of 12, the boy had an intellectual disability. On examination, fingernail abrasions, excessive biting of lips, and increased levels of serum uric acid were observed. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lesch-Nyhan disease

The above clinical scenario with findings showing self-mutilation and laboratory values of hyperuricemia is most likely suggestive of Lesch-Nyhan disease.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder due to a complete deficiency of the hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). This deficiency results in an inability to salvage hypoxanthine or guanine leading to increased levels of phospho-ribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP). Increased PRPP leads to increased purine synthesis, which is later degraded to uric acid. Increased hypoxanthine is also converted to uric acid.

The patients have intellectual disability, behaviors of self-injury like lip and finger biting, developmental delay, muscle dystonia, and extrapyramidal symptoms.

Diagnosis is made by the elevated levels of uric acid and by HGPRT enzyme assay.

The image given below shows the metabolism of hypoxanthine and guanine by HGPRT.

Orange diaper syndrome can be an early indicator of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. At birth, individuals with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome typically appear asymptomatic, with normal prenatal growth and development. The condition is often first detected through the presence of orange-coloured crystals in the diaper, resulting from hyperuricemia. Since hyperuricemia is a common feature across all variants of HGPRT deficiency, which causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, predicting associated neurodevelopmental abnormalities requires enzyme activity testing.
questions.learning: Lesch-Nyhan disease — The above clinical scenario with findings showing self-mutilation and laboratory values of hyperuricemia is most likely suggestive of Lesch-Nyhan disease.

options: Superior & medial quadrant has more tissue
Axillary tail of Spence crosses anterior axillary fold
Nipple is located at 4th intercostal space in most of the females
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Axillary tail of Spence crosses anterior axillary fold

The correct answer is Axillary tail of Spence crosses the anterior axillary fold.

The axillary tail is a superolateral extension of breast tissue that passes into the axilla across the anterior axillary fold, making it clinically important in breast examination and surgery. The axillary tail is an extension of upper outer quadrant, it passes through the foramen of Langer, enters the axilla and lies along the lateral border of pectoralis major.

The superolateral quadrant (not superomedial) has maximum breast tissue, breasts have 15–20 lobules, and the nipple is usually at the 4th intercostal space in males, not consistently in females.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text:
An 18-month-old child with a 3-day history of watery diarrhea and vomiting presented with altered sensorium. Which of the following are differential diagnoses?

1. Severe dehydration
2. HUS
3. Cerebral Venous Thrombosis
4. Hyponatremia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3, 4

The differential diagnoses in a child with a history of watery diarrhea and altered sensorium include severe dehydration, cerebral venous thrombosis, and hyponatremia.

The lack of dysentery(bloody diarrhoea) and the short period of interval between diarrhoeal episodes and the symptom complex, help to rule out Haemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS). HUS is a form of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia usually occurring in children less than 5 years of age. There are 2 forms of HUS:

1. Typical HUS which is usually followed by a gastrointestinal infection most commonly by E.coli. The infection in turn affects the gastric mucosa and alters the endothelial cells which promotes platelet activation and aggravation.
2. Atypical HUS which occurs due to deficiency in certain proteins like complement factor H, factor I, or CD46.

Clinical features of the condition include bloody diarrhea which occurs 5-10 days before the onset of hemolytic uremic syndrome, abdominal pain, fatigue, cramping, and vomiting. The most dangerous complication is renal failure requiring dialysis or renal transplantation. Treatment is mainly supportive and the nature of the illness is usually self-limiting.

Differential diagnoses in a child presenting with altered sensorium/ seizures with diarrhea:

• Hypo- or hypernatremia
• Hypoglycemia
• Encephalitis or meningitis
• Febrile seizures
• Cerebral or saggital sinus thrombosis
questions.learning: 1, 3, 4 The differential diagnoses in a child with a history of watery diarrhea and altered sensorium include severe dehydration, cerebral venous thrombosis, and hyponatremia.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 40-year-old male with a known HIV infection presents with cough and fever lasting for 3 months. Patient is diagnosed with a case of miliary tuberculosis. What is the next best step?
options: Start ATT now and start ART later and increase the dolutegravir dose
Start ART now, start ATT two weeks later and increase the dolutegravir
Start ATT now along with corticosteroids, start and increase the dolutegravir
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Start ATT now and start ART later and increase the dolutegravir dose

In HIV patients with active tuberculosis, anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) should be initiated first, followed by antiretroviral therapy (ART) after a short delay.

• Start ATT immediately in all cases of active TB
• ART is started after 2 weeks (early initiation reduces mortality but avoids severe immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, IRIS)
• Rifampicin induces hepatic enzymes → reduces levels of dolutegravir
• Therefore, dolutegravir dose must be increased when co-administered with rifampicin

Additional notes:

• Simultaneous initiation of ATT and ART increases risk of IRIS
• Steroids are reserved for specific indications (e.g., TB meningitis, pericarditis), not routine miliary TB

Thus, ATT is started first, ART is added after 2 weeks, and dolutegravir dose is increased due to rifampicin interaction.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic patient is diagnosed with gouty arthritis. What biochemical changes will be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased urate and lactate levels

This patient with chronic alcoholism and gouty arthritis will most likely have elevated levels of lactate and urate.

The oxidation of ethanol to acetate by alcohol dehydrogenase is accompanied by the reduction of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) to NADH. This results in a high concentration of NADH, leading to an increased NADH/NAD+ ratio (Option A).

Due to this, the following metabolic reactions that require NAD+ are inhibited:

1. Glycolysis
2. Citric acid cycle (ketogenesis favored)
3. Pyruvate dehydrogenase
4. Fatty acid oxidation

Decreased fatty acid oxidation leads to increased esterification and production of triacylglycerol, which causes fatty liver.

Also, there is an increase in two reactions:

• Pyruvate to lactate
• Oxaloacetate to malate

Increased lactate leads to hyper-lactic-acidemia, which leads to increased renal reabsorption of urate and decreased excretion of uric acid. This results in aggravation of gout. Alcoholics are deficient in thiamine which inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase and leads to lactic acidosis.

A decrease in pyruvate and oxaloacetate levels, which are substrates for gluconeogenesis, leads to a decrease in blood glucose levels, causing symptoms of agitation, impaired judgment, and combativeness.

Other options:

Increased urea and urate levels are not specifically associated with alcoholism and gouty arthritis. While urate levels may be increased due to gout, urea levels are not directly related to the condition (Option B).

Increased levels of alkaline phosphatase can be seen in alcohol-induced hepatitis due to intrahepatic cholestasis but is not directly related to gouty arthritis in a chronic alcoholic patient. Therefore, this option is less relevant compared to increased urate and lactate levels (Option D).
questions.learning: Increased urate and lactate levels — This patient with chronic alcoholism and gouty arthritis will most likely have elevated levels of lactate and urate.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient has come with sudden onset of chest pain and his CT scan shows the following picture. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aortic dissection

The given CT scan showing a double lumen and dilatation of the aorta is suggestive of an aortic dissection.

In this condition, blood enters the space below the intima of the aorta. This results in the formation of a true lumen and false lumen. The true lumen is often the smaller of the two because of being compressed by the false lumen, as shown below.

The beak sign in aortic dissection is a reliable sign to identify the false lumen. It refers to the acute angle formed at the edge of the false lumen in aortic dissection in axial cross-section. It is formed by the borders of the outer aortic wall and the intimal flap, and maybe partially thrombosed (blunted beak).
questions.learning: Aortic dissection — The given CT scan showing a double lumen and dilatation of the aorta is suggestive of an aortic dissection. In this condition, blood enters the space below the intima of the aorta.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with tachycardia, hypertension, tongue fasciculations, excessive salivation, dilated pupils, and mild redness at the bite site. The child reports that the biting animal had an upward-curved tail. Which animal is most likely responsible for this bite?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation—tachycardia, hypertension, tongue fasciculation, and hypersalivation—represents the "autonomic storm" characteristic of Scorpion envenomation. Scorpion venom contains neurotoxins that trigger a massive release of catecholamines (sympathetic) and acetylcholine (parasympathetic). The report of an animal with a "curved tail pointing upwards" is pathognomonic for a scorpion. Dilated pupils further indicate sympathetic overactivity. Sea urchins (Option A) cause localized pain and puncture wounds. Caterpillars (Option B) typically cause dermatitis or localized stings. Shellfish poisoning (Option D) usually presents with gastrointestinal symptoms or paralytic neurotoxicity but lacks the upward-pointing tail and the intense autonomic storm. In India, the Red Scorpion (Mesobuthus tamulus) is notoriously dangerous for children, often leading to pulmonary edema if not treated with Prazosin. Therefore, both the specific physical description and the systemic neuro-autonomic symptoms point definitively to a scorpion sting
questions.learning: The clinical presentation—tachycardia, hypertension, tongue fasciculation, and hypersalivation—represents the "autonomic storm" characteristic of Scorpion envenomation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The following is the bone marrow biopsy of a 60-year-old man with easy fatiguability, back pain, and multiple lytic lesions in the skull. Likely diagnosis is______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Multiple myeloma

The clinical history along with the biopsy picture showing Russell bodies is suggestive of multiple myeloma.

Russell bodies are eosinophilic, large, homogeneous immunoglobulin-containing inclusions usually found in a plasma cell undergoing excessive synthesis of immunoglobulins. It is characteristic of the distended endoplasmic reticulum in multiple myeloma.

Clinical features

* Bone pain is the most common symptom

* Renal failure -Acute oliguric or non-oliguric kidney failure may be present due to hypercalcemia, hyperuricemia, light-chain cast injury, or primary amyloidosis

* Pallor and soft tissue masses

* Fever occurs with infection

* Patients may have neurologic signs related to neuropathy or spinal cord compression

* Hyperviscosity syndrome (mucosal bleeding, vertigo, nausea, visual disturbances, alterations in mental status, hypoxia)

Bone marrow biopsy shows round or oval cells with an eccentric nucleus composed of coarsely clumped chromatin, a densely basophilic cytoplasm, and a perinuclear clear zone containing the Golgi apparatus.

Pearl PF0569: Some Pathological Cells/Bodies in Multiple Myeloma

Description

Russell bodies

They are globular intracellular accumulations of immunoglobulins (Ig).

Plasma cells filled with multiple Russell bodies are called Mott cells.

Dutcher bodies

PAS-positive intranuclear inclusions containing Ig seen in some of the plasma cells are called Dutcher bodies.

Flame cells

Plasma cells with fiery red cytoplasm are called flame cells.

PAS: Periodic acid Schiff

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Seizures are seen in what percentage of RTA patients with brain contusion/loss of consciousness?
options: No relation between trauma and seizures.
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic seizures (PTS) are a well-recognized complication of Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI). For patients who have sustained significant head trauma in a road traffic accident, characterized by brain contusion or a prolonged loss of consciousness, the incidence of developing seizures is approximately 17%. These are classified as "early" if they occur within the first week and "late" if they occur after seven days. Options B and C (45% and 75%) significantly overestimate the clinical risk for most contusion cases. Statement D is incorrect as the relationship between brain trauma and epilepsy is well-established. Because of this risk, prophylactic anticonvulsants like Levetiracetam or Phenytoin are often administered for the first 7 days following severe TBI to prevent early PTS, which can worsen secondary brain injury. Accurate knowledge of these statistics helps clinicians counsel families and plan appropriate neurological follow-up

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old male with a known history of diabetes came with a wound on his foot. Identify the given condition.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Trophic ulcer

The given picture showing an ulcer with punched-out edges over a pressure point is most likely that of a trophic ulcer/neuropathic ulcer.

A neuropathic ulcer is one that occurs as a result of peripheral neuropathy. In peripheral neuropathy, lack of sensation over the pressure points leads to cumulative microtrauma, minor wounds, or cuts that remain unnoticed but eventually develop into ulcers.

Features of a neuropathic ulcer include

* Painless ulcer

* Punched out ulcer with regular margins

* Often located on the plantar surface of the foot

* Ulcer margins show the presence of calluses

Underlying condition

Peripheral vascular disease- mainly atherosclerosis, thromboangiitis obliterans, cervical rib, Raynaud's phenomenon

Location
Toes, feet, legs, or even upper limb digits
Lower limb, commonly on the medial side of the ankle, never above the middle third of the leg
The plantar surface of the foot, toes
Neck, axilla, and groin

Characteristics

Deep, penetrates the deep fascia exposing the tendons, muscles, and underlying bone.

The ulcer is painful, tender, and hyperaesthetic.

Vertically oval, and painless, the floor may have pale to no granulation tissue, induration, and tenderness at the base.
Punched-out with regular calloused margins.

Edges are thin, reddish blue, undermined; pale granulation tissue, scanty discharge on the floor, and slight induration at the base

Other features
Features of ischemia in adjacent areas, like pallor, dry skin, brittle nails, loss of hair
Inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged, usually, the vertical group and the ulcer is recurrent; forms again after healing
Dry, cracked, insensate

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Serum glucose is normal, but CSF glucose is very low. The defect is most likely due to deficiency of which glucose transporter?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. GLUT 1

GLUT1 deficiency syndrome is caused by mutations in the SLC2A1 gene, resulting in defective GLUT1-mediated transport of glucose across the blood-brain barrier (BBB). As a result, serum glucose remains normal, but CSF glucose is markedly reduced (hypoglycorrhachia) because glucose cannot adequately enter the central nervous system. The disorder typically presents in infancy with seizures, developmental delay, acquired microcephaly, movement disorders, and intellectual disability.

Why not the other options?

• B. GLUT2: Found in the liver, pancreatic β-cells, kidneys, and intestine; functions in glucose sensing and bidirectional glucose transport. It is not responsible for glucose transport across the BBB.
• C. GLUT4: An insulin-dependent transporter present in skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and adipose tissue. It has no role in CSF glucose transport.
• D. GLUT5: Primarily transports fructose, not glucose, and is found mainly in the small intestine and sperm.
